News.title: I had a vasectomy in my 20s after the trauma of my sons' births
News.content:
Because he was asking for a vasectomy at such a young age, Sam had prepared for the questions his doctor was going to ask him: Don't you think you're too young to know you don't want kids? Could you change your mind in future? You do know reversals are expensive and aren't always successful?

"[The doctor] actually said he had very recently changed his view," says Sam. "And that, if I had come in half a year earlier, he would have turned me away instantly."

His vasectomy took place a couple of months after he first contacted the clinic.

The questions from Sam's doctor were designed to ensure he was making a decision he could live with; men under 30 are more likely to regret a vasectomy, according to guidance from NHS Scotland, external.

Dr Sarah Salkeld, a former GP who is now a medical director for MSI Reproductive Choices, a group of clinics offering various contraceptives to NHS and private patients, says a vasectomy is "very safe and effective".

But she cautions it is important for men to "really think about" whether a vasectomy is right for them.

"We offer everyone counselling to talk about it if they want to, just toâ¦ make sure they've got all the information they need to make that decision."

She says reversals are not routinely available on the NHS as there are strict criteria for having one.

The NHS website points out that other forms of contraception, external are available to men, including condoms and the fertility awareness method - avoiding sex or using condoms on the days when their female partner is most fertile.

Sam told his doctor that, while he loved kids and had a happy childhood himself, he wanted to stay focused on his job as a sound designer for video games.

News.title: Solitude as a new aspirational lifestyle: 'We are not lonely'
News.content:
It's a Friday night. A young woman trudges back to her apartment after a day of work. She enters a spotless kitchen, unloads a bag of groceries, and unwraps a frozen pizza before sliding it in the oven.

What follows is a nightly routine that is almost meditative in its mundanity: she lights a candle and gazes briefly at the snow-covered landscape outside her window, piles a premade salad onto a plate with the pizza, and settles on her sofa to eat in front of the TV.

The tagline that accompanies the scene reads: "POV you're a childfree and single girl that has no friends and lives alone so this is how you spend your Friday night."

At the centre of the video â which has amassed seven million views on TikTok â is Lana Isa, a software sales manager in her 20s based in Toronto.

In addition to chronicling her nightly self-care routines, she takes her almost 400,000 followers across TikTok and Instagram on late-night fast food drives, reading sessions perched on a rock by the lake, even a saga of getting locked out of her apartment in the middle of the night.

Isa is part of a growing, albeit niche corner of the internet where content creators, many of them women, share their daily rituals of living alone, choosing to spotlight a lifestyle that prioritises peace and solitude - the antithesis of social media excess.

For Isa, unveiling the "no friends" aspect of her life was less of a tagline, but the "reality" she had been living for several years.

News.title: Spider-Man fans hail Brand New Day as Holland's best yet
News.content:
Fans have been queuing outside cinemas to catch the latest Spider-Man film, with many hailing it as a spectacular return for the web-slinging superhero.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day marks Tom Holland's fourth standalone adventure as the protagonist and hero Peter Parker.

Picking up after the events of Spider-Man: No Way Home, the film follows Parker as he devotes his time to protecting New York City while adjusting to a life in which everyone, including his closest friends, has forgotten who he is.

The fourth Spider-Man film is director Destin Daniel Cretton's second project in the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU), having previously been at the helm of Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings.

Appearing together in the same film for a second time this summer, Holland reprises the role alongside his wife Zendaya, who stars once again as MJ.

There is also a return for Jon Bernthal's Punisher, making his first appearance in an MCU feature film, and an introduction to the MCU for Sadie Sink, whose role in the plot has been kept firmly under wraps.

News.title: Ginger hair portraits show unexpected 'golden thread' connecting Americans
News.content:
For Kieran Dodds, photographing people with red hair has become something of an obsession over the past decade.

The 45-year-old, from Edinburgh, who is himself a "proud ginger", began taking pictures in his homeland in 2013 as part of a series examining Scottish identity.

His interest in the subject soon took him to other ginger hotspots such the Russian city of Perm and Jamaica's Treasure Beach.

His 2020 book Gingers spanned the world but after its release he notice there was a "huge gap".

"I realised I didn't have any American citizens," Kieran told the BBC.

"Then all these people got in touch."

News.title: William and Kate bring children to second last day of Commonwealth Games
News.content:
The Prince and Princess of Wales have brought their three children to watch some of the final sporting events at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

Cheering crowds at the city's OVO Hydro were treated to exhilarating performances in the netball semi-finals where the family watched New Zealand's 61-54 win over England.

Known as the Duke and Duchess of Rothesay while in Scotland, the couple also spent time meeting athletes, staff and volunteers during a slightly blustery visit to the venue on the River Clyde.

They then made their way to the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome - where they chatted to British cyclist Dame Laura Kenny and sat one row behind another Olympic cycling champion, Sir Chris.

News.title: Mountaineer Nirmal Purja killed in Pakistan avalanche, his company says
News.content:
Purja's death was also confirmed by Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah, who said that "the tragic death of six Nepalese and four other foreign climbers, including world record holder Nirmal Purja, in the Karakoram mountain range of Pakistan, has shocked us".

"The history of their courage, dedication, and contributions will always remain inspiring," the prime minister added.

In a statement, Purja's older brother Kamal wrote: "It is with the heaviest heart that I share the devastating news that my beloved younger brother, Nirmal 'Nimsdai' Purja, and the other climbers are no longer with us.

"Although our hearts are broken, we are incredibly proud of you. Your legacy will live forever," he added.

UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said in a post on X: "Incredibly sad to learn of the passing of Nirmal (Nims) Purja and those he was climbing with.

"He was an inspirational man who served in our Armed Forces for many years - and whose incredible mountaineering adventures are known the world over."

Naila Kiani, a spokesperson for the Alpine Club of Pakistan which is involved in the rescue efforts, told BBC's Newshour programme that Purja had led many expeditions that she was on.

Praising his leadership skills, she described him as a "very experienced climber and fearless".

Kiani said the Alpine Club would only announce his death once the body has been recovered - but she added that "we are fearing them all dead".

She also said rescuers had seen some bodies - but were yet to reach them.

Teams in Pakistan have been searching for the climbers on the world's 12th-highest summit after an avalanche on the 8,047m (26,400ft) peak in the Karakoram range.

Pakistani officials earlier said the bodies of three climbers from his expedition - American Mallory Geis, Nadhira Ahmed Abdullah Al Harthy from Oman and Pur Bahadur Gurung from Nepal - had been recovered.

The multinational climbing group was being led by Purja. Also known as Nims, he rose to prominence in 2019 when he climbed all 14 of the world's mountains with peaks above 8,000m in 189 days - smashing the previous record by more than seven years.

He became widely known following a Netflix documentary chronicling his journey, 14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible, released two years later.

At the time, he said: "It has been a gruelling but humbling six months, and I hope to have proven that anything is possible with some determination, self-belief and positivity."

Purja served in the British military for 16 years, 10 of which were spent in the special forces, and he was awarded an MBE by the late Queen in 2018 for his achievement in extreme high-altitude mountaineering.

Purja, who lived with his wife and three-year-old daughter in Hampshire in southern England, said he was also the first Gurkha to climb Everest while serving in the British military.

In his last post on X, published on Monday, he said he had not intended to climb Broad Peak.

"Initially, the plan was to climb just G2," Purja wrote, referring to Gasherbrum II, another peak in the Karakoram mountain range.

But right before he set off for Pakistan, he realised that if he also managed to climb Broad Peak while he was there, he would have only one more mountain to conquer before becoming the "first person in history to climb all 14 eight-thousanders twice. Without oxygen."

An eight-thousander is a mountain that rises more than 8,000m above sea level.

"This wasn't planned," Purja wrote. "But opportunities don't scream: they whisper to those already working in silence."

"Broad Peak, I ask for nothing but safe passage up and back down. I take zero mountains for granted," he wrote.

Broad Peak is regarded as one of the more challenging mountains for climbers. The first successful ascent was in 1957, when an Austrian expedition reached the summit.

Since then, many more have climbed the mountain, but dozens have lost their lives.

One of Broad Peak's deadliest years was 2013, when at least six fatalities were recorded.

News.title: Peak District's rebrand deal brings in cash - but also criticism
News.content:
A deal between Peak District bosses and car firm Skoda to put up temporary signs welcoming tourists to "the Peaq District" in honour of the firm's new electric model has given the park authority's coffers a welcome boost.

However, it has also sparked protests from campaigners and residents unhappy about the commercial aspect of the arrangement.

One campaigner said: "If national parks are prepared to sell their very name to the highest bidder, then we're already on the path to industrial extraction of the most protected landscapes."

Park bosses have defended the "fantastic" deal and said the partnership brought in extra funds for conservation and heritage work.

With national parks continuing to grapple with funding pressures, could the partnership be a sign of things to come for the Peak District and beyond?

News.title: Cambridge professor at centre of plagiarism row defends his work
News.content:
A Cambridge University professor has defended his academic work after finding himself at the centre of a plagiarism row.

The row erupted after another academic - self-defined "race realist" Nathan Cofnas, who was sacked from his Cambridge role in 2024 - said he found numerous instances of plagiarism in Prof Jason Arday's work and questioned some of his stated achievements.

While some critics say the treatment of Arday, who is black, has been motivated by racism, others have said the claims of plagiarism were legitimate.

Arday admitted errors in his work, telling the Times, external in an interview on Saturday that he was accountable for those mistakes but that "what I am not is a liar".

He told the newspaper: "There has been, since I arrived at Cambridge, a very well orchestrated and co-ordinated campaign to unseat me from my position."

He argued this was "racially motivated" and that he had become a "lightning rod" for criticism of diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) policy.

Arday said some errors in his early academic work was because of his autism, as he relied on using mimicry to make sense of information, and that similar scrutiny would find similar errors in work by other academics.

"We're talking about academia here. I didn't murder somebody. I think the cruelty that I've experienced and the positioning of me as this kind of liar and fantasist is totally unacceptable," he told the newspaper.

In 2023, the then 37-year-old sociologist became the youngest ever black professor at Cambridge, telling the BBC at the time his work focused on neurodivergence and race in education.

He was diagnosed with autism and global development delay in his early years, to which his being unable to speak until the age of 11 and unable to read or write until 18 was attributed.

Arday worked as a PE teacher before earning his doctorate at Liverpool John Moores University and going on to teach at Roehampton, Durham and Glasgow.

News.title: Suffolk fire 'stable' and fundraiser set up
News.content:
The blaze that has devastated heathland in Suffolk is now "stable" but crews have continued to tackle hotspots on what is the fourth day since the flames took hold.

The fire affecting RSPB Minsmere and Dunwich Heath started at about 17:00 BST on Wednesday and engulfed 371 acres (150 hectares) at its height - equivalent to the size of 210 football pitches.

Wildlife habitats of some of the UK's rarest species have been destroyed.

The National Trust has launched a fundraiser to help the habitats "recover and thrive in a changing climate".

Meanwhile, some local people have started returning to normal life.

A scheduled market went ahead at nearby Westleton earlier, which an organiser said was the chance for people to take their minds off recent events.

News.title: Son of Wicker Man maker dies just weeks before his sequel to film premieres
News.content:
British filmmaker Justin Hardy, who directed a sequel to his late father Robin's 1973 cult horror classic The Wicker Man, has died aged 61.

His family said Hardy died on Friday night after suffering a heart attack, remembering him as "a man of family, of boundless creativity" and "so full of life right to the end".

A Bafta and Emmy nominated writer and director, Hardy was known for the documentary Children of the Wicker Man in 2024, made with his brother Dominic, which chronicled the legacy of their father's iconic film.

He had just completed production on Wrath of the Gods, the concluding chapter to the Wicker Man trilogy, which was due to premiere in London later this month.

Hardy also directed historical films and documentaries for the BBC, Channel 4 and CNN, including Princes In The Tower, Trafalgar Battle Surgeon, The Relief Of Belsen and Spanish Flu: The Forgotten Fallen.

His family said they were "devastated" by his death and "heartbroken" Hardy would not be able to see Wrath of the Gods open.

Dominic described his brother as having "an incredible appetite for life".

"We've lost him and we've lost that larger-than-life presence looking over us all," he said. "He really became a filmmaker his own right."

Dominic also praised Hardy's work on his last film as "incredibly beautiful", adding it was "a great satisfaction to him" to have made something new.

The Wicker Man, starring Christopher Lee, is the story of a police officer sent to a remote Scottish island community to investigate the disappearance of a local girl.

Wrath of the Gods was inspired by recently discovered scripts and storyboards by Hardy's late father Robin, marking the end of the trilogy that began with The Wicker Man and the 2011 follow-up The Wicker Tree.

Hardy, who also taught screenwriting at University College London, is survived by his wife Larissa, and their four children.

News.title: Manhunt after prisoner escapes from van outside court
News.content:
A manhunt is under way after a prisoner escaped from a van taking him to a court appearance.

Stephen Grzyb, 22, was being transported by contractor GEOAmey from Belle Vale custody suite to Liverpool Magistrates' Court to face burglary charges on Saturday.

As the van arrived outside the court building, at around 10:00 BST, Grzyb was able to flee and ran off down Red Cross Street towards the Strand.

Merseyside Police said: "Assisting him in any way will bring police to your own door, so it is not an association worth keeping."

News.title: Boaters race against clock as drained canals close
News.content:
Boaters are racing against the clock to beat canal closures as waterways run dry due to extreme heat.

Some channels connecting large parts of the Midlands and the North of England have lost several inches of water, leaving narrowboats stuck and those already on the canals facing being stranded miles from home for weeks on end.

Campaigner George Seward said he was getting up at 05:00 BST and cruising until dark to get his narrowboat through the Atherstone flight of locks, after a sudden closure was announced.

"They're unlikely to be open again for many weeks and I want to make sure I get through that flight so I can get my boat safely home," he said.

The locks on the Coventry Canal in Warwickshire are due to shut on Tuesday morning, with last entry on Monday afternoon, as the Canal and River Trust (CRT) tries to conserve dwindling supplies.

For Seward, who is Midlands regional chair of the Association of Waterways Cruising Clubs, the deadline is the difference between getting his boat home to Hinckley in Leicestershire and being potentially marooned for an unspecified period.

News.title: ‘They drive me nuts’: How Brits forgot the art of being a good neighbour
News.content:

Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. When I moved house this spring, I was immediately charmed by the community of my new road. We had not one but two WhatsApp groups – one for chatting, one for emergencies – in which people let each other know they’d taken in their parcels, shared local events like craft workshops, and in one instance even offered to donate blood to one neighbour’s family friend, who was in desperate need of a transfusion. It was, it seemed, the best of humanity, until helpfulness gave way to hatred; residents started to bicker about parking, made noise complaints, and even dubbed one disliked man a terrorist.

As Jean-Paul Sartre famously declared in his 1944 play No Exit: Hell is other people – and living alongside those you haven’t picked can prove a test for the body and the mind. In Olivia Wilde’s film The Invite, which hit cinemas this month, the director stars as one half of a San Francisco couple on the brink of a breakup, who invite their free-spirited neighbours (Penélope Cruz and Edward Norton) over for dinner. As Wilde buys flowers and makes soufflé, her husband (Seth Rogen) complains bitterly about the intrusion: He hates this couple who have loud sex and make strange small talk in the lift.

Although half of Britons said in a Nextdoor survey that they’d turned to their neighbours for help in the past year, one in 10 people happily admitted to researchers for GoCompare that they don’t actually like their fellow residents, with those in the South East most likely to have a problem with next door. In The Invite the two couples’ feud plays out for comedic effect: the gift of a homemade flan, followed by an attempt at swinging. In real life, cross-resident resolution is rarely so candied and curious.

“I extremely and aggressively hate my neighbours,” says 29-year-old Paige*, who lives in a house with her friends in south London. The feud began when a woman next door asked them not to turn their outdoor lights on past 8pm, because the light shone into her daughter’s room, who hadn’t managed to pick out curtains that she liked. “We told her that lights are meant to go on at night and that obviously didn’t go down well,” says Paige. Weeks later, the woman started construction on a conservatory that launched each day at 7.45am and coated their garden in inches of brick dust. “Our entire house, all of our garden furniture, all of our windows, are filthy,” says Paige. “We f*****g hate her for it.”

open image in gallery ‘The Invite’ tells the story of neighbours gone all wrong ( Film Nation )

In Edinburgh, 32-year-old Daisy* also “f*****g hates” her neighbours. “One woman in the bottom flat thinks she owns the entire shared garden and believes she should be feeding pigeons, seagulls and rats to encourage diversity in the garden,” she laments. “It makes the space completely unusual and she’s unable to be reasoned with because apparently it’s a detriment to the wildlife… She says dogs aren’t welcome despite the garden being shared by 12 flats. She calls herself the “designated garden lead”, but she’s not. It’s the most mundane drama ever, but it drives me nuts.”

These types of neighbour feuds are maddening and, often, hilarious to spectate. After Paige’s neighbour’s children mistakenly threw their basketball over her fence, she was so filled with rage that she wanted to stab it with a kitchen knife. “My housemates told me I wasn’t allowed,” she mourns.

One woman in the bottom flat believes she should be feeding pigeons, seagulls and rats to encourage diversity in the garden Daisy*, 32

Other instances have markedly less comedic value. Although grown up and in her own house now, 30-year-old Joy’s* neighbour from her childhood home in Surrey has haunted her family for decades. Mean-spirited and rude, he yelled at Joy as a child for having three friends over on New Year’s Eve and, more recently, made her family’s dog sitter cry because the fire alarm was triggered during an electrical storm while she was out. “That’s a brief overview,” she says. “Relations have been frosty. Basically he’s a bully, and he’d never speak to my dad or brother like that – only children and women.”

open image in gallery Recurring theme: Rogen also starred in the 2014 comedy ‘Bad Neighbours’ in which he moves next door to a rowdy fraternity ( Universal Pictures )

Even more alarmingly, recent university graduate Lucy* was hounded out of her new apartment in Warwickshire after the man next door started to film, harass and verbally abuse her. “He knocked on the door and told me that he’s having a mental health crisis and he’s got heart issues,” she says. “So, I offered him a cup of tea and told him to come in. I had to tell him to leave after two hours of being hospitable – he just wasn’t taking the hint.”

What ensued was nothing short of a horror film. The neighbour would listen at the front door until the early hours to try and hear if Lucy and her partner were having sex, then open their letter box to make sure. He’d pretend he’d locked himself out of his flat just to interact, blast music night and day, and call the couple various racial slurs and mime stabbing them, until he was evicted and continued to harass them online. “It hasn’t made me scared to interact with my neighbours,” says Lucy, who came close to being placed under witness protection. “But I wish the landlord had warned us.”

We told her that lights are meant to go on at night and that obviously didn’t go down well Paige*, 29

We are living on top of each other more than ever before. Over half of all homes in London are flats or apartments, according to the 2024 housing stock, and more than 50 per cent of homes built since 2002 are highrise flats. Go Compare found that being quiet and peaceful were the most important traits of being a good neighbour (with being friendly and chatty coming in second), but it can be increasingly difficult to embody quiet and peace in an environment that isn’t so.

Joe Painter, a human geography professor at Durham University, notes that neighbour relations can become particularly fraught, as it’s the only area of our lives – aside from family – where we can’t choose those closest to us. “At work, you can choose your company, you clock off and go home,” he says. With neighbours, whether you like it or not, they’re there when you go to sleep and wake up.

open image in gallery The women of Wisteria Lane had complicated relationships with their fellow residents on ‘Desperate Housewives’ ( ABC )

In 2023, research by King’s College London found the UK to be among the most trusting countries when it comes to neighbours, behind only Egypt, Sweden, and Norway. But that can feel hard to believe in 2026 when Facebook community groups, the road group chat – or neighbourhood apps like Nextdoor – are popping off over a missing parcel, or a misplaced recycling bin.

”They are forms of social media,” Painter concludes. “Like Twitter and Instagram, it allows people to hide behind the screen – except you know them,” he says. “So, you can certainly see why it exacerbates conflict.”

Painter posited in a paper published in 2012 that we should pay more attention to the figure of the neighbour, rather than focusing on neighbourhoods, or geographical units, for a better understanding of ethics, citizenship, and urban politics. “It brings a challenge, to live alongside people who you might not have anything in common with, or might not even like,” he says. “But I do think that’s probably a good thing for society, to address that in our personal lives, as well as our national political life.”

Unlike in families, which have their own hierarchies, rituals and traditions, there’s no system, standard or clear expectation of how to be a so-called good neighbour in modern urban societies. “It’s all about feeling our way,” says Painter, who notes we tend to stereotype our neighbours as being wonderful or the absolute opposite. “It’s always ‘a very close knit community’ or ‘neighbours from hell’,” he says. “Most of the time, it’s neither of those things. But we do become a little bit wary of our neighbours until we interact more, because there's that unknowingness and no clear codes for how to deal with people.”

The closest codes we have for strangers living among each other are reality television. Painter points to the first season of Big Brother (before it became “clickbait”) and the show that launched Ben Fogle’s career, Castaway, as useful examples that allow us to observe how we relate to one another in a confined environment. “You can imagine the research that could be done to try out different forms of neighbourhood living, neighbourliness, and different forms of neighbourhood interaction, to see what actually works,” he says. “Those social experiments would be quite interesting.”

Despite the spats, the rows and, in some cases, verbal abuse and violence (last year, a “much-loved” 74-year-old neighbour was killed by another resident in a row over shutting a gate), Painter makes clear that government policy interventions – beyond funding for local community projects – are unwise as a way to regulate interactions. “If we do that, we’ll end up in a bad place,” he says. “In the end, what it comes down to is the need for us to, somehow, work it out together – as neighbours.”

News.title: First Eurovision, now Strictly: Delta Goodrem is in her year of saying yes
News.content:

Look closely, and you’ll see we’re in the middle of a Delta Goodrem summer. The Aussie musician, who soared to fame in the early 2000s as the angel-faced, angel-voiced teenager behind such ballads as “Born To Try”, is seemingly everywhere right now: on stage, on tour, on telly.

In May, Goodrem, 41, made her Eurovision debut in style – propelled into the air on a platform that rose out from a golden piano, mid-key change. She has only just finished a set of live UK shows, a prelude to the world tour she will embark on next year in support of her forthcoming eighth album Pure. In a couple of weeks, Goodrem will touch down in London once again to begin rehearsals ahead of her stint on Strictly Come Dancing – though not before she closes out the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow tonight. “I feel it’s one of those years of saying yes to everything. I want to be adventurous. I’m ready for that in my life,” she says now, over video call from Sydney.

Back in Australia, where I grew up, the singer remains a national treasure. To some, particularly those who came of age in the early Noughties, Goodrem is as iconic as Vegemite or the Sydney Opera House, a venue she has played no fewer than five times, the most recent being last year when she sold out two anniversary shows of her 2005 album Mistaken Identity. Goodrem has been less of a constant presence over here, and this second shot at cracking the UK feels only right, given her first was cut short by tragedy.

It was in the same week that her debut album shot to No 2 in the UK charts that she was diagnosed with Hodgkin’s lymphoma, forcing her off the promotion circuit and into a hospital bed, and effectively slamming the brakes on a music career that had quite literally just got going. It was 2004 and Goodrem was just 18. The experience was surreal to say the least. “I tried the best I could with the duality of what was happening,” says Goodrem. “Cancer doesn’t discriminate based on what job you’re doing. It says, ‘You have to look after this now.’”

The country rallied around her; by then, she was already known to millions as Nina, the sweet, shy high schooler on Neighbours. Newspapers filled with messages from readers sending their love; Sony, her label at the time, set up a “Get Well Delta” postbox to get a handle on the massive influx of letters from fans. Australia’s prime minister sent his regards. As did Elton John “on behalf of the United Kingdom”.

“The entire press world was sitting outside my door,” recalls Goodrem. “My brother would hand out biscuits to them, that’s one of my strong memories. Our house was like a train station!” Today, the idea of reporters camped outside the home of a teenage star screams invasion of privacy – but that’s not how Goodrem remembers it. “I’m pretty neutral about it,” she says after giving the question a good deal of thought. “There are so many stories in my life that I have to go into the filing cabinet of my mind… but I mean, it was all well wishes coming from them. And I think, as an 18-year-old back then, I was just focused on being with my friends and family.” Outside her bubble, hubbub continued to grow; Innocent Eyes spent a record-breaking 29 weeks at No 1 in Australia.

After months of chemotherapy and radiation, Goodrem went into remission before she was given the all-clear. It’s a period she speaks of with grit and grace. “I’ve gone through a lot of different emotions about my changes in trajectory when I first started [...] but I’ve since been able to see that hopefully that’s symbolic of being a survivor,” she says. “Being able to give back and make a difference – that’s a gift from that chapter in my life.” In 2020, she established the Delta Goodrem Foundation in partnership with the hospital in Sydney where she was treated.

Goodrem is still the human equivalent of a glowstick: a 1,000-kilowatt smile and the sort of enviable perma-tan that only Australians seem to possess. Certainly, hers is not the hardened exterior you might expect from a woman who was signed to Sony at 14 and came of age in the media hellscape that was the early 2000s. “My journey was positive,” she says simply. “Everyone has a different journey. I really did have great industry mentors, wonderful men and women around me, including my mum who was this fierce woman. It doesn’t mean I didn’t have to fight for myself, of course, but there was enough respect and understanding to have collaboration and conversation.”

open image in gallery Golden Girl: Goodrem performs on behalf of Australia at the 2026 Eurovision Song Contest in Austria ( Getty )

Her parents made sure she maintained a normal life outside of music. “I never felt like I missed out on any childhood,” she says. “Also, I was the driver in my music. It wasn’t my parents. They just guided and protected me.”

Now, two decades later, Goodrem is still in the driver’s seat with an eighth album on the way. Set to be released in November, Pure has been described as “a return to myself” and follows on from her latest single “Hologram” – a big, gleaming gem of disco-pop. Sonically, it’s miles away from the heart-wrenching ballads on which Goodrem made her name, but spiritually it’s more similar than you think. It has that same bright-eyed, bushy-tailed optimism of “Not Me, Not I” – only this time filtered through a woofer-rattling bass.

Before then, though, Strictly… “I love the glamour of it!” Goodrem says of her decision to sign up to the BBC show. “My music has always been very piano-driven so this is my opportunity to learn something new and then I can take it on tour with me.” As for who she would like for a partner, she has just one request for producers. “I’m quite tall, so I’d love to have someone taller than me!” laughs Goodrem, who is just shy of 6ft. “I really don’t want to be the one that has to lift people.”

open image in gallery Blowing kisses: Goodrem pictured at the 2003 Aria Awards in Sydney wearing a wig following chemotherapy and radiation treatment ( Getty )

It’s fair to say that Strictly has been through the wringer recently, with this latest series arriving amid a spate of scandals. But Goodrem knows the game, having spent eight years on The Voice Australia where she was on the other side of things as a coach rather than contestant. “I can safely say that, being on the show for nine years, everyone worked very hard to make sure all the artists were shining on stage and getting to live out their dreams,” she says, “what you do with that moment is up to you. It is a TV show, and you have to create your next moment.”

The show also taught Goodrem the value of holding back sometimes. “I probably gave too much of myself [to the contestants],” she says. “I poured so much into it. I was always on the phone to the artists because I loved sharing; I’m an open book.” It’s her natural disposition, she says. “I’m such a ride-or-die person. When I love someone, I’ll do anything for them. And so when people are loyal to me, I’m so loyal back. Scorpio loyal.” It can come at a cost, though. “The show taught me about my own boundaries and pouring that back into myself and my own artistry.”

open image in gallery Picture perfect: Goodrem was 18 years old and riding the high of her No 1 debut album when she was diagnosed with Hodgkin’s lymphoma ( Getty )

Season six of The Voice saw Goodrem become the target of online bullies who questioned the sincerity of her on-air enthusiasm. The earnestness that had once endeared her to audiences suddenly became the very thing they used to dismiss her as fake. Seal, her co-judge at the time, was among those to defend her publicly. “There was so much that I saw change culturally when Twitter came into play, and obviously being the only female coach for a long time, it was a very different dynamic for me,” Goodrem says. “I was 26, but people treated me like I was a lot older because I started so young. So I had to navigate those chapters of intensity under a microscope.” Though, she reminds me, it certainly wasn’t the first time.

Never were more eyes on Goodrem than in the wake of her cancer remission, when her return to public life carried the weighty comeback narrative of a seasoned musician three decades her senior. In 2004, Goodrem released Mistaken Identity. The album had a different thrust: more dark than its predecessor, more grown-up. Whether she intended for it to be or not, Mistaken Identity pushed against the idea of Goodrem as the nation’s most beatific pop sweetheart.

open image in gallery From down under to the dancefloor: the Aussie star is competing on the forthcoming series of ‘Strictly Come Dancing’ ( PA )

“Heading back into the world was definitely a change of gears,” she says now. “That’s probably when it felt most like going into the washing machine, so to speak – definitely a rougher, more turbulent chapter. Your identity changes after going through something so extreme.” Her parents had divorced, and her body – “my physicality” – was no longer the same. “Everything had changed.” The spotlight turned up some after it was revealed that Goodrem was dating Westlife singer Brian McFadden that same year – it turned up more still after their nasty and very public split in 2011. “Do I wish that it ended earlier? Yes. Do I wish I had the courage to leave earlier? Yes, I do,” she told Vogue in 2012. On the subject of McFadden today, Goodrem is looking on the bright side: “Every single path that’s led me to today and this beautiful relationship I’m in now, I’m grateful for.” (At one point in our conversation, her husband, the guitarist Matthew Copley, pops his head in with a big smile and a glass of water for his wife.)

open image in gallery People’s princess: Goodrem has remained close to the hearts of millions of Australians ( Getty )

Goodrem might just be one of pop’s most resilient stars. The cancer wasn’t even her last major health scare. In 2018, she had a salivary gland removed after which she woke up from the surgery to find her speech altered; a nerve in her tongue was paralysed. Goodrem couldn’t speak, let alone sing. “The lesson that came out of that experience was sometimes you have to surrender and listen,” she says. “It wasn’t about talking or doing. It was a real reset. It is something you cannot rush.” In the end, it took over a year for Goodrem to regain her voice. She’s certainly putting it to good use now, with her year of saying yes.

‘Pure’ is out via Universal Records on 6 November, with ‘Strictly Come Dancing’ set to launch in September

Jeroen Wouda and Dirk Boom walk slowly along a Dutch dike, prodding at the bone dry surface with metal rods and scanning the parched grass for patches of green that could give away the location of a leak.

In a scene that brings to mind the fictional Dutch boy who heroically plugs a hole in a dike with his finger, the two men are hunting for cracks in the low-lying Netherlands’ famed water defenses caused a drought that is gripping Europe and has fueled raging wildfires in France and Spain and sent the Danube and Rhine rivers to record low levels.

Unlike the low-tech solution in American author Mary Mapes Dodge's 19th-century story, modern dike patrols are able to plot possible problems caused by drought in an app and send it to authorities who can then quickly carry our repairs.

In the Netherlands and neighboring Germany cargo ships that ply the Rhine and its offshoots have been forced to carry significantly less freight or risk running aground in shallow navigation channels. Farmers facing restrictions on irrigating their crops are warning of smaller fruit harvests and rising prices this season.

And for some houseboat owners, the drought has left their water-borne homes resting on sandy river bed.

Checking dikes for damage

Peter van Duijvendijk is a flood defense manager at the Schieland en de Krimpenerwaard water corporation, one of 21 such organizations covering the Netherlands that are responsible for issues including flood control.

He has a team of 140 volunteers who are responsible for checking about 100 kilometers (60 miles) of dikes, reporting any problems they find. So far this dry summer there have not discovered any major issues. But they remain alert now and likely into the fall.

The volunteers “are our eyes and ears on the dike,” Van Duijvendijk told The Associated Press.

Like many inland dikes, the barrier in agricultural fields near the small town of Waddinxveen, east of The Hague, is made of peat that needs to be damp to be strong enough to hold back water. It is in one of the lowest points in the Netherlands, some 5 meters (16 feet) below sea level.

“Because it is so dry right now the peat loses moisture, and because of that it becomes weaker,” Van Duijvendijk said. “If that peat becomes weaker, then there is a chance that water will flow through the dike and that waterway will drain into the polder,” referring to reclaimed Dutch land.

Cargo traffic choked by low river levels

Europe's major rivers face a lack of water flow.

In Cologne, Germany, people walk along parts of the dried-up bed of the Rhine, a river that is a major highway for European freight traffic.

On Saturday, the Rhine’s water level in Cologne dropped below the record low set in October 2018. Marcel Beck, manager of the western German ports of Neuss, Düsseldorf and Cologne at RheinCargo, a port and freight transport company, said the levels are having a “devastating impact” on shipping.

“A ship that would normally carry 2,000 to 2,500 metric tons of cargo can now only transport 400, perhaps 600, metric tons depending on the ship’s design,” he said. “This places an enormous burden on the entire transport chain to reorganize everything in order to still get the goods inland.”

In the eastern Dutch city of Nijmegen, a rusted bicycle and shopping cart are exposed on the dried bed of the Waal — the main Dutch arm of the Rhine — and houseboats are left almost high and dry by receding water.

Frans Schilte has seen the summer periods of low water levels get longer in recent years. They used to last a month, but “now it’s like three months,” he said.

His steel-bottomed boat is now resting on the sandy river bed.

“It’s a little out of level, it’s not a big problem,” said Schilte, who describes the drought as “the negative effect of climate change.”

Water levels are a Dutch dilemma

The Netherlands, about a third of which is below sea level, is involved in a balancing act between preventing winter floods and having enough water for crops and canals in the summer.

“Throughout the year, we have enough water in the Netherlands, there’s no shortage,” said Vince Kaandorp, a groundwater hydrologist at Deltares, an independent Dutch water research institute.

“But, of course, it is not evenly distributed over the seasons,” Kaandorp said. “In the winter we drain it away quickly because we want to keep our feet dry and we don’t want water on the land. How can you ensure that you do that slowly and give water time to sink into the ground?”

Such measures don’t have to be high-tech, Kaandorp said. Adding something as simple as a hedge near a river slows down water and gives it time to seep deep into the ground. Authorities are studying how to turn soil into “sponges” to better hold water throughout the year.

The low-lying parts of the western Netherlands that are reclaimed land suffer increasingly from salinity in droughts, posing problems for farmers who grow fruit and vegetables in the fertile soil. Water authorities trying to maintain adequate supplies of fresh water have banned farmers in some parts of the country from pumping water out of canals to irrigate their crops.

“It is an extremely challenging year for growers,” John Kusters, chair of the Netherlands Fruit Growers' Organization, said in a statement.

___

Associated Press journalists Ahmad Seir in Nijmegen, Netherlands, Daniel Niemann in Cologne, Germany, and Stefanie Dazio in Berlin contributed to this report.

A fast-moving wildfire driven by strong winds and high temperatures swept across northwest Spokane on Saturday before jumping the Spokane River and prompting the evacuation of thousands of people.

The Old Trails Fire started around noon, burning brush and grass in an open area, but quickly spread north and east toward residential areas. Cars lined the roads as people fled their homes, and orange and red flames were visible from the highway.

The blaze sent a plume of smoke billowing over the region, and as of the evening almost 4 square miles (10 square kilometers) of terrain had been burned, said Courtney James, spokesperson for the Washington State Department of Natural Resources.

The cause was under investigation.

“We urge residents of Spokane to heed evacuation orders and to stay alert to changing conditions and evacuations as they are rapidly changing,” James said.

Some structures were lost but officials did not yet have a solid count, said Jessica Watson, a DNR spokesperson for the fire. Firefighters had zero containment as of the evening and the wind continued to blow, she said.

Power company Avista said it implemented public safety shutoffs in the area due to elevated fire risk.

Gov. Bob Ferguson declared a state of emergency Saturday after unusually high temperatures and high winds exacerbated record wildfires across the state. The National Weather Service issued a “particularly dangerous situation” red flag alert for eastern Washington.

News.title: Idaho shooting updates: At least 3 dead and 2 injured in mass shooting at Idaho In-N-Out with casualties expected ‘to increase’
News.content:
( AP )

The latest headlines from our reporters across the US sent straight to your inbox each weekday Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

At least three people were killed and two others were injured in a mass shooting at an In-N-Out in Twin Falls, Idaho, on Saturday, according to police and local officials.

The suspected shooter — an unidentified male — is dead, Twin Falls Police Chief Matthew Hicks said at a press conference. He described the scene as “tragic” and “chaotic.”

Joshua Palmer, a city spokesperson, told The Independent that the number of victims is expected to rise. “We want to emphasize that that number may change,” Palmer said. “That was just the first number we got.”

An “active shooter incident” was first reported at 4:29 p.m. ET at the In-N-Out on Blue Lakes Boulevard North. Police urged people to avoid the area, saying roads nearby would be closed as officers responded.

Shelter-in-place orders have since been lifted, Palmer said.

Hicks said the FBI is assisting the investigation, adding that information about the suspect and his motivations are expected to be revealed in the coming days.

Twin Falls, a city of about 56,000 people, is located roughly 130 miles southeast of Boise. There have been over 300 mass shootings in the U.S. this year, according to the Mass Shooter Tracker.

It was 1989, George H.W. Bush was in the White House, Madonna was on the radio and the country was in the grips of its last major measles outbreak - until today.

“People were scared to death to come to the city. I mean, schools canceled trips to the city. We were pulling one dead child out of the house after another,” pediatrician Dr. Paul Offit, an infectious disease expert at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia who was working in the city as cases exploded, told The Independent.

By the time the outbreak ended in 1991, there had been 55,467 cases and 166 deaths across the country, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention records show.

It was the worst outbreak the country had seen since the measles vaccine, which also targeted preventable illnesses mumps and rubella, was introduced in 1963. Public health officials blamed the crisis on low vaccine coverage.

Now - with more than 2,300 cases of the potentially-deadly disease in the U.S. and numbers rising weekly - there are no such vaccine barriers. But different obstacles exist: beginning with the White House.

open image in gallery College students stand in line for measles vaccinations at Georgia’s Auburn University in April 1989 - the year of the last major measles outbreak in the US - until today ( AP )

A skeptical White House

President Donald Trump’s public health agenda, spearheaded by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., has seen vaccine skeptics added to advisory panels and conspiracy theories about vaccines spoken about inside the federal government.

Trump himself has repeatedly claimed that young children are given 80 different vaccines.

"They give — I mean, for a little baby to be injected with that much fluid?" Trump told reporters in September. "Even beyond the actual ingredients, they have sometimes 80 different vaccines … It’s like you’re shooting up a horse."

The number of vaccinations before the age of 18 is typically between 30 to 50, doctors say.

The president has also recently pushed Kennedy - long known as a vaccine skeptic - to be more aggressive on cutting federal recommendations for annual child vaccines over the debunked ties to autism, The Wall Street Journal reported earlier this month.

open image in gallery Measles is a nasty virus that can lead to life-threatening brain swelling in children who are unvaccinated. Distrust in vaccines has been at the heart of America’s measles resurgence, with vaccine skepticism rising 15 percent since 2019 ( CDC )

open image in gallery President Donald Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. have both made misleading comments that are skeptical of vaccines for children, including related to debunked ties between vaccines and autism ( Getty )

Last year, Kennedy said he directed the CDC to abandon its longstanding position that vaccines do not cause autism.

“The whole thing about ‘vaccines have been tested and there’s been this determination made,’ is just a lie,” he told The New York Times in November.

White House spokesperson Kush Desai also previously told the The Independent that people worried about “skyrocketing autism rates have long been ignored if not mocked.”

He added that the administration is “committed to leaving no stone unturned to finally address these concerns with Gold Standard Science.”

In vaccines we distrust

Distrust in vaccines in the U.S. came long before Trump but has grown in recent years because of misinformation that circulated online during the Covid-19 pandemic and in podcasts and social media since then.

That distrust has been at the heart of America’s measles resurgence, with vaccine skepticism rising 15 percent since 2019, according to a study from the University of Arkansas.

About one in five parents are not confident childhood vaccines have been tested enough or that the annual vaccine schedule for kids is safe, according to a 2025 Pew Research Center survey.

“Here we have a skeptical, mistrustful, conspiratorial population goaded on by people like Bobby Kennedy Jr. And now we have a very different kind of problem – and a dangerous one,” Dr. Irwin Redlener, co-founder of non-profit healthcare organization Children's Health Fund with the musician Paul Simon, told The Independent.

open image in gallery This map from the CDC shows measles cases across the U.S. so far this year. The states with the highest case levels are shown in darker blues and those with the lowest levels are shown in lighter blues ( CDC )

Since last year, there have been several large measles outbreaks affected by vaccine skepticism, including in a Mennonite community in West Texas and an evangelical Christian community in South Carolina. There were two child deaths reported in Texas.

Measles appears as an angry red rash dotting all areas of the skin, with cases causing a high fever, pink eye and runny nose. Normal cases typically last for a week or two but some who are infected develop a progressive brain disorder that is often fatal.

The virus spreads quickly through the air after an infected person coughs or sneezes - even if they are no longer in the room a couple of hours later.

Fortunately, the answer to stopping the spread is the same as it was 35 years ago: vaccines.

open image in gallery Ethan Turner holds his 14-month-old son, Niko, while he gets the measles vaccine at a clinic in Lubbock, Texas, in March 2025. Increased vaccination helped to end the measles outbreak in Texas last August ( Getty )

open image in gallery Medical workers assess a patient with symptoms of the measles in a parking lot in Spartanburg, South Carolina, in January. Spartanburg was the site of one of the nation’s biggest outbreaks since last year ( The Washington Post/Getty )

A deadly cost

During the last major outbreak, in 1991, Philadelphia saw 1,400 cases, with about a third in middle-class Christians, accounting for six deaths in under a year, according to Offit.

Religious exemptions to vaccines were legal in Pennsylvania, as remains the case across more than 40 states, and these communities “just didn’t believe in modern medicine,” he recalled.

“And you know, they believed in prayer. And if you prayed and your child died, then you hadn’t gotten close enough to God,” Offit said.

Several months into that surge, Philadelphia doctors were issued an order from a judge to vaccinate children, regardless of the parents’ wishes - something that hasn’t been done since. The decision helped stop cases in their tracks.

In states with other outbreaks, free vaccine clinics at universities played a role in slowing the spread of measles at a time when the jab wasn’t always without a cost. Georgia’s Auburn University, Illinois’s University of Chicago and Ohio’s Kent State University offered the shots free of charge.

Cost was the primary hurdle for children in the U.S. not getting vaccinated during the 1989 outbreak, according to the CDC. At the time shots cost over $30, a 1989 New York Times article reported.

Many low-income families also did not have access to primary care physicians who could give children vaccines, Redlener explained.

“[Back then it] was problems of access along with, ‘Oh, is it really serious, anyway?’” he said. More than half of children infected in the that outbreak had not been vaccinated.

It took a national effort to pull America out of the crisis. New guidelines for a second dose of the vaccine were released in 1989, giving Americans an added layer of protection from the virus. Two doses of the vaccine are 97 percent effective against infection, whereas one dose is 93 percent effective.

In 1993, President Bill Clinton’s administration launched the federal Vaccines for Children initiative, providing vaccines for kids whose parents who may have not been able to afford them.

By 2000, 76 percent of children in the U.S. had the measles vaccine - which helped stop the continuous spread of the disease for more than a year and brought cases to a record low.

'I think people don't remember measles'

Now, more than 90 percent of children have had their measles shots. But coverage needed to limit spread among kindergarteners is lower than it should be and has been declining since before the pandemic.

So an illness that many doctors thought they had resigned to history has come roaring back and as a far murkier and complex problem to solve.

“Now we have a challenge that none of us have formally been trained for. What do we do with recalcitrant, anti-science ideologues who have bought into the conspiracies being sold by the likes of Bobby Kennedy Jr.?” Redlener asked.

open image in gallery Incoming kindergartener Jeremy Conner, 5, reacts to a measles shot in Santa Ana, California, in August 2002. Measles was declared eliminated in the US in 2000 ( Getty )

While Kennedy denied being anti-vaccine during his confirmation hearings to become health secretary, he’s also touted unconventional treatments for measles and previously falsely claimed that outbreaks were tied to the fact the vaccine didn’t offer lifelong protection. The measles vaccine offers lifelong protection, per the CDC.

“As long as we have a federal government that’s committed to promoting misinformation and conspiracy theories, it’s going to be very difficult to fix anything,” Redlener added.

In response to today's rising cases, HHS says Kennedy has been clear that vaccination is the most effective way to prevent infection and that the department has focused its response on supporting affected communities and strengthening local and state response.

"Under Secretary Kennedy's leadership, HHS has mounted an aggressive outbreak response, providing more than $8.5 million to states and local partners, expanding technical assistance, and surging CDC personnel and resources to support containment efforts where needed most,” Press Secretary Emily Hilliard told The Independent.

Offit believes the measles outbreaks will continue in an era of medical freedom, and as people believe they have the right to make their own health decisions and stop caring about the health of their neighbors.

Part of the problem is that people don’t remember past outbreaks, he said, and some younger doctors working at his hospital had never seen a measles case before.

“I think that not only did we eliminate the disease, we eliminated the memory of the disease. I think people don’t remember measles,” he said.

News.title: Dowman weaves his magic and new signing shines as Arsenal hit ground running
News.content:
Hello and welcome to our live coverage for this pre-season friendly between Girona and Arsenal at Estadi Montilivi in Catalonia.

With the transfer speculation surrounding Vinícius Júnior’s and Bruno Guimaraes’ potential moves to Arsenal ramping up, the reigning Premier League champions are in action against Girona as they step up their preparations ahead of the upcoming campaign.

Unlike other Premier League heavyweights, Arsenal have kept their pre-season tour relatively local with a selection of games in Spain, Ireland and England, before they face Manchester City in the FA Community Shield on August 16 at the Millennium Stadium in Cardiff.

Arsenal beat League One side MK Dons 3-0 in a behind-closed-doors friendly on July 25 at the Sobha Realty Training Centre, thanks to goals from Reiss Nelson, Ethan Nwaneri and Ceadach O’Neill.

After featuring in this victory and setting up Nelson for the opener, Christos Tzolis will be looking to continue his positive momentum with his new club, after joining Arsenal for £34m earlier this summer. Many fans will be keeping a close eye on the recently-signed winger given that various core members of last season’s Premier League-winning squad are yet to return from their post-World Cup breaks, having progressed deep in the competition.

Tournament winners David Raya, Martin Zubimendi and Mikel Merino, Norway captain Martin Odegaard, as well as England internationals Bukayo Saka, Declan Rice, Eberechi Eze and Noni Madueke are all missing for this game, while France’s William Saliba is out injured and set for an extended period on the sidelines.

Those who exited the World Cup earlier than the aforementioned players, including Gabriel Magalhaes, Gabriel Martinelli, Piero Hincapie, Kai Havertz, and Viktor Gyokeres, have all joined up with the squad in northern Spain.

Mikel Arteta’s men will play a wounded Girona, who suffered relegation from the top flight of Spanish football last season due to a 19th-place finish.

Kick-off is at 19:00, with team news arriving shortly.

News.title: Kerr wins by a mile: Scot claims Commonwealth gold to emulate Bannister
News.content:
“It means everything – absolutely incredible,” said Kerr, who joined the rendition of Flower of Scotland before closing his eyes to soak up the moment in a stadium where he had competed as a child in even the shot put.

“To do it in front of a Scottish crowd, where I learned how to race, doesn’t get any better,” he added. “I came here week after week growing up as a kid. This was the championship of my season with the world indoors and going after the record. This was on the calendar before any of that. I think a British crowd deserved more from me and I owed them that.”

Of the tactics compared to his world record, where he had to hold an even pace throughout, Kerr stressed the importance of staying calm and not being tempted into pushing too soon. “London was a big stress, pushing my body to the extreme limit,” he said. “Doing a championship race is a nice clean slate; using your brain instead of your body. It’s how I love to race.

“When you’re running that slow, your job is not to waste energy and I did that. I knew an opportunity would open up. Then it was about staying awake and alive and trying to get some space. felt like I had plenty of gears left in me.”

Kerr had emerged to a huge home ovation and, with the Proclaimers booming out as the runners completed the first two laps, he was content to stay in the pack even as Myers followed. There was then only one brief moment of concern as the runners began gathering themselves during the penultimate lap and Kerr became momentarily boxed in.

News.title: Exciting young talent JJ Gabriel makes debut as Man Utd beat Atletico Madrid
News.content:
Manchester United 2 Atletico Madrid 1

JJ Gabriel showed glimpses of his potential as he made his Manchester United debut in their 2-1 win over Atletico Madrid in Stockholm.

The 15-year-old may have been introduced with only eight minutes remaining, but, given how highly rated he is, it was a significant move by Michael Carrick to give him game time in the senior team.

There were hints of why Gabriel is so well regarded during those eight minutes, as he found space in the centre of the pitch and linked well with Leny Yoro. But he was also on the receiving end of some physical challenges – something he will have to grow accustomed to the more he plays at senior level.

Yoro, who himself made his senior debut as a 16-year-old for Lille, was impressed by Gabriel and said: “He’s a really good player. He is still really young and still has a lot to learn and a lot to improve on but he’s really humble and still working, so I’m happy for him to get his first minutes. I hope, for him, it’s going to continue like that.”

News.title: City fire blanks in shoot-out as Maresca’s opening game ends in defeat by Inter
News.content:
Manchester City 1 Inter Milan 1; Inter win 3-1 on pens

Manchester City lost the Asahi Super Dry Trophy 3-1 on a penalty shoot-out against Inter Milan.

Enzo Maresca took charge of the Premier League runners-up for the first time since his arrival as Pep Guardiola’s replacement, though he was without many of his stars who had yet to return from World Cup duty.

One of the players missing was Elliot Anderson, the £116m signing from Nottingham Forest, though Jeremy Monga, 16, was an unused substitute after being brought in from Leicester City in the summer transfer window.

City took the lead on 14 minutes through Divin Mubamba as he tapped in an Antoine Semenyo cross, but Inter’s experienced defender Benjamin Pavard levelled just six minutes later when City failed to clear a corner.

The Premier League side dominated possession in the second half after an even first 45 minutes but could not find a way through. Phil Foden, the captain, was again underwhelming after a difficult year last season, but with the season still to come he had plenty of time to show his best form once more after signing a new contract at the Etihad.

The game went to penalties after full-time with no extra time played, and only Claudio Echeverri held his nerve for City as Inter Milan scored three of theirs, Matteo Lavelli netting the winning spot-kick.

Both teams learnt little from the match as Inter made 11 changes and City eight, though Maresca will have been impressed by Ryan McAidoo’s performance as a second-half substitute, as he regularly threatened from the right wing. The 18-year-old forward will surely be in demand from other clubs looking to loan him, and City may yet be tempted to keep him around for the coming season.

Match details

Manchester City Donnarumma; Lewis, Khusanov, Gvardiol (Reis, 46), Mfuni (Alleyne, 46); Kovacic (N González, 46), Reijnders (Ait-Nouri, 46); Savinho (Braithwaite, 78), Foden (Echeverri, 68), Semenyo (Sangare, 68); Mubama (McAidoo, 46).

Substitutes not used Bettinelli, Wint, Chabot, Monga, Mukasa, F. Samba, Heskey, Henderson-Hall, Parker.

News.title: Massage guns vs compression boots: Which is better for muscle recovery?
News.content:
Looking after your body is no longer just about getting a good workout in; it’s ensuring that you’re properly recuperating afterwards, too. Luckily, in 2026, there is a huge range of products designed to aid recovery.

In fact, the recovery tech boom is playing a big role in the growth of the sports technology market overall. Estimates show it’s projected to grow from $39.6 billion in 2026 to $192.3 billion by 2034.

Two of the most popular products in this category are massage guns and compression boots. Both claim to ease muscle soreness and help you bounce back to training sooner, but they sit at very different price points. You can pick up a basic gun from around £40, whereas the cheapest boots we tested were £300. But which method is actually better for improving workout recovery?

Massage guns can help to improve flexibility in older muscles

Massage guns work by delivering repeated percussion and vibration to one specific area, which helps improve the mobility and flexibility of a specific muscle. In turn, this can make your muscles feel less tense and stiff. These gadgets can be used before and after workout sessions.

While useful for all ages, massage guns can be helpful for anyone looking to improve range of movement, ease muscle stiffness and boost blood flow – whether exercising or not.

“It will help temporarily improve your mobility so that you feel like you’ve got a bit more flexibility in that muscle,” explains Jonathan Wreaves, clinical physiologist at preventative health clinic Viavi.

But how do they actually work?

Most massage guns offer a revolutions per minute (RPM) range, which refers to how many times the massage head moves back and forth every minute. This tends to be somewhere between 1200 and 3500. The lower range is ideal for gentle massage and warming up, while a higher RPM is better for targeting bigger muscle groups and more intense tightness.

News.title: Battle rages over access to new ‘miracle’ HIV drug
News.content:
For the first time in the four-decade fight against HIV there is a “miracle” drug that can all but eliminate the risk of infection, but in the Latin American countries where it was tested almost no one can get it.

Trials show that Lenacapavir, made by Gilead Sciences, is almost 100 per cent effective in preventing HIV infection. With just two shots a year, those taking it will avoid contracting the virus even when frequently exposed.

The drug, which many believe could bring an end to the global HIV pandemic, costs $14,000 a dose in the United States. Gilead has agreed to licence generic versions of the pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) medication at around $40 a dose in 120 low-and middle-income countries, but almost all of Latin America is excluded.

Brazil, Mexico, Argentina and Peru are among those with serious HIV epidemics that are shut out, despite having run some of the clinical trials that proved the drug works.

Their status as “upper-middle income countries” means they are too rich to qualify for the cut price generic version and yet they remain too poor to pay the US price.

News.title: Senior dating: a guide to finding love later in life
News.content:
Whether you’re a widow, widower or divorcee, the thought of online dating in later life can feel daunting. However, more and more people are turning to the internet to find romance. Roughly 16 per cent of UK adults are using online dating services to meet a partner, according to Statista. Among them, there are lots of singles over 50 using dating sites.

So here’s how to navigate your senior dating online, with expert advice from psychologist and dating coach Dr Pam Spurr, and sex and relationship coach Angela Vossen.

How do I know if I'm ready to date again as a senior?

Coming out of any relationship is hard. If you’re hoping to date after a divorce, bereavement or break up, it can take a long time to feel ready to date again. Dr Spurr advises taking your time.

“Many people feel bruised, even traumatised, after coming out of a long-term relationship or having been bereaved,” she explains. “Your feelings naturally vary from day to day about whether you're ready to get back out to look for love – or even for fun. A crucial factor is if you've come to the point where you have more good days compared to bad days”.

Dr Spurr explains that good days are the days on which you feel more optimistic about life generally, and you find your thoughts turning to meeting someone new. “That's an important sign that you are healing,” she says. “However, if you're still feeling deeply insecure or are riddled with self-doubt about your worthiness, take your time. When you feel worthy, you will find someone worthy of you”.

Feeling heartbroken? Learn how to get over a break up

How to start senior dating online

If you’re new to online dating, it can feel intimidating at first. The secret is taking things step by step so that you do things at your own pace. The first step, however, should be choosing a senior dating site that will help match you with like-minded people. This will narrow your search and ensure your dating experience is more successful.

Step 1: Create an online profile

Once you’ve decided on a dating site or app and signed up, you’ll be asked to write a dating profile. This should reflect who you are along with your passions, values and what you seek in a partner.

Try to be authentic rather than creating a fantasy version of yourself. If you exaggerate your accomplishments, your date will only feel deceived once they get to know you. Likewise, don’t be tempted to use a photo of yourself from 10 years ago.

What are you waiting for? |  Single and looking to find true love? Sign up today for Telegraph Dating and join more than 220,000 like-minded people. Join today

Step 2: Spark meaningful chats with potential dates

Once you have signed up to a senior dating site and created a profile, you will be free to start looking at other people’s profiles and sending messages to anyone that catches your attention. But how can you initiate a conversation after an introduction?

“When messaging people on dating sites, ask open-ended questions to spark meaningful chats,” says Angela. A good example would be, ‘I can see you enjoy travel. What place have you always wanted to visit but haven’t yet?’ or “tell me more about your love of tennis? Did you watch the US Open?” If things go really well and the chat seems to flow naturally, you may decide to organise a phone chat or ask them out on a date. An initial chat over the phone can help gauge how well you get on and how easily the conversation flows. If this goes well, meeting in person may feel less nerve wracking and a little less ‘blind’.

Step 3: Prioritise your safety

“While most people are well intentioned online, it’s important to protect your safety,” advises Ms Vossen. “Keep personal details private (like where you live or your social media profiles) until you’ve met in person and built trust”. You should also arrange first dates in public places, share your plans with a friend, and trust your instincts if something feels off.

If the first date or two doesn’t quite hit the mark, try not to be too disappointed and remember that you can say no to another date. Ms Vossen says: “Be patient – online dating takes time, but with practice, you’ll gain confidence and enjoy the journey”.

Traditional ways to meet senior singles

Of course, couples continue to meet in a manner that predates online dating sites. If you’re keen to join the older dating scene but find the online world overwhelming, there are plenty of ways to meet people in real life.

1. Holidays and group trips

We are often our best selves on holiday, so it’s the ideal place to find a single senior woman or to meet men if the opportunity presents itself. Why not organise a trip on which you meet new people while doing what you love, whether that’s cycling, walking, sightseeing or just travelling around a new part of the world. There are many escorted tours that cater to specific age groups and interests. They also take away the stress of organising a trip yourself.

“An organised holiday or trip can be a great place to meet someone new and there are many organisations offering these for the over 50s,” says Dr Spur. “A word of caution though, you can spend a lot of money and there's no guarantee that you will meet that special person. However, if it's a place you've wanted to travel to then go with the mindset that you're going to have a great trip. If you meet someone, that's an added bonus”.

2. Activities and social groups

Whether you enjoy walking, reading or volunteering, taking up a new hobby or joining a social group is a great way to enhance your social life and increase your chances of meeting a new romantic interest.

“Joining a club or taking up a hobby can be a fantastic way of meeting singles who enjoy the same pastimes,” says Dr Spur. “You're doing an activity you enjoy knowing that there might also be someone there that will catch your eye”.

If you do meet someone that you’re interested in at a social event, Dr Spur advises starting with a simple ‘hello’ and an easy question such as how long they've been doing that particular activity or hobby. “This can open-up a friendly conversation that might lead to flirting down the line,” she says.

Start online dating for seniors today

Whichever way you decide to start looking for love, approach it in a way that you feel comfortable with. Signing up to an online dating service is a great way to meet other seniors. Remember, it’s never too late to begin a new chapter.
