World.title: Labour holds Greater Manchester mayoralty after counting goes to second round
World.content:
Speaking at the Co-Op Live arena to the east of the city, Craig said she stands “ready to serve” her 3 million constituents.

“Every single decision I take as your mayor of Greater Manchester will pass the test of making your life better,” Craig pledged.

The vote was triggered after three-time mayoral contest winner Burnham resigned the job in June to return to Westminster, where he swiftly claimed leadership of the governing Labour Party and became prime minister. There had been concern that Burnham’s move would allow Reform UK — which performed strongly in local elections in England earlier this year — to seize the mayoralty.

Craig will now be have to deal directly with Burnham, who has promised to devolve more powers to England’s mayors as a part of a devolution package. The post currently comes with powers over transport, policing, and housing.

Turnout for the special election was noticeably lower than when Burnham last ran back in 2024, with only 25 per cent of voters heading to the polls this time, compared to 32 per cent at the last vote. POLITICO witnessed some voters on doorsteps Thursday evening learning of the election for the first time.

Counting continued late into the night as the re-instated supplementary voting system took the contest to a second round for the first time ever.

World.title: Almost all of Ceuta migrants have returned to Morocco, Spain says
World.content:
People gather on a hilltop near Bab Sebta on the Morocco-Spain border, near Ceuta and the Moroccan town of Fnideq on July 30, 2026. | Abdelmajid Bziouat/AFP via Getty Images

“Most of the people that came yesterday are now back in Morocco,” an official said.

BRUSSELS — More than 48,300 of the approximately 50,000 people who entered the Spanish exclave of Ceuta from Morocco have returned, a Spanish government official told POLITICO.

“Most of the people that came yesterday are now back in Morocco,” said the official, who was granted anonymity to speak freely, adding that the situation was “on the path back to normality.”

The influx of migrants could be linked to a recent Spanish court ruling that limited the use of the country’s immediate-return procedure for migrants, the official added.

The European Commission said “there are no onward movements towards the European continent or other member states” by the migrants.

World.title: Trump administration slams Spain’s Sánchez for migrant ‘invasion’ of Ceuta
World.content:
“This unacceptable incident is the direct result of the Spanish Government’s deliberate efforts to enable and facilitate mass illegal migration into Europe. We are considering actions to defend Americans at home and abroad from this threat and stand ready to assist other European allies considering similar options,” wrote the department.

Sánchez will hardly be surprised by the scathing American reaction, having emerged as the fiercest Trump critic among EU leaders, slamming U.S. military action in the Middle East and barring U.S. military planes from using Spanish air bases.

“Thank God POTUS was elected and our country’s border no longer looks like this. These images out of Spain are an unfortunate reminder of the consequences of mass migration and the radical left-wing globalist policies that have enabled the Invasion of the West,” wrote U.S. Vice President JD Vance.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security made the same argument, saying: “If Spain had their own President Trump, this wouldn’t be an issue.”

The U.S. criticism came as the situation in Ceuta escalated into a Europe-wide political flashpoint in little more than a day. Neighboring governments moved to tighten their response on Friday, with France restoring border checks and Italy calling for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen area, exposing divisions over the bloc’s migration policy.

Former Trump adviser and world’s first trillionaire Elon Musk initially shared a video comparing footage from the Ceuta migrant crisis with scenes from the 2013 zombie film “World War Z.” “Wow, the situation in Spain looks crazy!” he posted.

Clarifying the comparison was a joke, he then shared footage from 2023, showing hundreds of Venezuelan migrants attempting to cross into the U.S., captioning it: “This is what America looked like under Biden.”

World.title: Northern Ireland misses a deadline to fix its budget crisis
World.content:
Bryant, a former Anglican priest who’s never held a Cabinet post before, held his first press conference as Northern Ireland secretary shortly before meeting delegations from the region’s two main government parties, Sinn Féin and the Democratic Unionists.

Bryant emphasized that the U.K. government expects Stormont to get more bang for its buck by reforming the delivery of local services, most crucially hospital care, where Northern Ireland suffers the worst waiting lists in the entire National Health Service.

“Look, we need to get to a budget,” Bryant said. “And I understand the financial pressures. I know everybody expects me to come with a checkbook. I’m actually coming with a checklist of things that I want to get sorted.”

Sinn Féin, which holds the key finance and economy ministries, has shied from taking any significant decisions on raising local taxes—not that the DUP wouldn’t immediately veto such moves. Nothing much can happen in Northern Ireland’s system of cross-community government unless the largest parties on each side of the divide can agree.

The two parties blame each other for delivering so little and agree that it’s up to the U.K. Treasury to break the budgetary impasse by providing them much more annually to spend. An independent budgetary watchdog, the Northern Ireland Fiscal Council, recently concluded that the region wasn’t being subsidized by English taxpayers to the same levels as in Scotland and Wales — and if it was, Northern Ireland could gain an extra £1 billion to £3.5 billion annually.

While few expect the Burnham administration to come anywhere close to that, both sides in Belfast do expect Bryant to take charge of key budget decisions — which is what his predecessors did when the Northern Ireland Executive collapsed in 2017 from a Sinn Féin walkout, and again in 2022 from a Democratic Unionist walkout.

World.title: London mayor Sadiq Khan accuses Palantir of bypassing procurement rules
World.content:
Palantir claims that Khan’s office blocked the contract unlawfully and “irrationally,” citing comments attributed to the mayor’s spokesperson which referred to the company’s unspecified “values and ethics.”

Louis Mosley, Palantir’s U.K. CEO, has argued that Khan’s decision puts politics above Londoners’ safety, while Met Police Commissioner Mark Rowley has said that the force’s inability to access Palantir’s technology would worsen the impact of cuts to the force’s budget.

In a pre-trial defense statement filed last Thursday and seen by POLITICO, lawyers for MOPAC said Palantir’s claim is “without merit and should be dismissed,” stating that the Met Police “conducted an award process that was unlawful.”

It says the Met Police and Palantir designed a pilot of the technology in 2025 so that the value remained below a £500,000 threshold at which it would have required MOPAC approval. MOPAC, led by Khan’s deputy mayor for policing and crime, oversees the Met Police.

Prior to the conclusion of that pilot in April 2026, the Met Police and Palantir started discussions on directly awarding Palantir a much larger contract to extend the pilot, according to the statement.

The Met Police intended “at each stage” to award the larger contract to Palantir, the statement says, adding that the approach that was “supported/encouraged/assisted” by the company.

World.title: UK to hold budget on Oct. 28, chancellor announces
World.content:
“Fiscal credibility is the bedrock of economic stability and national security,” said the chancellor in the letter. “That is why we will abide by the fiscal rules, ensuring we retain a buffer to protect us against uncertainty and the impact of instability in the Middle East.”

Healey also pledged the budget will move “money and power out of Westminster, and into every postcode around Britain.”

Burnham announced today that local English mayors will be given powers to retain and spend business rate taxes to boost growth in their regions.

The prime minister said mayors will soon have power over income taxes, but Healey will unveil a whitepaper and a “roadmap” on the topic at the autumn budget.

World.title: Explosion in Moscow restaurant killed three and injured 21
World.content:
An explosion Saturday at a Moscow restaurant that killed three people and wounded 21 others was a bombing, Russia's national anti-terrorism committee said.

 

"A homemade explosive device blew up at a restaurant in Kudrinskaya Square in Moscow, killing three people," said the committee, quoted by the Tass state news agency.

The three people killed were a woman carrying the device into the restaurant, a security agent who stopped her and a customer.

Telegram channel Baza, known for its ties with Russian security forces, first talked about a gas explosion that would have come from the restaurant's kitchen.

The restaurant had been booked for a private birthday party and Alexandre Tchaïko, the commander of the Russian Air Force, was present, reports say.

An earlier statement by Moscow police to the Ria Novosti news agency said investigators and police forensic specialists were at the site.

Images posted on Russian Telegram channels showed fire engines and ambulances outside the building.

Several terrorist attacks in past years

Russia has been the target of several terrorist attacks in the past.

Since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, Ukraine's secret service has claimed or been accused of several attacks on Russian military officers and public figures backing the conflict.

Russia blamed Ukraine for the killing of a senior general, Yaroslav Moskalik, in a car bomb in April 2025.

In August 2022, the nationalist Darya Dugina, daughter of hardline Russian ideologue Alexander Dugin, was killed outside Moscow when a bomb attached to her car detonated.

Many believe her father was the intended target.

In April 2023, pro-Kremlin military blogger Vladlen Tatarsky — real name Maxim Fomin — was killed when a statuette he was handed exploded at a cafe in Saint Petersburg.

A bomb attached to a scooter outside a Moscow apartment block killed General Igor Kirillov, head of the Russian army's chemical weapons division, and his assistant in December 2024.

And the pro-Kremlin writer and nationalist Zakhar Prilepin was seriously wounded in a May 2023 car explosion that killed another person near the city of Nizhny Novgorod.

World.title: EU rules on AI models become enforceable. What's going to change?
World.content:
As of today, the EU's rules on AI models become enforceable, cementing the European Commission's role as the world's most prominent regulator of this disruptive technology. Euronews takes a deep dive into what the rules mean for Europe and beyond.

 

The AI Act is the first comprehensive law regulating artificial intelligence. Passed in 2024, some of its most significant provisions — notably those regulating large language models — become applicable this August.

As the law introduces first-of-its-kind rules, enforcing them presents a unique set of challenges, not least because new generations of AI technology emerge every few months. Brussels' experience is likely to resonate well beyond Europe's borders.

What are the rules about?

Initially, the AI Act was only meant to regulate AI applications. But when the public launch of ChatGPT took the world by storm in 2022, EU policymakers decided also to cover the underlying technology: large language models.

The rulebook sets out rules for all models that lack a specific purpose but can be adapted to a variety of use cases, requiring transparency on how a model was built, disclosure of any copyright-protected content used for training, and enough information for downstream users to understand the model's capabilities.

Additional requirements fall on companies developing the most powerful "frontier" models — those pushing the boundaries of the technology — compelling AI firms to identify and mitigate risks to society at large.

Last year, the Commission endorsed a voluntary code of practice drafted by world-leading experts, including Yoshua Bengio, detailing how developers should comply with the rules. Most leading Western AI labs, with the notable exception of Meta, signed the code.

"We've collaborated closely with the European Commission and the wider ecosystem on implementing the AI Act, including its Codes of Practice, and will continue working together to help Europe realise the benefits of the Intelligence Age," Tom Duff Gordon, OpenAI's Vice President and Head of EMEA Policy, told Euronews.

What challenges lie ahead?

The Commission set up the European AI Office to drive enforcement of the AI Act's rules on AI models. The task is enormous, taking on one of the most complex technologies of our time and some of the richest companies in the world.

The EU's resources are knowingly limited, and AI talent is in high demand, with public authorities competing with the private sector. The Commission is therefore seeking to tap into external expertise, namely a panel of scientists and a pool of highly specialised AI safety firms.

Still, AI in general, and frontier models in particular, remain a moving target: officials will have to keep pace with fast-moving technological developments without much prior experience or scientific consensus on how to prevent harm at scale.

At the same time, any decisive action from Brussels in this area is bound to draw the attention, if not the ire, of Washington, with the Trump administration particularly assertive in attacking the EU's digital rules when they affect American companies.

"The danger is that the current US administration treats this as an attack on US commercial interests, as it did when the Commission sought to implement its digital markets' rules in December 2025 and more recently this month when it sought to fine Google under the EU's Digital Markets Act," MEP Michael McNamara (Ireland/Renew) told Euronews.

What does it mean for Europeans?

The AI Act's core purpose is to make technology safer for European citizens, ensuring it does not harm their safety and fundamental rights. As such, it also applies to foreign companies that commercialise their AI technologies in the EU.

The industry has repeatedly attacked the law, arguing that it will slow innovation by placing an unnecessary burden on tech companies, forcing them to divert money from hiring engineers to hiring lawyers to handle the paperwork.

In practice, for European consumers and businesses, that might mean some of the most advanced AI models launch in the EU a few weeks later than in other markets, as firms ensure they have done their compliance homework.

Still, it will also mean that, at least in theory, Europeans can trust that if an AI model is available in the EU, it is safe to use. Given how embedded AI is becoming in everyday products and services, that time lag might be worth it.

MEP Axel Voss (Germany/EPP) called on the Commission to enforce the AI Act in close alignment with other digital issues, since AI technologies are increasingly embedded in connected products and online services.

"Taking the AI Office's lack of capacities into account, I very much hope that they do not waste their energy on niche concerns but instead align strongly with the priorities of their platform regulation colleagues," Voss told Euronews.

Is the EU setting the benchmark?

As the Commission has become the world's most prominent AI regulator, it will inevitably set the benchmark for how public authorities approach the technology, especially since other jurisdictions have taken a more wait-and-see approach.

That is why the enforcement priorities the AI Office sets for itself are bound to have an impact well beyond Europe's borders — not to mention the so-called "Brussels effect," the EU's capacity to set compliance standards for global companies.

There are two main schools of thought on the main risks AI regulation should address. The AI ethics tradition focuses on fundamental rights violations, such as discrimination and privacy, and the need to ensure human oversight.

Effective altruism, by contrast, emphasises so-called existential risks: the possibility that AI could cause catastrophic harm by helping build nuclear or biological weapons, enabling massive cyberattacks, or escaping human control altogether.

Recent episodes — Anthropic's Mythos-based model being pulled under US export control restrictions over concerns about its cyber capabilities, and an OpenAI AI agent hacking into an AI firm during testing — might push the Commission to focus its scarce resources solely on existential risk scenarios.

"The Commission must resist the temptation to devote its enforcement resources solely to cyber-offence and loss-of-control systemic risks," Laura Lazaro Cabrera, a director at the Center for Democracy & Technology, told Euronews.

"Enforcement should not be headline-driven, but should address the full spectrum of risks and ask whether fundamental rights and societal risks have been adequately considered," she said.

World.title: Solar car parks could cut electricity bills by €32,00 a year. Why is Europe so resistant?
World.content:
Europe’s car parks could be turned into mini solar farms to slash electricity bills and bolster decarbonisation targets – but not every country is on board. Solar power has been described as a “shining star” of Europe’s clean energy transition, which is already helping cushion the continent from the soaring costs of oil and gas amid the war on Iran. Thanks to plummeting costs and fast installation, solar has become the most competitive source of electricity in many parts of the EU. According to the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), in 2024 solar panels were on average 41 per cent cheaper than the lowest-cost fossil fuel alternatives. This has inspired a whole host of solar panel innovations beyond the traditional ground-mounted solar farms and rooftop installations. Europeans are already harnessing free electricity from their garden fences, while solar railways could soon pop up in Italy following a successful trial in Switzerland. Are solar car parks a smart idea? Car parks could be another way city infrastructure adapts to the renewables boom, and has become part of several European countries' long-term strategies. “Car parks can generate electricity without taking up additional land, which is an important consideration given the planning challenges that ground-mounted solar can encounter,” Rob Stait of Alight, one of Europe’s leading solar developers, tells Euronews Earth. “The infrastructure pairs with electric vehicle (EV) charging, making it easier and cheaper to install charge points where they’re required, which supports broader decarbonisation targets and creates a further benefit to car park users as well as the wider public.” Stait adds that solar car ports can also provide sheltered parking to help reduce vehicle cabin temperatures in summer. He says this is becoming “increasingly important” given Europe’s warming summers – which has already sweltered through a series of back-to-back heatwaves this year. France leads the way with solar car parks In 2022, France approved legislation to require all existing and new car parks with space for at least 80 vehicles to be covered by solar panels. The owners of car parks with between 80 and 400 spaces were told they had five years (until 2027) to comply with the measures, while operators of those with more than 400 had just three years (2025). At least half of the area of the larger sites must be covered by solar panels The French government said the measures could add 11 gigawatts of power to its grid, enough to power around 12 million homes. Operators ignoring the mandate risked fines of up to €40,000 a year. You get the electricity generation without the land use trade-offs, and with the added benefit of EV charging integration built in.
Rob Stait Managing Director of Alight Last year, France eased the solar mandate, allowing outdoor parking lots over 1,500 square metres to cover at least half the area with either solar panels, shade-providing trees, or a combination of both. Similar rules exist in Slovenia, where all reconstructed and new parking lots of more than 1,000 square metres are obliged to install solar panels. In Germany, new car parks in several regions, including Baden-Württemberg, North Rhine-Westphalia, Schleswig-Holstein, Rhineland-Palatinate and Lower Saxony have solar mandates depending on the number of parking spaces provided. UK U-turns on its solar car park plans Last year, the UK government launched a call to evidence to understand how to “harness the untapped potential” of solar in car parks across the country. Initial government estimates suggest that an 80-space car park could save around £28,000 (approximately €32,00) per year in electricity bills by installing solar carports and using all of the electricity generated. Companies could also recover the costs of installing solar panels in car parks by selling energy generated back to the grid. “Right now, the sun is shining on hundreds of thousands of car parking spaces across the country which could be used to power our homes and businesses,” former Energy Secretary Ed Miliband said last year. “We want to work with businesses and car park operators to turn our car parks into solar carports to save families and businesses money with clean, homegrown British energy.” The government pointed to several case studies that are already demonstrating the impact such a policy can have, including the UK’s first ever solar park and ride carport in Leeds. The system is estimated to generate 852,000 kWh per year, offsetting 471 tonnes of carbon annually, which is the equivalent of removing 203 cars from the roads. Because the park and ride can store excess energy harnessed from sunlight during the day, it provides lower cost electricity compared to buying energy from the grid. Payback for the EV charging points is estimated to be less than 10 years, based on an average of two charges per day in year one. ‘Huge missed opportunity’ However, following a call for evidence – which is used to collect data, research and expert views to shape new policies or laws – the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESZN) concluded that the policy “will not be taken any further at this point”. Euronews Earth asked DESNZ why the plans have been shelved given the potential earnings. “After careful consideration and close engagement with industry, we have decided against mandating solar panels on new car parks,” a spokesperson says. DESZN says that solar remains “central” to its clean power mission, adding that it continues to support solar panels on new buildings, including car parks, through the Future Buildings Standard scheme. Stait branded the decision a “huge missed opportunity”, telling Euronews Earth that relying on market forces rarely stacks up without policy support. “The type of debates that typically slow solar deployment – visual impact, biodiversity, land use (despite such matters being comprehensively addressed by the industry) – largely disappear when you’re building on existing infrastructure like car parks,” he adds. Stait says that France’s mandate has proven the model is “viable at scale”, arguing that there is a “strong case for the rest of Europe to follow”.

World.title: Historic sporting events in Europe worth travelling for
World.content:
It’s been a massive year for sport in 2026, with both the Winter Olympics and FIFA World Cup held over the past six months.

 

Even non-sporting fans are getting in on the sports tourism action, with people travelling to soak up the atmosphere at baseball games in Japan, ice hockey games in Canada and Muay Thai bouts in Thailand.

If you’re planning your next trip and thinking about dipping your toes in the sporting waters, why not combine it with your love of history and culture?

These historic sporting events date back centuries, and offer a fascinating glimpse into the traditions of the countries they are held in.

The famed Palio di Siena horse race takes place twice a year AP

Palio di Siena, Italy

Held twice a year on 2 July and 16 August since the 17th century, the Palio di Siena horse race takes over Siena’s main square.

The historic city is split into 17 contrade (districts), and jockeys from 10 of these take part – the seven that didn’t participate last time, and three picked at random – with horses completing three laps of the piazza.

If you’re not a fan of horse racing, schedule your visit to Siena for the day after, when residents of the winning contrade parade through the streets of the losing districts wearing outfits in their colours and sporting dummies, which are meant to symbolise rebirth.

Calcio Storico Fiorentino combines football, rugby and wrestling Lorenzo Noccioli/Creative Commons

Calcio Storico Fiorentino, Italy

Elsewhere in Italy, Florence also has its own competition – Calcio Storico Fiorentino – that splits the city into its four historic wards.

Dating back to the 16th century, the sport combines football, rugby and wrestling, with 50-minute matches held in the dirt-covered square in which teams must score in the opposing team’s net.

Unlike football, there are no substitutions for injuries, of which there have been plenty.

There are two semi-finals held early to mid-June, followed by the final on 24 June, the feast day of St. John the Baptist.

The Velká Pardubická Steeplechase is considered to be among the most difficult in the world Copyright 2005 AP. All rights reserved.

Velká Pardubická Steeplechase, Czechia

The oldest cross-country steeplechase in Europe (and considered to be among the most difficult) has been held in Pardubice annually since 1874.

Taking place on the second Sunday in October, between 15 to 20 horses and jockeys are allowed to attempt the 6,900-metre long track which has 31 obstacles, including the infamous taxis ditch.

The Velká Pardubická Steeplechase lasts between nine and 10 minutes, and there have been years where nobody has reached the finish line.

Castells are inscribed on UNESCO’s Masterpieces of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity list Copyright 2024 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

Concurs de Castells, Tarragona, Spain

Catalonia’s 18th-century human pyramid building tradition, also known as castells, is part of UNESCO’s Masterpieces of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity list.

While there are human tower shows throughout the summer on various feast days, the best known competition is the Concurs de Castells in Tarragona, held every two years.

Teams win points based on the number of levels in each tower as well as the number of people in each storey. The next event is in September, but tickets have already sold out.

Kırkpınar Oil Wrestling Festival, Edirne, Türkiye

Kırkpınar, a Turkish oil wrestling tournament, holds the Guinness World Record for being the oldest continuously sanctioned sporting competition, having first been held near Edirne in 1350.

Taking place over three days in late June, matches are won when one of the competitors gets an effective hold of the other’s kisbet, aka leather trousers, which they can demonstrate by picking their opponent up and walking three steps, or by spinning him around.

Bouts last 40 minutes, with additional time coming in at 15 minutes if there is no clear winner.

The Federal Swiss Wrestling and Alpine Festival is held every three years AP

Federal Swiss Wrestling and Alpine Festival, Switzerland

ESAF, or the Federal Swiss Wrestling and Alpine Festival, has been held every three years since 1895.

The competition includes Swiss wrestling, aka Schwingen; Hornussen, where teams attempt to strike a puck as far as possible; and the Swiss stone throwing sport of Steinstossen.

The last competition in 2025 had more than 50,000 spectators in the stands, and the festival prides itself on being the only major event that allows knives and glass bottles in the arena, as toasting and sharing cheese and bread is a key part of the watching experience. In 2028, Thun will be the host.

Knights taking part in the Sinjska Alka tournament must strike a loop with their lance L. Carević/Creative Commons

Sinjska Alka, Croatia

Ever wanted to step back in time? You can do just that at Sinjska Alka, a chivalric tournament that has taken place annually on the first weekend of August since the 18th century.

Included on UNESCO’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, the competition sees knights riding horses at full gallop along the main street while aiming their lance at an iron ring hanging on a rope.

The iron ring is split into three, with the smallest ring worth the most points. There are three races, and in its entire history, only a dozen knights have managed to hit the middle ring each time.

Highland Games, Scotland, UK

The Highland Games, which see competitors take on strength sports such as the caber toss, stone put and Scottish hammer throw, have been taking place across Scotland and countries with a large diaspora of Scots since the 19th century.

Events are held throughout spring and summer. The biggest is the Cowal Highland Gathering in Dunoon, held on the final weekend in August, while the Braemar Gathering, held on the first Saturday in September, is traditionally attended by the British royal family. You can find a full list of events on the Visit Scotland website.

World.title: Memorial Day of Sinti and Roma: The genocide Europe struggles to remember
World.content:
The opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not represent in any way the editorial position of Euronews.

Victims of persecution can be lost twice: first when their lives are taken, and then when their names are quietly mislaid by history.

 

Victims of persecution can be lost twice: first when their lives are taken, and then when their names are quietly mislaid by history.

For decades, one of the most haunting images of Nazi persecution was known simply as the “girl with the headscarf”. She was filmed looking through the closing doors of a train leaving the Westerbork transit camp and widely assumed to be Jewish. The image became famous. The girl did not. Only years later did historical research restore her identity.

Her name was Settela Steinbach. She was Sinti.

Photograph of Settela Steinbach at the exhibition ‘The Nazi Genocide of the Sinti and Roma’ – January 2008, Weimar, Germany (AP Photo / Jens Meyer) AP Photo

Settela was nine when she and her family were deported to Auschwitz-Birkenau in May 1944. She was most likely murdered there with her mother, two brothers, and two sisters on the night of 2-3 August 1944. Only the photograph survived. Her name, her identity, and the history of the people to whom she belonged almost vanished from the story attached to it.

Hundreds of thousands of Roma and Sinti people were persecuted and murdered during the Nazi era

Every year on 2nd August, Genocide of the Roma Memorial Day, Europe remembers Settela and the hundreds of thousands of Roma and Sinti people persecuted and murdered during the Nazi era. The real question is what happens on 3rd August – and every day thereafter. It is crucial not to allow a memorial day to become an annual exercise in solemn words followed by institutional amnesia.

Roma and Sinti people were subjected to racist laws, imprisonment, forced labour, deportation, mass shootings and murder across Europe – yet their genocide remains one of the least recognised chapters of Nazi persecution.

Roma and Sinti victims were denied recognition from national histories. Many survivors received neither justice nor proper acknowledgement.

That neglect did not end in 1945 – for decades, Roma and Sinti victims were denied recognition from national histories. Many survivors received neither justice nor proper acknowledgement. The prejudices that had helped make persecution possible did not obligingly disappear when the war ended.

Recognition remains patchy

Of course, some progress has been made. Some memorials have been established and research has certainly deepened. Survivors, descendants, scholars and organisations have painstakingly recovered names and histories. Indeed, it was such difficult and important work that gave the “girl with the headscarf” her name again.

But recognition remains patchy. In too many classrooms and museums, the genocide is still presented as an optional appendix to the history of the Nazi era rather than an integral part of it. Ask what happened to Roma and Sinti people under Nazi rule and the answer may still be a blank look. That silence is not the fault of young people born decades later – they cannot know what they have never been taught.

Nazi crimes did not begin with mass murder. They began with stereotypes, exclusion, paperwork, racial classification, and the steady removal of rights – the bureaucratic preliminaries to barbarism. Teaching this history shows how prejudice emerges as administrative and legal and eventually becomes lethal.

Teaching history must show Roma and Sinti as more than anonymous victims

It must also show Roma and Sinti people as more than anonymous victims. They had families, professions, communities, and ambitions. They resisted persecution and rebuilt lives afterwards. Settela was not merely the frightened child caught on film for a few seconds: she was a daughter and sister; her father was a trader and violinist. These facts restore the individuality that persecution tried to erase – they are not decorative detail.

As opportunities to hear directly from living survivors and witnesses become fewer, responsibility passes increasingly to institutions.

As opportunities to hear directly from living survivors and witnesses become fewer, responsibility passes increasingly to institutions. Because recognition came so late, many Roma and Sinti voices were never recorded in the first place, making the testimonies that remain all the more precious. We must preserve the historical record while continuing to document the experiences of those who are still able to share them. Archives must be opened, sites connected to the genocide safeguarded, photographs correctly identified, and Roma and Sinti perspectives placed at the centre of education and commemoration.

Europe’s commitment to remembrance cannot be measured only by ceremonies held on 2nd August

The International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s “Recommendations for Teaching and Learning about the Persecution and Genocide of the Roma during the Nazi Era” were developed to turn that obligation into something more useful than good intentions. Designed for governments, policymakers, teachers, museums, memorial sites, archives and civil-society educators, they provide a practical framework for why this history should be taught, what students should learn, and how it can be approached responsibly. The Recommendations help countries bring this history into mainstream education and memory culture, safeguard the historical record, counter distortion, and ensure that teaching includes Roma voices, resistance and crucially – agency. They also offer guidance on curricula, educational resources, and teacher training, while recognising national and local experiences and involving Roma communities themselves.

But our Recommendations cannot manufacture political will. They can, however, remove the excuse that nobody knows what practical action looks like. Europe’s commitment to remembrance cannot be measured only by ceremonies held on 2nd August, however moving or well attended. It must be measured by what happens in classrooms, archives, museums, and public institutions throughout the year.

Europe cannot return those who were murdered. It can at least refuse to lose them twice

The test is whether future students will still encounter silence where this history should be taught– and whether people like Settela remain merely an anonymous face in an old film, or are remembered as people with names, families, and a history.

Europe cannot return those who were murdered. It can at least refuse to lose them twice.

A career diplomat, Michaela Küchler has held a range of positions including Press Attaché in Santiago de Chile, Cultural Attaché in former Czechoslovakia, and Consul General in Chennai. She also served as a negotiator for European Union enlargement and as a European policy adviser to two Federal Chancellors and three Federal Presidents. As Chair of the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) German presidency in 2020, she spearheaded initiatives to counter distortion of the Holocaust and the genocide of the Roma.

World.title: UEFA declares to have 'lost confidence' in Infantino over 'shabby, back room, opaque deal'
World.content:
Gianni Infantino's FIFA presidency remains in crisis as football associations around the world targeted his leadership after a controversial private investment plan was dropped on Saturday.

 

“No option should be off the table,” said European soccer body UEFA just hours after FIFA announced it was withdrawing its private equity plan.

FIFA had floated the plan on Tuesday, saying it could raise up to $4.2 billion based on a valuation of $20 billion for a new commercial subsidiary, called the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), which it proposed would run events such as the World Cup and Club World Cup.

It said that, if approved, the project could provide each of FIFA's 211 member associations with a one-off payment of $20 million in early 2027, and increase their funding allocation for the 2027-2030 cycle from $8 million to $20 million.

UEFA President Aleksander Čeferin has led the fight against Infantino in a seismic week for FIFA.

In a blistering statement, UEFA declared “the current FIFA leadership has not only lost UEFA’s confidence but also that of many other members of the football family.”

“We cannot keep going on like this with secret schemes on fast-track timescales, cooked up by faceless individuals and of dubious benefit to the game," UEFA said. “We must identify those responsible and hold them to account.

“It is right that, in the coming days and weeks, UEFA will work with its associations and in close cooperation with other confederations to reflect on how this happened and devise a plan to make sure that it cannot occur again.”

UEFA said that Infantino had "failed to deliver" on promises he made when he successfully first sought election in 2016 -- namely to be "transparent" and that FIFA's money was "your (the member associations) money" and "not the money of the FIFA President".

"The shabby, back room, opaque deal he hatched and tried to force through were anything but transparent.

"And with reserves standing at over $5bn, he has also failed to use associations' money for the benefit of the game."

UEFA President Aleksander Ceferin, right, and FIFA President Gianni Infantino pose during the 48th UEFA congress in Paris, Thursday, Feb. 8, 2024. AP Photo/Christophe Ena

CONCACAF calls for 'a comprehensive reckoning with this presidency'

Later Saturday, the governing body for North and Central American and Caribbean soccer (CONCACAF) called for accountability, calling for "a comprehensive reckoning with this presidency" while slamming Infantino's "poor governance and leadership".

Infantino's plan had "advanced outside every established governance framework, without transparency, consultation or due process."

CONCACAF's statement added that FIFA leaders have “a duty of service over power. Where that duty is not upheld, accountability cannot be optional.”

It was not just continental bodies condemning the move.

English football's Football Association (FA) said there should be "a full and robust review of FIFA's leadership and governance to ensure that the global game is run transparently".

The German FA (DFB) called for a complete overhaul within FIFA.

"Together with UEFA and other confederations, we must ensure that a fundamentally different culture takes hold at FIFA — a culture where, above all, decisions are once again discussed and made by members within the governing bodies."

World.title: Ceuta trying to regain calm and return to normality 'with caution'
World.content:
Euronews is reporting from Ceuta, where authorities are working to restore order after the unprecedented influx of migrants. Along the breakwater where at least 60,000 people crossed irregularly, workers have begun installing new protective barriers in an effort to prevent another mass arrival.

 

Despite those efforts, the effects of the crisis remain visible. Euronews found migrants still wandering the streets, while authorities believe an unknown number are hiding in the homes of friends and relatives.

Speaking to Euronews, one resident recalled the moment the crowds arrived.

"Honestly, it was frightening. When that whole crowd came rushing in... yes, we were scared. We really were. Then the Armed Forces arrived—thank God—and they managed to restore some order."

The Ceuta Business Confederation says local businesses have resumed operations, albeit "with caution", after residents spent more than 24 hours sheltering in their homes. During the lockdown, most shops remained closed, leaving parts of the city facing shortages of basic goods, including fresh bread.

Among those still in the city is a young migrant who told Euronews he came in search of a better future.

"I came here to find a new life. My father, my whole family, they're poor. Now we're here, trying to survive, sleeping on the streets. Life is really hard."

He said this is not his first time in Ceuta and that he has no intention of leaving for now.

Normally, the city would now be celebrating its Patron Saint festivities in honour of the Virgin of Africa. This year, however, the celebrations have been cancelled - an extraordinary decision that underlines the scale of the crisis. While authorities are trying to restore normality, the mood in Ceuta remains one of fear, uncertainty and anger, but also compassion, as the city continues to grapple with the aftermath of one of the largest irregular border crossings in its history.

World.title: Fears of wheat price surge amid Ukraine-Russia clashes in the Black Sea
World.content:
Intensifying clashes between Ukraine and Russia in the Black Sea are threatening a crucial trade artery responsible for nearly a third of the world's wheat supply, stoking fears of soaring prices and shortages.

Advertising

Earlier in July, a Russian cruise missile struck the grain carrier Golden Leo, claiming ten lives. This marked the deadliest blow yet in a mounting campaign by both Russian and Ukrainian forces targeting cargo ships in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.

"This is a new development in recent months," claims shipping analyst Yoruk Isik, who runs the Istanbul-based Bosphorus Observer consultancy. Isik warns that cargo vessels are caught in a deadly tit-for-tat.

"Ukraine has been targeting Russian seaborne bulkers in particular, the ones transporting stolen grain from the occupied territories of Ukraine," explains Isik, "Russia retaliated and hit Ukraine's civilian port infrastructure in Odesa; a mid-sized vessel carrying corn out of Odesa was totally sunk, other vessels were damaged, and sailors died," he adds.

Turkey’s Shipowners’ Association, having logged 136 incidents involving commercial vessels in recent months, is now urging its members to avoid the Black Sea altogether.

Beyond its role as a key channel for Russian oil, the Black Sea is a lifeline for global grain exports, with Russia and Ukraine among the top suppliers.

"It is very important to note that most of Russia's agricultural commodities are exported through the Black Sea, and that almost all of Ukraine's agricultural commodities are shipped via Ukraine's ports," warns Isik.

Bad timing for harvest

Around a third of the world's wheat moves through these waters. The surge in attacks across the Black Sea and the neighbouring Sea of Azov has brought exports to a near standstill.

"No port is officially closed, but almost no shipowner wants to go there, so trade is close to zero," claims Istanbul-based international grain dealer Can Atbasoglu. "Sellers want buyers to handle the vessels, and buyers want sellers to handle the vessels, but shipowners don't want to risk it."

This deadlock arrives at the worst possible moment: harvest time. "Normally, Russian sellers would have sold all their August cargoes by now; I don't know if anybody has any sales on their books at present," says Atbasoglu.

Turkey agrees deal to clear Black Sea of mines that threaten Ukrainian exports

Wheat prices are already reacting. "The price in Romania is, say, 20-25 percent higher – that's the clearest effect we're seeing. But everybody is waiting for some kind of intervention, and soon," adds Atbasoglu.

Turkey now leads a NATO mission, along with Bulgaria and Romania, to safeguard navigation in the Black Sea. However, former Turkish ambassador and navigation rights expert Mithat Rende believes Ankara will be wary of any effort to enforce passage for commercial ships. "It's very important that the Ukrainian war should not be transformed into a regional war," cautions Rende.

"Where would it stop? Would you fire missiles and intercept Russian missiles in the Black Sea? They (Russia) already accuse all of us of fighting Russia as NATO. It's very important to avoid such operations," he adds.

Full impact yet to be felt

Rende argues Ankara’s priority is diplomacy, having played a pivotal role in brokering the 2022 United Nations-backed grain export deal after Russian forces blocked Ukrainian shipments. "Turkey maintained a dialogue with both the Russian and the Ukrainian sides at the same time," says Rende, "But is there political will for a ceasefire now? I don't see it at present."

Grain trader Atbasoglu warns the full impact of the disruption is not yet reflected in prices. "Buyers are still not fully reacting. It's seen more as an August, or at the latest a September issue, and the markets still want to believe both sides will get together and talk," he says.

However, Atbasoglu cautions that time may be running out. "In 2022, Ukraine was completely closed off, and there was a major panic. We saw the effect: wheat prices jumped 50 percent in 2022, and we could expect something similar if this continues," he concludes.

Africa and the Middle East, which are heavily reliant on Black Sea grain, are beginning to seek pricier alternatives. Europe, too, may soon feel the strain, as drought-hit wheat harvests threaten to push global food prices even higher.

World.title: No new Iran strikes for now amid deal hopes — Trump
World.content:
Skip next section Trump says no new strikes on Iran if peace deal is reached soon

08/02/2026 August 2, 2026 Trump says no new strikes on Iran if peace deal is reached soon

US President Donald Trump said Saturday that the United States and Israelhad agreed to refrain from carrying out threatened attacks on Iran under the condition that a peace deal with Tehran was reached quickly.

Trump said the US was "locked and loaded and ready to go against the Islamic Republic of Iran," but that Tehran and other Middle Eastern countries had asked him not to carry out fresh strikes.

"Based on this request, I have agreed, for the future benefit of the WORLD and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL," Trump posted on his Truth Social platform.

"The Country of Israel joins me in this commitment. Get to work, everybody, and get it DONE," he added.

His remarks come after he on Friday threatened to hit Iran "very hard," with reports saying US attacks on Iranian energy infrastructure were being considered.

According to the US media reports, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman spoke with Trump before Saturday's social media postings to express concerns over the reports of planned new attacks.

The report, which cited US sources close to the talks, said the crown prince urged Trump to de-escalate.

World.title: US: Multiple dead in shooting at In-N-Out Burger in Idaho
World.content:
Multiple people were killed in a shooting at an In-N-Out Burger restaurant in southern Idaho. The suspected shooter is dead, police said.

Multiple people were killed and others were injured after a gunman opened fire at an In-N-Out Burger restaurant in a city in the northwestern US state of Idaho.

The shooting unfolded near a busy shopping area in Twin Falls where hundreds of people were present, police chief Matthew Hicks said in a news conference.

The suspected shooter was among the dead, Hicks said. Police were still trying to determine the shooter's identity and motive.

Local media broadcast video footage from the scene showing what appeared to be a young man carrying a long gun outside the restaurant that had only been open for a week at the Twin Falls location.

Police to confirm exact number of fatalities

The shooting at the burger chain "resulted in fatalities" but authorities were still working to determine the number of victims, Hicks said.

"We are working to try to ascertain his identity and the motivations behind [the shooting] and we'll be able to figure that out in the next coming days," he said, adding that it was a "very chaotic scene."

Local public radio station KTVB reported that three people were killed and two were injured. A city spokesperson said the number of victims is expected to be higher.

Multiple people hospitalized after shooting at Idaho In-N-Out

Police said multiple people were taken to St. Luke's Magic Valley Medical Center.

Hospital spokesperson Taylor Marschner said in a statement that it was "working closely with law enforcement and emergency responders as they manage the situation."

Twin Falls, a city of about 56,000 people, is about 130 miles (205 kilometers) southeast of Boise and about 75 miles (120 kilometers) north of the Nevada border.

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

World.title: Hungary to shut sole nuclear plant for first time on Sunday
World.content:
Hungary will shut down the Paks nuclear power plant on Sunday for the first time in its 44-year history, Prime Minister Peter Magyar said.

He made the announcement on social media late Saturday night, saying the decision was taken after a further drop in the Danube's water level.

The plant, located 120 kilometers (74.5 miles) south of the capital, Budapest, uses water from the Danube to cool its reactors. It provides more than 40% of Hungary's electricity generation.

Record-low Danube levels necessitated the shutdown

The Danube has fallen to record-low levels in some areas after months of below-average rainfall and successive heat waves since May.

Hungary's water authority projected that the Danube, which flows from Germany to the Black Sea, would fall further in the coming days.

It measured the Danube's water level in Budapest at 23 centimeters (9 inches) on Wednesday morning, well below the previous record low of 33 centimeters (13 inches) set in 2018.

As a result, output at the Paks nuclear power plant had already been cut earlier in the week and some reactors shut down.

"Due to a further decline in the Danube's water level, the second-to-last generating unit at the Paks nuclear power plant will be shut down at 1:30 a.m. (2330 GMT)," the prime minister said.

"As a result, the plant is now producing only 240 megawatts (of electricity), and tomorrow (on Sunday), for the first time in 44 years, it will be completely shut down," Magyar added.

Hungary's large power users asked to cut power

The surge in imported electricity prices could cost Hungary between 120 billion and 240 billion forints ($315 million to $630 million, €273 million to €546 million), Tisza Party Vice Chairman Mark Radnai said on Facebook.

Magyar warned the Paks plant could remain offline for weeks and said his government would seek voluntary power cuts from large users, in addition to the 240 megawatts already pledged, with penalties for noncompliance.

No significant rain is in the forecast for the next few days and temperatures expected to rise to over 38 degrees Celsius (100 degrees Fahrenheit) across the region Image: Robert Nemeti/Anadolu/picture alliance

A decree would also allow grid operator MAVIR to mandate consumption cuts and temporarily disconnect large users if necessary.

"Households will be the last to face restrictions," Magyar said.

World.title: Homemade bomb goes off outside upscale Moscow restaurant state officials say
World.content:
Russian authorities said the blast occurred outside a restaurant on Kudrinskaya Square when a woman allegedly carrying explosives was stopped by a security guard.

An explosion at a restaurant in central Moscow killed at least three people, including the suspected bomber on Saturday night, authorities said.

Russia's Anti-Terrorism Committee said a woman carrying "a homemade explosive device" tried to enter the restaurant on Kudrinskaya Square but was stopped by a security guard.

The device exploded at the entrance, killing the woman, the guard and a restaurant patron.

What do we know about the explosion?

State news agency RIA Novosti reported that at least 21 other people were injured in the blast, which occurred shortly before 8 p.m. local time (5 p.m. UTC).

The restaurant's website said the venue had been closed on Saturday for a private event.

The explosion occurred at an Italian restaurant located in one of ​Moscow's seven Stalin-era skyscrapers Image: Sergei Vedyashkin/Moscow News Agency/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Heavily armed law enforcement officers sealed off the area and launched an investigation.

Authorities did not immediately identify those they believed to be behind the attack.

Russia has faced several attacks since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022. They blamed a ‌series of assassinations and attempted killings on Kyiv.

World.title: 13 killed in tourist plane crash in Peru
World.content:
The plane was taking tourists to see the Nazca Lines, a group of geoglyphs etched into the deserts of southern Peru.

A small plane carrying tourists to see Peru's famed Nazca Lines archaeological site crashed, killing all 13 people on board, authorities in Nazca province said on Saturday.

"We have information that 11 passengers and two crew members have died," said Police Major Jorge Andrade at the crash site in southern Peru.

Andrade also said that "given the severity of the accident, there are no survivors," adding that four bodies have been recovered so far.

Peru's local news site RPP reported that seven Italians, two Germans and two Spaniards were killed in the accident. There's no official confirmation about the nationalities of those aboard the plane.

The plane crashed shortly after 1:00 p.m. local time (1800 GMT) after taking off from the airport in the city of Pisco, located about 240 kilometers (150 miles) south of the capital, Lima.

What else do we know about the crash in the Peruvian desert?

​RPP reported that the small plane lost contact with the control tower minutes after takeoff.

The crash occurred in the area of Pueblo Viejo, about six kilometers from the city of Nazca and ​around 12 kilometers from the Nazca Lines site, according to local authorities.

Nazca's government said the plane was operated by local Peruvian company Aerodiana.

The airline was not immediately available for comment. However, on its website, Aerodiana says it has operated scenic flights over the Nazca lines for the last 14 years.

The reasons behind the plane crash are still unknown. Peruvian authorities said the incident is under investigation.

Tourist planes over Nazca Lines have crashed before too

Stretching across the desert near the city of Nazca, the Nazca Lines are a vast collection of geoglyphs created hundreds of years ago by Peru's Indigenous inhabitants.

The famous desert geoglyphs, many depicting animals, can only be fully appreciated from the air or elevated viewing platforms.

The latest incident is not the first plane to crash near the site in recent decades.

In 2022, a plane crash killed seven people on board, including two Chileans and three Dutch nationals.

In 2010, another fatal crash killed four British tourists and two Peruvian crew members.
