By Daniel Tilles If Mateusz Morawiecki cuts his final ties with PiS and forms a new party, it may help broaden the opposition’s appeal by offering voters a more moderate, centre-right option. While the strings have not yet been fully cut, Poland’s main opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), is splitting in two. A group of 40 MPs led by former Prime Minister (and PiS deputy leader) Mateusz Morawiecki have now formed a separate parliamentary caucus of their own, after last week refusing to sign a pledge of loyalty and quit the association they had formed – as had been demanded by PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński. Former Polish PM @MorawieckiM says 41 lawmakers aligned with him will form their own parliamentary caucus, deepening a split in conservative opposition party @pisorgpl. The proposed group would become the third-largest bloc in Poland's Sejmhttps://t.co/coOdpS7pia — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 29, 2026 The move means that Morawiecki’s caucus, known as Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), is now the third largest in parliament, while PiS, which is down to 147 MPs, has lost its status as the biggest. For now, most of Morawiecki’s followers officially remain members of the PiS party, a situation that will only change if they either resign or are thrown out following a disciplinary process that could take weeks. But unless either or both sides make major concessions, it seems only a matter of time before Development Plus becomes a separate party. A lot of international reporting has suggested that these developments will harm Poland’s right-wing opposition and boost the re-election chances of Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s more liberal coalition at next year’s parliamentary elections. In fact, PiS’s split could well help the opposition win a majority. Over the last year, PiS has found itself in an increasingly difficult position. Its support in the polls has fallen below 25%, the party’s lowest level in 14 years. Meanwhile, combined support for two far-right opposition groups – Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) – has risen to over 20%, threatening PiS’s longstanding dominance on the right. In response, Kaczyński has pushed his party in a more rightward direction, picking a hardline figure, Przemysław Czarnek, as PiS’s prime ministerial candidate in March. That signalled that PiS was aiming to compete head to head with the far right on many issues, taking tougher positions on Ukraine, the EU, migration and climate policy. In many cases, that meant disowning the legacy of the PiS government led by Morawiecki from 2017 to 2023. It also meant that the party was ceding the centre ground, something Morawiecki, who represents the more moderate, technocratic side of PiS, was particularly concerned about (alongside his own waning influence). When in power, PiS launched a revolution in Poland's energy transition. But now, in opposition, it has disowned those achievements and returned to an emphasis on coal. This could be a missed opportunity to win back centrist voters, writes @OrzelBartlomiej https://t.co/8cGvubn7N2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 29, 2026 Should Morawiecki now, as expected, launch his own centre-right party, focused on economic development, it would appeal to moderate conservatives who are opposed to the Tusk government but put off by the far right and PiS’s own hardline turn. Inevitably, some of the support for Development Plus would come at the expense of PiS – but not all of it, and possibly not even most of it. An example of something similar happening can be seen elsewhere among the opposition. Until last year, KKP was part of Confederation. However, its leader, Grzegorz Braun, was expelled after announcing a run for the presidency against Confederation’s official candidate, Sławomir Mentzen. In June 2025, KKP formed its own parliamentary caucus. Since then, support for Confederation has remained stable at around 13-14%, while KKP has risen to over 9% in the polls. So, by splitting, the two groups actually increased the size of their potential electorate, with KKP successfully appealing to an even more radical pool of voters than Confederation. It is possible that Morawiecki could do the same in the opposite direction – his new party winning over moderate conservatives while PiS continues to appeal to its most loyal supporters as well as competing with the far right. There certainly seems to be fertile ground for such a party. Regular polling by the state research agency CBOS shows that the proportion of Poles with a negative view of Tusk’s government rose to its joint-highest level this month, at 48%, while only 29% have a positive view. The last time that positive views outnumbered negative ones was in February 2024, the second full month of the current ruling coalition’s time in power. Among those who voted for Tusk and his allies in 2023, dissatisfaction is strongest among moderate conservatives. Both Tusk’s centrist KO and one of his coalition partners, The Left (Lewica), are polling only slightly below the proportion of votes they received in that year (30.7% and 8.6%, respectively). However, the most conservative part of the coalition, the centre-right Third Way (Trzecia Droga) alliance, has fallen from 14.4% of the vote in 2023 to only around 4-5% today for the two parties that constituted it, Poland 2050 (Polska 2050) and the Polish People’s Party (PSL) (which last year decided to go their separate ways). An IBRiS poll for Polsat News in April this year found that, whereas 84% of KO voters and 57.1% of Left voters have a positive view of Tusk’s government, that figure falls to 42.5% for Third Way voters, a majority of whom (51.6%) have a negative opinion. PSL and Poland 2050, the two parties that make up the Third Way alliance, have confirmed that they are splitting and will stand separately at the next elections. They will, however, remain part of @donaldtusk's ruling coalition https://t.co/NduEJY25eE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 18, 2025 Moderate conservatives’ disillusionment with the government, combined with PiS’s shift away from the centre ground, gives a clear opportunity for Morawiecki. And Tusk’s coalition itself showed in 2023 the advantages for the opposition in offering a broader set of options. While some – in KO in particular – had pushed for centrist and left-wing parties to stand jointly on a single list at that year’s elections, instead they campaigned as three main blocs. That gave voters opposed to the PiS government a genuine choice, and likely played a big part in the record turnout that helped bring Tusk’s coalition to power. It is similarly possible now that a four-branched opposition, ranging from Morawiecki on the centre right, through PiS and Confederation, to Braun on the radical right, could together win a parliamentary majority. Polls currently show those four groups with combined support of around 50% (though polling regarding support for Morawiecki’s prospective party should for now be treated with caution). Jestem dumny z tego, co wspólnie zrobiliśmy dla Polski. I wiem jedno – nasza misja wciąż trwa💪🇵🇱#RozwojPlus pic.twitter.com/xOnxKDoroS — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) July 31, 2026 However, even if they do win a majority, it is far from certain what would happen then. In 2023, the three opposition blocs were, although standing separately, clearly aligned with one another and focused on removing PiS from power. When they together won a parliamentary majority, it was absolutely clear they would form a coalition government. By contrast, today’s opposition is deeply divided. Confederation and KKP regularly attack PiS. It is not at all clear that Confederation would be willing to form a coalition government with PiS, while Kaczyński has explicitly ruled out working with the pro-Russian, anti-American Braun. Meanwhile, Morawiecki’s split has followed months of bitter infighting within PiS, which has often been carried out in public. The manner in which he and his allies are now departing the party means that relations with PiS are likely to remain difficult. The national-conservative opposition PiS party's newly named candidate for prime minister has made overtures to the far-right Confederation. But he also ruled out Grzegorz Braun, an even more radical far-right figure, serving in a PiS-led government https://t.co/i3zOZJWdUN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 9, 2026 It would therefore be hard for the opposition to form a government, even if they do win a majority. In this situation, the role of President Karol Nawrocki may be vital. Though elected with the support of PiS last year, he was technically an independent and maintained good relations with Confederation and even, to some extent, Braun (who endorsed Nawrocki after being eliminated in the first round). When Morawiecki this week announced the “ten pillars” of Development Plus’s programme, he made clear his loyalty to Nawrocki: the second of those pillars is “respect for the president”. Nie ma silnej Polski bez wielkich ambicji. Nie ma wielkich ambicji bez ludzi, którzy je zdefiniują i będą gotowi wziąć odpowiedzialność za ich realizację. Bezpieczeństwo. Rozwój. Suwerenność. Ambicja. Tożsamość. Patriotyzm. To nie hasła wyborcze, ale fundamenty państwa, które… pic.twitter.com/G0YBbfhLye — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) July 28, 2026 Many on the right hope that Nawrocki can play a role next year in helping the opposition present a more united front during the election campaign. It is also the president who decides who gets the opportunity to try to form a government after the elections. That role would be of particular significance if, as is very possible, Tusk’s KO emerges as the biggest individual party but the opposition together may be able to form a parliamentary majority. Given that we are still over 14 months away from the elections, and Morawiecki has not even yet officially split from PiS, it is still far too early to make confident predictions. However, while Morawiecki’s likely departure is clearly a personal blow to Kaczyński – and a sign of the 77-year-old’s waning influence over not only the Polish right but even his own party – it may conversely provide a boost to the opposition as a whole. World.title: Poland bans use of smartphones by children in primary schools and kindergartens

Poland has banned children from using smartphones and other electronic devices in primary schools and kindergartens in a bid to improve their wellbeing and safety. The new legislation, signed into law by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki on Thursday, will take effect at the start of the school year on 1 September, but schools will have until the end of 2026 to adjust. Prezydent podpisał nowelizację, która zakazuje korzystania z telefonów komórkowych w przedszkolach i szkołach. (PAP)#PAPInformacje pic.twitter.com/CK7YFU7sru — Polska Agencja Prasowa/Polish Press Agency (PAP) (@PAPinformacje) July 30, 2026 Under the new rules, pupils in primary schools and kindergartens will be prohibited from using smartphones and other electronic devices allowing communication or audio and video recording for the entire school day, including breaks and lessons held outside of school grounds. Schools will be allowed, but not required, to create designated places where pupils’ devices can be stored in a safe way and with respect for their privacy. The law, however, allows for some exceptions. When pupils need a device because of illness, disability or other special needs, school headteachers can permit their use. Phones could also be used in emergencies where there is a direct threat to life, health or property. Furthermore, pupils will be permitted to use mobile phones if a teacher deems them necessary for educational purposes and gives approval. The law also allows secondary schools to introduce bans on smartphone use if they choose, but does not make this compulsory, with such schools retaining autonomy to set their own rules through their statutes. The draft law banning phones from primary schools was first approved by the government in June. It then went to the Sejm, the lower and more powerful chamber of Poland’s parliament, which introduced amendments, including extending the measures to kindergartens. The Sejm then approved the bill in a rare near-unanimous vote, with only some MPs from the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) voting against it. Subsequently, the Senate passed the bill without amendments, sending it to Nawrocki, who could have signed it, vetoed it, or sent it to Poland’s constitutional court for review. Poland’s government has approved a ban on mobile phones in primary schools as well as tougher age-verification requirements for online pornography. Both measures still require parliamentary and presidential approval before becoming law https://t.co/y4Ycf46FQD — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 2, 2026 The president ultimately decided to sign the law, with his office noting that the measures aim to “create safer learning conditions” and support the “healthy and responsible” use of digital technologies by pupils. Poland’s education minister Barbara Nowacka said last month that the law would “improve teachers’ power, autonomy and agency, as well as order and digital wellbeing in schools”. She added that, although many schools already have such bans in place, teachers had asked for legal backing to help enforce them. For more on the measures, see our earlier report from when the bill was approved almost unanimously by parliament, with only the far right voting against it https://t.co/9Mx0SfkE5V — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 According to a survey conducted in April by the Polish state research institute CBOS for the Polish Press Agency (PAP), 85% of Poles support a ban on the use of smartphones in primary schools. Poland has been recently stepping up efforts to protect young people from various digital threats. The topic has been a rare area of consensus between the government and Nawrocki, who has vetoed a record number of bills. Earlier this month, Nawrocki signed a law banning online content depicting illegal acts or other forms of abusive and degrading behaviour – known in Polish as “patostreaming”. Another measure approved by the government that is now being considered by parliament is the introduction of stricter age-verification requirements for accessing online pornography. In January, the digital affairs ministry also announced that it hoped to introduce measures blocking children from access to social media. Poland hopes this year to introduce measures preventing children from accessing social media, says the country's digital affairs ministry. It is working on tools that would require platforms to verify the age of users https://t.co/G7qeEl2q9x — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 5, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Russian missile that crashed in Poland carried “significant amount” of explosive material

Polish authorities have confirmed that the object that violated Polish airspace and crashed in eastern Poland was a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile carrying a significant explosive payload. The missile entered Poland during a period of intensive overnight Russian attacks on Ukraine, travelling around 100 km over Polish territory before exploding in a field in the Lublin region on Thursday morning. Nie miejmy żadnych złudzeń. Tego typu sytuacje albo tego typu prowokacje będą się zdarzać – powiedział wiceminister obrony Cezary Tomczyk w @faktypofaktach, komentując wybuch rakiety na Lubelszczyźnie.https://t.co/IKxuGNwe05 — tvn24 (@tvn24) July 30, 2026 “We can confidently confirm that it was a Russian Kh-101 missile, a cruise missile capable of carrying even nuclear warheads, which exploded on impact,” deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk told broadcaster TVN24 late on Thursday. The object was “a potentially very dangerous missile,” Tomczyk added. Asked whether the incident could have been a deliberate move by Moscow, he said that no possibilities could be ruled out. “We don’t know, and if we do find out, it will mainly be through intelligence. I’m sure the coming weeks will provide us with more answers,” the deputy minister said. Tomczyk said Poland was working closely with Ukraine, adding that 20 of the roughly 70 missiles fired by Russia overnight from Wednesday to Thursday were at one point heading towards Poland. “It is also worth noting that the vast majority of these missiles were shot down by Ukraine over Ukrainian territory, which clearly bore the full brunt of the attack,” he said. He added that a Ukrainian pilot had tracked the missile that later fell on Polish territory but was unable to intercept it. “He turned back 20 seconds before reaching the border,” Tomczyk said, adding that the pilot “could not have flown into” Polish airspace. An object crashed into a field 100 km from Poland’s border with Ukraine overnight after a major Russian attack. Ukrainian officials said it was a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile, while Poland reported an "extremely difficult night for our air defence"https://t.co/QIpRQfej5S — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 30, 2026 Prosecutors who concluded their work at the site on Thursday said the missile contained a “significant amount of explosive material”. Investigators collected fragments and soil samples from the impact site, where the explosion left a crater around 10 metres wide and 5 metres deep. “The crater has been filled and the site handed back to its owner. The Territorial Defence Force combed through an area of approximately 3 km² and found numerous rocket debris, including propulsion components,” the Lublin prosecutor’s office said. Prokuratorzy właśnie zakończyli swoje czynności na miejscu zdarzenia. Lej został zasypany, a teren przekazany właścicielowi. WOT przeczesał teren o powierzchni ok 3 km2 znajdując liczne szczątki rakiety w tym elementy napędu. — Prokuratura Okręgowa w Lublinie (@Prok_Okreg_Lub) July 30, 2026 The incident came amid a political dispute in Poland over its air-defence capabilities. Earlier this month, the government confirmed it had transferred PAC-3 missiles for Patriot systems to Ukraine, prompting opposition criticism that the move had weakened Poland’s defences. Following the latest incident, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the government would, paradoxically, consider providing Ukraine with further military aid, including additional Patriot air-defence systems if necessary. “Our intention is to ensure that Ukraine does not lose this war,” Tusk said. The Polish government has confirmed that it has transferred Patriot missiles to Ukraine following opposition criticism It also released a list of all military donations to Ukraine since 2022, showing that the former PiS government gave much more equipment https://t.co/8BmDy5BjiB — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 7, 2026 The incident also prompted reactions from NATO allies and other world leaders. The US ambassador to Poland, Thomas Rose, said that Washington was in close contact with Polish authorities and NATO allies following the incident. “Any breach of a NATO ally’s territory is a matter we take extremely seriously,” Rose wrote on X. “We are coordinating closely with Polish authorities as the investigation proceeds and remain committed to defending Allied territory and upholding NATO’s collective security.” We are in constant contact with the Government of Poland —including @KosiniakKamysz @sikorskiradek @marcin_przydacz @CTomczyk and @POTUS @usambnato Matt Whitaker following this morning’s violation of Polish airspace by a Russian fired projectile that impacted deep inside Polish… — Ambassador Tom Rose (@USAmbPoland) July 30, 2026 NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte called the incident “yet another reckless act by Russia and a dangerous consequence of its war against Ukraine”. He said that NATO would continue to strengthen its readiness to defend against all threats. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz condemned the the attacks on Ukraine, saying that the violation of Polish airspace that accompanied them demonstrated “Russian ruthlessness and readiness to escalate”. Johann Wadephul, Germany’s foreign minister, said the violations of Polish and Romanian airspace showed that Russia remained “the greatest threat to our security”. He reaffirmed Berlin’s support for Ukraine, as well as European Union and NATO allies. Wir verurteilen die massiven russischen Angriffe auf die Ukraine scharf. Viele Zivilisten mussten wieder ihr Leben lassen. Und der Einschlag in Polen zeugt auch von russischer Rücksichtslosigkeit und Eskalationsbereitschaft. Wir stehen unverbrüchlich an der Seite unserer Partner. — Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz (@bundeskanzler) July 30, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland to deport foreigner who performed Nazi salute at Auschwitz Museum
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland will deport a Colombian citizen who performed a Nazi salute during his visit to the former German-Nazi death camp of Auschwitz-Birkenau. He is banned from re-entering Poland and the Schengen area for five years. The 34-year-old was charged with promoting Nazism, an offence carrying a maximum sentence of three years in prison, and desecration of a memorial site. “A place that symbolises one of the greatest tragedies in human history requires special respect, and insulting it does not go without consequences,” said the border guard. @PolskaPolicja zatrzymała ob. Kolumbii 🇨🇴, który na terenie Muzeum Auschwitz-Birkenau propagował nazizm i znieważył miejsce pamięci. Komendant #PlacówkaSGwKrakowie wydał wobec cudzoziemca decyzję o zobowiązaniu do powrotu oraz 5-letni zakaz wjazdu do 🇵🇱 i państw strefy Schengen. pic.twitter.com/kzfw1Kzw8w — Straż Graniczna (@Straz_Graniczna) July 30, 2026 Police in Oświęcim, the town where the museum is located, said in mid-July that they had detained a man after being notified by museum guards of a possible offence. A police probe found that the man, who had been living and working in the Wielkopolska province, had “posed for a photo making the Nazi salute” at the museum while visiting it. Prosecutors were informed of the case, police said, adding that the man was subsequently charged with two crimes: public promotion of Nazism and the desecration of a memorial site. He admitted to the offences and voluntarily submitted to his punishment, which consisted of a 2,000 zloty (€464) fine along with a decision for his verdict to be made public, they added. He was then handed over to Poland’s border guard, which decided to deport him and ban him from entering Poland and other Schengen countries for five years. The border guard said that the decision was “immediately enforceable”, and was based on “considerations of security and public order as well as the interests of the Republic of Poland.” It also noted that a court decided to place the man in a facility for foreigners in the city of Przemyśl, where he will await deportation. Polish prosecutors have indicted an Iranian-born German citizen for making statements denying the Holocaust during a tour of Auschwitz, which he then published in an online video Denying Nazi crimes carries a prison sentence of up to three years in Poland https://t.co/WCSm7O4gAx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 4, 2026 The Auschwitz Museum has in recent years dealt with various cases of visitors misbehaving, including in ways that are punishable by law. Earlier this month, prosecutors in Poland indicted an Iranian-born German citizen for making statements denying the Holocaust during a tour of Auschwitz. In 2025, an Israeli teenager who was seen doing a fascist salute at the former German-Nazi camp was fined for propagating Nazism. Auschwitz was first set up by Nazi Germany in occupied Poland in 1940 during World War Two as a camp to house Polish “political” prisoners, before later becoming primarily a site for the murder of Jews. At least 1.3 million victims were transported there, with at least 1.1 million of them killed at the camp. Around one million of those victims were Jews. The second largest group of victims – around 70,000 people – were ethnic Poles. On the 80th anniversary of the liberation of Auschwitz, we look at the extraordinary story of Anna Odi, who has lived her entire life in the grounds of the former concentration camp as the daughter of survivors who helped establish the @AuschwitzMuseum https://t.co/d2enYJRjMk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 27, 2025 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland appoints new official to promote country’s brand internationally

Poland’s government has appointed a marketing and branding expert to develop a unified strategy for promoting the country abroad, saying the move will help boost tourism, support Polish products and attract foreign investment. Barbara Mróz-Gorgoń, a professor at Wrocław University of Economics, noted that her appointment signals “a shift” from simple promotional activities to “managing the reputation of our great country”. The move comes as Poland seeks to capitalise on its economic success, including growth in tourism and continued investments. But the government says that current promotion efforts lack a single strategy and are fragmented. Czas na markę Polska! Witamy na pokładzie prof. Barbarę Mróz – Gorgoń 🇵🇱 pic.twitter.com/PPX2eWTRSm — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 29, 2026 Last year, Poland’s sport and tourism ministry appointed Mróz-Gorgoń, who also advises companies and institutions on branding strategy and founded a think tank dedicated to promoting Poland, to an interministerial team tasked with developing a comprehensive new branding strategy for Poland. The government said, however, that efforts to promote Poland were so far fragmented and lacked a single strategy, which is why it created the post of commissioner for promotion of the Poland brand. As the first specialist to take the position, Mróz-Gorgoń will be tasked with preparing a strategy to build a national brand and help implement it, coordinate activities to help grow tourism, support investments, and improve Poland’s position on the world stage. “We will create one programme resulting in the joint promotion of our country’s brand,” said Tusk. According to the government, this will come at no further cost, but ensure that existing funds will be spent in a more “coherent and effective way”. Mróz-Gorgoń, meanwhile, noted that “the Poland brand is not the property of the government. It is created by entrepreneurs, artists, athletes, local governments and millions of Poles at home and abroad”. Developing this brand “means more investment, recognition of our brands and products abroad, and it also provides greater strength in international relations,” she continued. Poland saw the EU's second-fastest growth in tourism in 2025, behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta https://t.co/WVkRbHtU7o — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 19, 2026 Poland has been one of the world’s fastest-growing economies in recent decades. The growth has coincided with the international expansion of its firms, more foreign investments, and a rapidly expanding tourism sector. Last year, the sport and tourism ministry announced that it wants tourism to contribute 9% of GDP annually within a decade, from about 5% now, and for Poland to become a leader in the sector in central and eastern Europe. Foreign direct investment in Poland grew from just under 15.5 billion zloty in 2003, a year before the country joined the European Union, to around 61.3 billion zloty last year, according to figures from the National Bank of Poland (NBP). Various state and private companies – such as delivery giant InPost, insurer PZU, and train manufacturer Pesa – are establishing themselves abroad by buying some of their rivals. The international success of some Polish athletes – including football player Robert Lewandowski and tennis star Iga Świątek – has also helped improve Poland’s visibility. With its historic cities, natural landscapes and growing culinary scene, Poland is hoping to boost the role of tourism in its booming economy, writes Olivier Sorgho The government wants tourism to contribute 9% of GDP within a decade, up from 4% now https://t.co/3wfyIkZMHm — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 2, 2025 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: PM Tusk says Russian Kh-101 missile likely crashed in eastern Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. This is a breaking news story and may be updated as events unfold. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Thursday that Polish airspace had been violated during a massive missile attack by Russia on western Ukraine overnight, adding that there were no casualties or immediate threat to civilians. A suspected Russian Kh-101 cruise missile crashed in eastern Poland, around 100 km from the Ukrainian border, prompting the deployment of police counter-terrorism officers and other security services to the site. The fall of the object, which is reported to have caused a powerful explosion, left a crater about 10 metres wide and scattered fragments in a field between Tarnawa-Kolonia and Tokary in Lublin province, about 2 km from the nearest buildings, according to local police. TYLKO U NAS! Wybuch i ogromny krater na #Lubelszczyźnie. Mamy zdjęcia! >> https://t.co/BrX7XneP7F Fot. Radio ESKA pic.twitter.com/BgzlhpSVag — ESKA (@eska_pl) July 30, 2026 Lublin prosecutor Grzegorz Trusiewicz told reporters at the site of the incident that the crater was about 5 metres deep and that fragments had been scattered across an area of roughly 200 metres. Ukraine has offered Poland assistance in investigating the scene, he added. Earlier in the morning, Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command (DORSZ) said that air defence radars had detected at least a dozen missiles over western Ukraine overnight whose trajectories could have posed a potential threat to Polish airspace. An unidentified object was detected in Polish airspace at 3:40 a.m. travelling westward, DORSZ said. An F-16 fighter jet was dispatched to identify and intercept it. At 3:46 a.m., before the object could be clearly identified, it disappeared from the radar. An Mi-24 helicopter was then sent to the area of the last radar detection to verify the indications. Its crew located what was believed to be the crash site. W trakcie rosyjskiego zmasowanego ataku rakietowego na zachodnią Ukrainę doszło do naruszenia polskiej przestrzeni powietrznej. Zwołałem w związku z tym zespół koordynacyjny z udziałem Ministra Obrony i odpowiednich służb, które od wielu godzin pracują na miejscu zdarzenia i… — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 30, 2026 Tusk said the initial information suggested the object was likely a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile, echoing earlier comments made by Ukraine’s acting foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, but stressed that investigators would need to establish the precise type and origin of the object. “We will want to be 100% certain: what kind of missile, who launched it, whether it was the explosion of the payload or the impact of the missile itself that caused this crater,” he said at a press conference in Lublin. The prime minister added that Polish forces had been prepared to shoot down the object had it continued flying in a way that posed a threat. Tusk added that another missile approached the Polish border but did not enter Polish airspace. “This initial information clearly indicates that the relevant services, the military, our pilots, and our aircraft acted very quickly and efficiently. There was no immediate threat due to the missile falling in an undeveloped area,” Tusk said. He added that he had discussed the incident with opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki. Niezwykle ciężka noc dla naszej obrony powietrznej, systemów obserwacji i wykrywania zagrożeń. Dziękuję gen. I. Nowakowi i @DowOperSZ, wszystkim, którzy dziś koordynowali, obserwowali, analizowali i reagowali na wydarzenia nad Ukrainą i w naszej przestrzeni powietrznej.… https://t.co/RssjKTKAec — Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) July 30, 2026 This morning, Polish defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz described the night as “extremely difficult for our air defence, surveillance and threat detection systems”. Later, speaking alongside Tusk, he said Polish F-16 fighter jets had been operating near the Polish-Ukrainian border since about 2 a.m. “In addition, reconnaissance aircraft operating over Polish airspace and allied aircraft for aerial refuelling, which took off from Germany, have been activated,” he said. An early warning system was activated in Lublin and several other areas of the province because of Russian air attacks on Ukraine. The alarm lasted about 13 minutes, according to the interior minister. The opposition criticised the authorities for not providing residents with further information about the reason for the alarm. “A few minutes of alarm, no information in the mainstream media about what was happening, some residents didn’t even hear the sirens, and no text messages with an alert from the Government Centre for Security (RCB),” wrote Michał Dworczyk, a Law and Justice (PiS) MP, on social media. Digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski defended the decision to sound the alarm. “If it hadn’t been for that alarm, if those sirens hadn’t gone off, and if the object hadn’t landed in a field but instead in a block of flats, a house or any other place where it could have caused injury or, God forbid, death,” he told Polsat News. Polish airspace has been violated several times in recent years by objects entering from the direction of Ukraine amid the war there. In September last year, an estimated 20 Russian military drones were recorded repeatedly violating Polish airspace. In 2022, a stray missile struck the Polish village of Przewodów, killing two people. Poland has signed an agreement for a new anti-drone system that it claims will be the first of its kind in Europe. World.title: Record number of Poles opposed to Ukraine’s EU membership
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. Support for Ukraine joining the European Union has fallen sharply in Poland, with opposition reaching a record high of 40%, a survey carried out by the Polish state research agency CBOS shows. The figures show that 50% of Poles still support Ukraine’s EU membership, but that is a significant decline from 74% in October 2023, when the question was last asked, and from a record 90% in March 2022, shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The shift comes as public sentiment towards Ukrainians in general in Poland has deteriorated in recent years. The latest CBOS poll shows that, among those who support Ukraine’s EU accession, most favour a gradual process, with 41% of all respondents saying Ukraine should join the EU but “without undue haste”. “Only 9% of respondents currently support Ukraine’s earliest possible EU membership, which is the lowest figure in the history of these surveys,” CBOS reported. Meanwhile, opposition to Ukraine’s EU membership has increased by 23 percentage points since October 2023, reaching its highest level in the history of CBOS surveys. People with right-wing political beliefs are most likely to be opposed to Ukraine’s accession (53%), while the age group with the highest percentage of people opposed is those aged 18-24 (58%). The survey also found that a majority of Poles expect the war in Ukraine to end with territorial concessions from Kyiv – 55% of respondents said they believed Ukraine would lose some territory, a view that has remained dominant since December 2024. Compared with the previous survey, however, pessimism has eased. The proportion of respondents who expect Ukraine to lose part of its territory fell by 8 percentage points, while the number expecting Russia to take control of the entire country declined from 8% to 6%. On Western support for Ukraine, 39% of respondents said the military, financial and humanitarian assistance provided by countries in the West was sufficient. Meanwhile, 27% said aid was excessive, while 22% said it was insufficient. Russia has published purported archival documents relating to massacres of Poles by Ukrainians in WWII. Kyiv had warned that Russia was planning to release the files in order to stir tensions, while Polish media note that the material contains nothing new https://t.co/CI0cfAlDle — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 6, 2026 Ukrainians are Poland’s largest foreign national group, with almost 1.6 million living in the country, but recent polls have shown growing hostility towards them, fuelled in part by anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from far-right parties and a tougher stance towards Kyiv from some opposition politicians. In its annual survey of attitudes towards national and ethnic groups, CBOS found earlier this year that the proportion of Poles who said they disliked Ukrainians increased by five percentage points this year, the largest rise recorded among all groups surveyed, reaching 43%. Tensions between the two countries have also been heightened by disputes over historical issues and a series of recent incidents targeting Ukrainians in Poland. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show. The figures come following recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are Poland's largest immigrant group https://t.co/pcTsJddDz7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians rose by 30% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, according to newly reported police data. Last weekend, three men were filmed violently attacking a Ukrainian woman and her partner outside a shop in Wrocław, apparently because of her accent. Two of the assailants have since been detained by police, while their victims required treatment in hospital. In response, Prime Minister Donald Tusk called for Poles to “wage war on violence”, saying that the perpetrators of such acts “have become emboldened precisely because they now have political role models, political patrons, and political support”. World.title: Spaniard Santi Denia Named Coach of the Czech Republic National Team
World.content:
Spanish coach Santi Denia took over the Czech Republic national team on Friday to become the first foreigner in the post.

The Czech soccer association said the 52-year-old signed a two-year contract with an option to be extended by another two years.

Czech football association head David Trunda introduced Denia at a news conference in Prague.

“We greatly appreciate that an expert with such a credit and immense experience at the international level is joining the Czech national team,” Trunda said.



“I’m happy to be here and I’m extremely motivated, because I consider it a great opportunity to lead the Czech national team,” Denia said. “Czech football has a magnificent history and I honestly regard it as a great honor to be here.”

Denia replaced Miroslav Koubek who resigned after the team’s early exit from the World Cup.

Denia was a center-back in Atletico Madrid (1994-2005) and has two games on the national team to his credit.

As coach, he led Spain to gold at the 2024 Paris Olympics. He also claimed the European titles with Spain´s under-17 (2017) and under-19 teams (2019).

He was most recently in charge of Al-Shahania, a club in Qatar.

His first major task in the post will be to face tough opponents in League A of the Nations League. The Czechs open the competition by hosting Croatia on Sept. 26 in a group which also includes England and World Cup champions Spain.

World.title: Czech PM Calls for Closing Schengen to Spain due to Migration Crisis in Ceuta
World.content:
Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš called for temporarily excluding Spain from Schengen due to the migration crisis in Ceuta, where about 49,000 migrants entered uncontrollably from Morocco.

Italy has already suspended Schengen rules in connection with Spain.

Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš called for closing the Schengen zone to Spain after a sharp escalation of the migration crisis in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta.

According to Babiš, the situation in Ceuta is “absolutely scandalous,” and the cause of the crisis was the overly lenient migration policy of the Spanish authorities.



According to the publication, since Thursday, about 49,000 migrants have entered Ceuta uncontrollably from the territory of Morocco. At least 19 people have died trying to cross the maritime border.

Foreign Minister Petr Macinka (Motorists) described the situation as a serious challenge for the entire Schengen Area but stopped short of calling for Spain’s exclusion, saying he wanted to hear Madrid’s position before drawing conclusions.

What is the Schengen Agreement?

The Schengen Area allows people to travel between 29 European countries without routine passport checks at internal borders.

While border controls are normally abolished, member states can temporarily reinstate them if they believe there is a serious threat to public order or internal security.

Italy does not share a land border with Spain, so the decision to reintroduce border controls for a month will impact people travelling by plane or boat between the two countries.

Where is Ceuta?

Ceuta is an autonomous Spanish city on the northern coast of Africa that borders Morocco.

Spain also controls the nearby city of Melilla. Together, the two enclaves form the European Union’s only land borders with Africa.

Roughly the size of inner Sydney, Ceuta has a population of just over 83,000, according to Spain’s Instituto Nacional de Estadistica. It is home to Christian and Muslim communities, including Spanish and Moroccan residents and cross-border workers.

World.title: Prague’s Online Heat Map Shows Where to Find Water and Shade
World.content:
As another spell of extreme summer heat approaches the Czech Republic, Prague has published an online map showing where residents can cool down, find drinking water or spend time near water.

Temperatures in the capital could reach 38°C, with the hottest conditions expected toward the end of the week.

This map is designed to help people find relief across the city and includes public drinking fountains, misting systems, fountains, wells and locations suitable for swimming or relaxing beside the water.

The project was prepared by the City of Prague in cooperation with the Prague Institute of Planning and Development (IPR Prague) and the municipal technology company Operátor ICT.



The initiative is part of the city’s broader efforts to prepare for more frequent periods of extreme heat. Prague says it is increasingly focusing on measures that can reduce the effects of rising temperatures over the longer term, rather than relying only on temporary interventions.

More trees, water and shade planned

Prague is also looking to incorporate more greenery and water into public spaces as part of new development projects.

The city is supporting measures including new fountains and other water features, green roofs, rainwater collection tanks, climbing plants, permeable surfaces and additional tree planting. The expansion of parks is also among the measures being considered.

Temperatures could approach 40°C

The current heatwave is expected to reach its peak on Friday, when temperatures could climb as high as 39°C in parts of the Czech Republic.

Friday night could also remain exceptionally warm, with overnight temperatures staying above 20°C in some areas.

A temporary change is expected on Saturday, particularly in parts of the country where showers and thunderstorms could bring some relief. The cooler conditions, however, are not expected to last.

At the beginning of next week, temperatures are forecast to rise again, with daytime highs between 32°C and 37°C.

World.title: Canadian International High School in Prague: Your Pathway to Top Universities Worldwide
World.content:
Earning an internationally recognized high school diploma and preparing for admission to top universities no longer requires moving abroad.

Canadian International High School in Prague (CIHS) offers students in Grades 10-12 a fully English-language education based on the Canadian curriculum.

Located in the heart of Prague, CIHS combines the strengths of Canada’s education system with the quality of life and accessibility of the Czech Republic. Students receive a globally recognized diploma while studying in a familiar European environment, avoiding the higher costs and challenges of relocating overseas.

An International Diploma Recognized Worldwide

Graduates earn the Ontario Secondary School Diploma (OSSD), Canada’s official high school credential, recognized in more than 20 countries. The diploma provides access to over 30,000 universities and colleges worldwide, including leading institutions across Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Europe.

Unlike the Czech education system, which typically spans 13 years, the Canadian program is completed in 12. As a result, students graduate a year earlier, begin university sooner, and gain an additional advantage as they build their academic and professional future.

Learning the Canadian Way

CIHS delivers its academic program in partnership with Toronto Imperial School, ensuring that students follow authentic Canadian educational standards. Courses are taught using modern curricula, teaching methods, and learning resources aligned with those used in Ontario schools.

English is the language of instruction across all subjects. An international faculty, including teachers from Canada, creates an immersive English-speaking environment that helps students strengthen their academic language skills and confidently transition into universities abroad.

To maintain high academic standards, all teachers undergo a rigorous selection process followed by professional training led by Canadian educators and the school’s academic partners.

Outstanding Value

Tuition is, on average, two to three times lower than at many international schools in Prague while offering an extensive range of included benefits.

Tuition covers:

the Ontario Secondary School Diploma (OSSD)

an iPad for both academic and personal use

for both academic and personal use a complete school uniform

an annual gym membership

continuous academic guidance and support

and support educational trips to the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Switzerland, and Germany

to the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Switzerland, and Germany participation in the Exchange program in the United States.

International Experience Beyond the Classroom

Education at CIHS extends well beyond the classroom. Each semester, students have the opportunity to join educational trips to Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Switzerland, and other destinations. These experiences include university campus visits, meetings with admissions representatives, and valuable insight into international higher education systems.

Students may also participate in the Exchange USA program, spending one or two semesters at one of 40 partner high schools across the United States. The program offers full immersion in American school life while strengthening English proficiency and developing valuable intercultural experience.

For students planning to continue their education in the U.S., CIHS also offers the opportunity to transfer to an American high school during Grade 12 on an F-1 student visa, complete their final year there, and graduate with a U.S. high school diploma.

A Modern Campus in Central Prague

The school is located in Holešovice, one of Prague’s fastest-growing and most vibrant districts. Its central location makes the campus easily accessible from virtually any part of the city by public transportation, while convenient parking is available for families.

The campus occupies a modern business complex close to parks and the Vltava riverfront, providing an ideal balance between study and recreation. Students also benefit from an on-site cafeteria and access to medical professionals, including general practitioners, dermatologists, immunologists, and allergists. Sports facilities, swimming pools, cafés, and shops are all within walking distance.

Personalized University Preparation

Beginning after Grade 10, students choose one of two academic pathways: Business & Social Science or Engineering, allowing them to focus on subjects aligned with their future university studies.

Throughout the program, experienced teachers and academic advisors provide personalized guidance, helping students develop essential academic skills, explore career options, and build competitive university applications.

Graduate Outcomes

By the time they graduate, CIHS students have gained far more than a high school diploma. They leave with:

the internationally recognized Ontario Secondary School Diploma

strong academic English proficiency

experience studying in an international environment

university admissions guidance

a global network of peers

participation in international educational programs

access to leading universities across Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, Europe, and beyond.

Canadian International High School in Prague welcomes prospective students and their families to visit the campus, meet the faculty, and learn more about its Canadian curriculum.

It’s an opportunity to experience a truly international education and earn a globally recognized diploma – while staying in the heart of Europe.

World.title: Prague Pride Strengthens Security Measures Following Berlin Attack
World.content:
Security will be tightened at this year’s Prague Pride festival following a deadly attack at a similar event in Berlin.

Czech police are preparing additional measures to protect participants in the week-long festival, which begins Monday.

The measures will also reflect changes to this year’s festival route and venue.

Prague Pride is moving its main festival area from Letná Plain to Štvanice Island. The traditional Saturday parade will also follow a new route, starting in the lower section of Wenceslas Square, continuing through the historic center and ending at Štvanice.



Organizers will begin the parade with a minute of silence on Wenceslas Square to remember the person killed in the Berlin attack.

“Thousands of people standing in silence will be a reminder that we will definitely not remain silent about violence motivated by prejudice,” Prague Pride director Kamila Fröhlichová said.

This year’s Prague Pride will feature more than 100 cultural, educational and social events. Dozens of associations, institutions, companies and individuals will organize programs at venues across the capital.

While many events will focus on the lives and experiences of LGBTQ+ people, the festival will also address wider questions surrounding human rights and civil society. A full program is available on the Prague Pride website.

Prague Pride was first held in August 2011. Its inaugural edition was met with strong opposition from conservative groups and politicians, who described the parade as obscene and accused its organizers of promoting what they called an “ideology of homosexuality.”

Then-President Václav Klaus was among the most prominent critics, arguing that society needed to oppose what he described as the spread of homosexuality.

Protests continued in subsequent years but gradually declined in size and intensity.

World.title: Prague Opens Air-Conditioned Space in City Centre to Help Beat Heat Wave
World.content:
People looking for relief from the heat in central Prague can use the air-conditioned ground floor of the Škoda Palace in Jungmannova Street on Thursday and Friday.

The city has opened the space to the public as temperatures across the Czech Republic are expected to rise well above 30°C. The building will be accessible from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. on both days.

Visitors can sit on benches and chairs, refill their water bottles at drinking fountains and use the toilets. Drinks and snacks are also available for purchase.



The measure comes as the Czech Hydrometeorological Institute has warned of very high temperatures in parts of the country. Forecasters are advising people to drink regularly, stay out of direct sunlight where possible and avoid strenuous physical activity, particularly during the afternoon.

The Czech Republic is facing several days of intense heat, with Friday expected to be among the hottest day of the current spell. Temperatures above 35°C are possible in some areas.

Individual Prague districts are taking similar steps. Prague 3, for example, plans to make air-conditioned areas in its town hall, information centre and Žižkostel available to the public when temperatures are forecast to exceed 35°C. Visitors will be able to sit down, drink water and take a break from the heat.

The city says the cooling spaces are intended to provide temporary relief during the hottest periods, particularly for people who may struggle to cope with high temperatures.

World.title: Revolut Opens Private Market Funds to Czech Investors
World.content:
Revolut is expanding its investment services in the Czech Republic, giving retail customers access to funds focused on private equity, private credit and infrastructure.

The new products will become available in the Revolut app from July 31. The fintech has signed distribution agreements with four major asset managers — Apollo, Ares, Hamilton Lane and Partners Group — which collectively manage more than $2.8 trillion in assets.

The move gives Czech retail investors access to parts of the private markets that have traditionally been aimed largely at institutional investors.



Private market investments have often required substantial minimum commitments, frequently above €100,000, or around CZK 2.5 million. Revolut’s new offering is designed to lower that barrier and allow customers to add private assets to portfolios that may already include stocks, bonds and exchange-traded funds.

Investments will be available directly through the Revolut app.

The funds will be offered through the European Long-Term Investment Fund framework, known as ELTIF 2.0.

How ELTIF 2.0 works

The structure is intended to provide investors with greater flexibility than traditional private equity funds, where capital can remain committed for several years and withdrawals may not be possible during that period.

The products offered through Revolut use an “evergreen” structure. This allows investors to put money into funds with existing portfolios rather than waiting for a traditional investment cycle to begin.

ELTIF 2.0 also provides scheduled liquidity windows during which investors can request the redemption of their holdings, subject to the conditions of the individual fund.

That does not mean the investments are as liquid as publicly traded shares. Private market assets remain difficult to sell quickly, and investors should expect to hold their money for the long term.

Revolut already offers Czech customers access to a range of traditional investments, including US and European stocks, ETFs, bonds and commodities. The addition of private market funds expands the investment options available through the same app.

World.title: From Old Town to Main Station: Tourist Charged €150 for Short Taxi Ride
World.content:
A tourist has reported an alleged taxi scam in Prague, claiming that a journey from Old Town Square to Prague Main Railway Station ended with an unexpectedly high fare and a disputed payment.

The incident reportedly took place on July 25 at around 16:15. According to the complaint, the driver charged CZK 980 for the ride, an amount the passenger said was far higher than the expected price for such a short distance.

The tourist claims that the driver refused to accept payment by card and requested cash instead.



“I paid him 100 Euros for the fare. He just took the note, swapped it and lied to me saying what I gave was 100 in Czech currency, and demanded me to pay the remaining 50 euro taxi fare,” the tourist said in his complaint.

“So I paid the initial 100 euro that was swapped, plus the 50 euro taxi fare.”

According to the passenger, the total amount paid for the ride was therefore €150 (over 3,600 CZK). He said he was rushing to catch a train to Bratislava and was unable to resolve the dispute at the scene.

The tourist also claimed that no receipt was provided after the payment. According to his account, the driver said an invoice would be sent by email, but it was never received.

The case has been reported to the relevant authorities, while details of the incident have also been shared online to raise awareness among other visitors.

Travellers are also encouraged to use established taxi applications or services recommended by hotels, restaurants, and official tourist information centres. Paying by card and confirming the expected price in advance can help avoid disputes.

World.title: Premium property at Lake Balaton: what the numbers don’t tell you
World.content:
My previous columns covered the logic of Budapest’s premium market – from the step-by-step purchase process and discreet transactions to inheritance and the golden visa reality. This piece moves one step beyond the capital. Premium property at Lake Balaton has quietly overtaken Budapest in a telling metric: in 2024, the average sum spent per transaction on the northern shore reached HUF 67.7 million, against Budapest’s HUF 60.4 million average. The numbers, however, only show the surface. What lies behind them – the structure of supply, the legal constraints and the mechanism that has made this one of the most protected premium asset classes in Central Europe – is what genuinely deserves attention.

Author: Emese Széll, Private Real Estate Advisor to Premium Clients in Hungary

Premium property at Lake Balaton: two very different markets

The Balaton property market divides sharply into two characters. The northern shore – Balatonfüred, the Tihany peninsula, Csopak, Badacsony, Balatonalmádi – is the prestige side: volcanic hills, a national park, historic wine regions and the inherited distinction of a 19th-century spa town. Average square-metre prices on the north shore moved between HUF 1.01 million and HUF 1.25 million in 2024; prime waterfront stock reached HUF 2–3.5 million per square metre. Tihany is in its own category: with an average of HUF 1.8–2.2 million per square metre it is one of the country’s most expensive settlements, and around 90 percent of its transactions close in cash.

The southern shore – Siófok, Zamárdi, Balatonszemes, Balatonlelle – has traditionally traded at lower prices. That hierarchy is shifting. In 2024, Balatonszemes reached HUF 1.55 million per square metre, making it the second most expensive Balaton settlement after Tihany; Szántód ranked third at HUF 1.53 million. The flatter southern topography allows direct-waterfront luxury villas and penthouse developments that are drawing increasing volumes of urban capital.

Balatonfüred: the capital of lakeside development

Balatonfüred has seen the most dramatic transformation of recent years. In the Fürdő utca district and the former Greek village area, luxury developments stand side by side, having added hundreds of premium homes to the market within a few years. Prices across the current new-build offering typically range from HUF 80 million at entry level to over HUF 400 million for top-floor and penthouse units, depending on location within the town, views and apartment size. These developments match international luxury standards in both scale and specification: underground parking, pools, saunas, smart-home systems and heat-pump engineering.

The Káli basin: where law creates value

Further inland from the lake, the Káli basin – Szentbékkálla, Köveskál, Monoszló, Kővágóörs – operates by a different logic entirely. A 2012-built luxury villa of 1,615 square metres on a ten-hectare vineyard estate with a wine cellar and pools in Monoszló is listed at close to HUF 2 billion, around €5 million. This is not exceptional; this is the area’s standard pricing logic.

The Káli Basin. Photo: premiumingatlanok.hu The Káli Basin. Photo: premiumingatlanok.hu

Behind these prices lies scarcity created not by the market but by regulation. The Káli basin falls within the Balaton Uplands National Park and the EU’s Natura 2000 network. Building coverage on rural plots is typically capped at three percent, and in many locations new building permits are simply not issued. The National Park was expanded by a further 8,500 hectares in April 2026. The supply of genuinely premium property at Lake Balaton and in the surrounding highlands is not growing – it is shrinking.

Tokaj-Hegyalja and Szekszárd: where wine country meets investment

Beyond the Balaton, Tokaj-Hegyalja is Hungary’s other rising premium market. Representative surveys consistently rank Tokaj as Hungarians’ favourite wine region, ahead of Eger and Villány. The area’s appeal rests on its natural landscape, the historic tradition of aszú production and a rapidly maturing premium gastronomy scene; long-established wineries and estate hotels have built an international-calibre tourism ecosystem that makes the region compelling even for the most discerning buyers. Average property prices here still trail the Balaton highlands, but sustained investment in infrastructure and gastronomic tourism is generating capital appreciation potential that few other Hungarian regions can match.

The wine-country premium market, however, does not end with Tokaj. Szekszárd – home of Bikavér and Kékfrankos, set in the historic heart of southern Transdanubia – is quietly moving onto the radar of considered buyers. The gently rolling loess hills, a near-Mediterranean microclimate and distinguished estates – among them Vesztergombi, Vida and Takler – offer a quality of life and sense of provenance that once seemed the exclusive preserve of the northern Balaton shore. What genuinely distinguishes the top tier of Szekszárd’s estate offering is sustainability as a real value dimension: at the finest properties, solar generation, heat-pump heating, a private well and a historic wine cellar are not separate features but components of a coherent, grid-independent ecosystem. At Szekszárd, a buyer is not yet paying Tihany prices, but a self-sustaining vineyard estate or country manor already represents an asset class whose supply cannot expand freely, constrained as it is by landscape and heritage protection.

Who is buying and why

According to KSH and ingatlan.com data, approximately 8,000 foreign nationals buy property in Hungary each year, with two-thirds of transactions now taking place outside Budapest. Among foreign buyers, Germans are the most active: their numbers grew by more than two-thirds in recent years, and every second German buyer chose the Balaton region – Somogy or Zala county. Price advantage is increasingly secondary as a motivation; macro-political stability, public safety and climate resilience have become the primary decision factors.

Hungary’s tax environment is a genuine draw. France, Spain and Norway operate annual wealth taxes that steadily erode invested capital; Hungary has no general net-wealth tax. Property taxation is limited to the one-off transfer duty and a local building tax – a position that compares favourably with the Mediterranean alternatives many buyers also consider.

Photo: premiumingatlanok.hu

What buyers need to know before stepping in

Entering Hungary’s rural premium market is considerably more complex than buying a Budapest apartment. The Agricultural Land Act draws a sharp distinction: non-EU nationals may not acquire farmland at all; EU nationals without a registered farmer qualification may acquire a maximum of one hectare of arable land, rising to 300 hectares with the relevant agricultural certification. Act XLVIII of 2025 – the Local Identity Act – has empowered municipalities to enforce pre-emption rights, restrict permanent registration and levy a settlement contribution on newcomers; over 200 municipalities already exercise these powers, and the effect is increasingly felt around the lake. On the other side of the ledger, the heritage building corporate tax incentive – which allows the cost of renovation to reduce the corporate tax base by twice the expenditure, producing a threefold tax-base reduction in practice – is one of the most powerful optimisation tools in the Hungarian legal system.

Position, not speculation

Premium property at Lake Balaton and in the Hungarian countryside has undergone a structural shift: it is no longer a seasonal asset but a standalone investment class. Supply is kept tight by conservation and legal constraints; demand is sustained by both domestic and international capital; and value growth rests on genuine scarcity rather than speculation. Anyone making meaningful decisions in this market needs more than price data – navigating the legal and physical landscape calls for experienced local representation, and that is the only reliable compass in a market this complex.

Emese Széll, an expert in the Hungarian premium real estate market. www.premiumingatlanok.com

This article is intended for general market and economic information purposes.

World.title: Hungary to suspend freight trains during evening peak to save electricity amid energy crisis
World.content:
Hungary will temporarily halt most rail freight traffic during the evening peak from Monday as the government introduces further emergency energy-saving measures following the sharp reduction in output at the Paks Nuclear Power Plant. The move is expected to reduce electricity demand by up to 90 megawatt-hours per day.

Evening freight rail services to be suspended

Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced in a video message on Saturday that the government had ordered the suspension of rail freight services between 5:00 PM and 10:00 PM from Monday.

According to the prime minister, the measure is designed to lower electricity consumption on the railway network during the most critical hours of the day and free up additional capacity for the national power grid.

Essential freight services exempt

Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy said the restriction would apply to most freight trains, with exemptions only for services considered essential to the national economy or critical infrastructure. These include trains transporting supplies needed to keep power stations and other key facilities operating.

Vitézy noted that similar restrictions have previously been introduced during periods of heavy snowfall, when freight traffic was temporarily limited to help maintain railway operations.

Up to 90 MWh of electricity could be saved daily

Government estimates suggest the temporary suspension of freight traffic could save between 70 and 90 megawatt-hours (MWh) of electricity each day.

The measure forms part of a broader package of emergency actions introduced as Hungary prepares for a significant reduction in domestic electricity generation linked to the ongoing problems at the Paks Nuclear Power Plant, whose output has been severely reduced due to the exceptionally low water level of the Danube.

Government expands energy-saving measures

Alongside the freight restrictions, the government has also announced:

Mandatory home working for eligible public administration employees during the first three days of next week.

A request for private-sector employers to allow remote working wherever possible and minimise office energy consumption.

The switch-off of decorative and non-essential lighting at all state institutions.

A call for all municipalities to implement the highest possible level of energy-saving measures.

Public urged to reduce electricity use

Vitézy also called on both businesses and households to cut electricity consumption wherever possible, particularly during the late afternoon and evening peak.

“Hungary is facing an unprecedented situation because of the shutdown of Paks, but with attention, cooperation and responsible decisions, we can keep the country running,” the minister said, urging the public to contribute to the nationwide effort.

The latest measures are part of the government’s wider response to an energy crisis triggered by the Danube’s historically low water levels, which have forced the gradual reduction of electricity generation at Hungary’s largest power plant.

World.title: Hungary Weekly Briefing: Energy emergency, political investigations and the challenges ahead
World.content:
Hungary faced one of its most challenging weeks of the year as an unprecedented drought pushed the Danube to record-low levels, threatening electricity generation, drinking water supplies and critical infrastructure across the country. At the same time, the government launched new investigations, unveiled major energy investments and continued reshaping key state institutions.

In the latest edition of Hungary Weekly Briefing, we examine how the unfolding energy emergency could affect Hungary’s economy and daily life, why the country’s reliance on the Danube has become a strategic concern, and what the government’s response reveals about its priorities. We also analyse the investigation into the relocation of Slovak Roma families, the launch of Hungary’s new Asset Recovery Office, the latest political polling, and the week’s most important business and diplomatic developments.

At Daily News Hungary, we believe the biggest stories deserve more than a headline. Every week, our editorial team explains the context behind Hungary’s political, economic and international developments, helping readers understand how individual events fit into the country’s rapidly evolving landscape.

World.title: Hungary recalls 25 more ambassadors, including from Washington, London, Brussels, Moscow and Kyiv
World.content:
Hungary has recalled another 25 ambassadors in one of the country’s biggest diplomatic reshuffles in recent years. The latest changes, initiated by Foreign Minister Anita Orbán, affect several of Hungary’s most strategically important diplomatic posts, including Washington, London, Brussels, Moscow and Kyiv.

Key diplomatic posts to change hands

The list of ambassadors whose appointments have been terminated was published in the latest issue of the Hungarian Gazette on Friday evening. Among the most high-profile recalls are Hungary’s ambassadors to:

Washington – Szabolcs Ferenc Takács

– Szabolcs Ferenc Takács London – Ferenc Kumin

– Ferenc Kumin Brussels – Tamás Iván Kovács

– Tamás Iván Kovács Moscow – Norbert Attila Konkoly

– Norbert Attila Konkoly Kyiv – Antal Heizer

– Antal Heizer Belgrade – József Zoltán Magyar

– József Zoltán Magyar Bratislava – Csaba Sándor Balogh

The changes also extend to Hungary’s permanent missions to major international organisations, including NATO, the United Nations, the World Trade Organisation (WTO) and the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE).

Part of a broader diplomatic overhaul

This is the second major wave of ambassadorial recalls since the new government took office. At the end of June, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs ended the mandates of 37 heads of diplomatic missions, describing the changes as part of a wider professional renewal of Hungary’s diplomatic service.

At the time, Foreign Minister Anita Orbán said the ministry aimed to build “a professional diplomatic corps operating at the highest standards” with ambassadors capable of advancing Hungary’s foreign policy objectives and strengthening the country’s international influence.
