Stronger voice of Central Asia

Addressing the meeting, Tokayev said Central Asia’s role in global affairs is steadily growing and that the region’s voice is becoming increasingly prominent on the international stage.

“Kazakhstan remains committed to the agreements reached and will continue advancing constructive initiatives aimed at strengthening friendship, good-neighborly relations and strategic partnership among our countries. I am confident that, through our joint efforts, we will achieve even greater progress,” Tokayev said.

The expanded format does not amount to a closed regional bloc. Instead, it reflects an effort by Central Asian states to coordinate more effectively, reduce their vulnerability to external shocks and approach larger powers with a clearer sense of shared interests.

World.title: How Trans-Caspian Cable Fits Kazakhstan’s Evolving Connectivity Strategy
World.content:
ASTANA — For decades, Kazakhstan’s connectivity strategy was measured in highways, railways and pipelines. Today, that vision is expanding. As global competition increasingly depends on the movement of data alongside the movement of goods, the country is investing in a new layer of strategic infrastructure — one designed not to carry cargo, but information.

Among the clearest examples of this shift is the Trans-Caspian fiber-optic cable project. The first-ever underwater telecommunications link across the Caspian Sea will connect Aktau and Sumqayit, creating a new digital corridor between Central Asia, the South Caucasus and Europe.

The project reflects a broader vision articulated by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, who has increasingly framed Kazakhstan’s connectivity agenda as extending beyond physical transport routes to include cross-border digital infrastructure. In his September 2024 State of the Nation Address, he called for the project to be completed, describing it as essential for “creating a digital infrastructure linked with international corridors and cross-border data flows.”

Several months later, speaking at an informal meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Organization of Turkic States in Budapest, Tokayev expanded that vision beyond Kazakhstan.

“This project will significantly improve digital communication between our countries and will be a strategic step towards strengthening regional integration. Such initiatives open up opportunities to create a new digital corridor across the Eurasian continent,” he said.

The regional context continues to evolve. As the cable enters its final construction phase, regional leaders are once again gathering, this time in Cholpon-Ata for an informal Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan, underscoring how cooperation between the countries increasingly extends across transport, energy and digital connectivity.

Nearly two years after Tokayev first identified the project as a strategic priority, it is entering its most tangible phase. Kazakhstan is now carrying out the final stages of the project, with commercial commissioning expected by the end of 2026. The latest phase has shifted from engineering preparation to offshore construction.

According to the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development’s release from July 31, regulatory, customs and organizational procedures have been completed, including the approval of equipment required for the offshore works, allowing construction to proceed without administrative delays.

Preparatory work in 2025 included desktop and offshore engineering surveys, selection of the optimal route avoiding anchorage zones and military training areas, environmental approvals from the Mangystau Region authorities, and the production and factory testing in China of a specially armored submarine cable equipped with ROPA optical amplifiers.

With the planning phase complete, attention has shifted from engineering design to execution at sea. The cable, previously delivered from China to the port of Kuryk together with three cable baskets weighing a combined 600 tons, was transported to Baku aboard a specialized logistics vessel. It has now been transferred into the cable tank of the cable-laying vessel, which has departed Baku and is laying the line toward Aktau.

The operation is being carried out by a cable-laying vessel with a displacement exceeding 20,000 tons and equipped with dynamic positioning technology to ensure precise installation on the seabed. Around 70 crew members are involved, including technical supervisors and representatives of Kazakhtelecom. The project is being implemented by CaspiLink B.V., the joint venture established by Kazakhtelecom and AzerTelecom.

A dedicated jointing room has also been installed onboard to allow engineers to repair or reconnect the cable if required during installation. Both the Kazakh and Azerbaijani cable ends have already undergone testing. Subject to favorable weather conditions, installation of the submarine cable is expected to be completed within the next 15 to 20 days, while the overall commissioning process remains on schedule for completion by the end of 2026.

The significance of the project, however, extends well beyond the technical operation. As economies become more deeply integrated through both physical and digital infrastructure, international corridors are no longer defined solely by the goods they carry. They are increasingly shaped by the data they enable to move across borders. While the cable spans just 380 kilometers across the Caspian seabed, the vision behind it reaches much further. The Trans-Caspian fiber-optic cable reflects Kazakhstan’s ambition to remain an important link in the movement of both goods and data across Eurasia.

World.title: Russian woman faces prison after calling Armenians ‘rat-like’ people
World.content:
Russian calls Armenians ‘rats’

A criminal case has been opened in Armenia against Russian national Nadezhda Pirozhkova. A blogger who has lived in Armenia for the past year and a half, Pirozhkova came under fire after criticising Vardavar, the Armenian tradition of pouring water over one another on the holiday. She described the custom as an act of aggression. In another video, she referred to Armenians as a “rat-like people”.

Armenia’s Investigative Committee has initiated criminal proceedings against Pirozhkova under the article on “public statements aimed at inciting hatred and discrimination through the use of the internet”. Armenia’s Criminal Code provides for a prison sentence of up to four years under this article. If Pirozhkova is found guilty in court, she could therefore face imprisonment.

For now, however, she has been banned from leaving her place of residence as a preventive measure. The blogger may leave Yerevan only with written permission from a prosecutor or a judge.

Vardavar is one of the principal feasts of the Armenian Apostolic Church, celebrating the Transfiguration of Jesus Christ, although its origins date back to pagan times. It is virtually impossible to stay dry on the streets that day, but taking offence is not customary, as drenching someone with water is considered a way of congratulating them on the holiday. The water is believed to bring health, good fortune and purification.

Pirozhkova’s Instagram posts sparked outrage among social media users—not only Armenians, but also fellow Russians.

Many have not only criticised Pirozhkova but have also called on law enforcement authorities to punish her as severely as possible or deport her from the country.

Political commentator Artyom Yerkanian did not rule out the possibility that certain actors interested in damaging Armenia’s image as a tourist destination were behind the spread of such videos. He pointed to the large number of Russian tourists visiting Armenia. In the first half of 2026 alone, Armenia received 1.042 million foreign visitors, around 40% of whom were from Russia.

“It’s interesting, isn’t it? On the one hand, the Russian government imposes trade restrictions [on imports of Armenian products and goods], while on the other, Russians happily travel to Armenia, enjoying its nature, its people and, why not, its traditions,” Yerkanian said.

What else Pirozhkova said

In a video about Vardavar, the Russian blogger said that the holiday made her want to leave Yerevan more than anything else. She described the tradition of pouring water over one another as “the height of tactlessness”. In her view, Armenians do not understand the concept of “personal boundaries” and routinely violate them.

Pirozhkova argued that splashing passers-by with water was disrespectful towards those who did not wish to take part in the celebration.

“If I’m in your country, I’m not obliged to follow your traditions. This is a direct manifestation of aggression.“

Following the video, Pirozhkova has periodically posted about the wave of online abuse directed at her. She has also publicly apologised several times, saying:

“I understand that many people saw it as disrespect towards the Armenian people. And I’m truly sorry. That was never my intention, and it still isn’t.”

At the same time, the blogger has acknowledged that she is using the controversy to promote her Instagram page.

“People recognise me now. Why shouldn’t I make use of something I’ve been through after putting in so much effort? I’ve worked hard for this. Why shouldn’t a person take advantage of circumstances and situations they have rightfully earned? I just want to change my life.“

Foreign nationals are required to respect Armenia’s national customs and traditions

The legal status of foreign nationals in Armenia is governed by the Law on Foreigners. Article 5 of the law states that foreigners in Armenia enjoy the same rights, freedoms and obligations as Armenian citizens. At the same time, it stipulates that “foreigners in the Republic of Armenia are obliged to respect the Constitution and laws of the Republic of Armenia, other legal acts, as well as national customs and traditions.”

The same article also provides that foreign nationals bear the same legal responsibility as Armenian citizens while in Armenia.

Armenia’s Criminal Code provides for penalties for “public statements aimed at inciting or promoting hatred, discrimination, intolerance or hostility against an individual or group of persons on the grounds of race, nationality or ethnicity, as well as the dissemination of materials or objects for that purpose.”

The available penalties include fines, community service, restriction of liberty and imprisonment.

Under Article 329, offences committed “through publicly displayed works, the mass media, or information and communication technologies” are punishable by one to four years’ imprisonment

Commentary

Political commentator Artyom Yerkanian said in an interview with a local television channel::

“After the Russian blogger publicly apologised, this story could have ended there. But some social media users continued calling on the Armenian law enforcement authorities to examine Nadezhda Pirozhkova’s actions and determine whether they amounted to a criminal offence. The authorities decided to respond to those calls.

Perhaps there was no need to be so severe. The court will, of course, take all mitigating circumstances into account.

Perhaps we should not politicise everything. It is obvious that the aim was not to incite ethnic hatred but simply to increase her audience through provocative videos.

In two weeks, the video attracted more than 250,000 views and over 5,000 comments. As a result, the number of followers on her page increased more than fifteen-fold.

In other words, this blogger simply found a ridiculous and foolish way to grow her audience.

Nevertheless, perhaps such cases should be monitored more closely, because this is not an isolated incident.

In recent weeks, there have been several similar cases in which foreign bloggers, particularly Russians, have made remarks discrediting Armenians and damaging Armenia’s reputation as a tourist destination.

There was one case in which a young woman accused an Armenian taxi driver of attempting to rape her. I also recall another similar incident, and there are probably many more. But what is more important?

Notably, these videos are deliberately amplified by non-existent users. An army of fake accounts is spreading this material in pursuit of a specific objective.

It cannot be ruled out that certain forces are behind these fake accounts and are interested in ensuring that Armenia is not perceived as a safe destination for tourists.

Every tourist who enjoys visiting the country indirectly becomes its ‘agent of influence’. Perhaps that is exactly what some people dislike.

I don’t know whether it is a coincidence, but it was precisely during those days that the Russian Foreign Ministry added Armenia to its list of countries where Russians cannot feel safe, citing the possibility that the Armenian authorities could extradite them to third countries. Perhaps it is a coincidence—or perhaps it is not.”

Social media reaction

“If, after a year and a half of living in Armenia, she still allows herself to speak like this, it cannot be dismissed as an accident or naivety.”

“The police should investigate her actions. She’s a planted agent.”

“She should be fined heavily and deported.”

“She should be tried and deported from our country. It’s a matter of the nation’s dignity.”

“If an Armenian had behaved like this in Russia, he would already have disappeared.”

“Foreign visitors are obliged to obey the law, respect the country and its people, and behave like guests.”

World.title: Meet Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver: Pine martens at Tbilisi Zoo. Video
World.content:
Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver are young pine martens and the newest residents of Tbilisi Zoo. A local resident found the orphaned cubs alone in an attic and took them home after discovering they had no mother.



However, pine martens are wild predators with powerful teeth and strong natural instincts. Once the cubs had grown up, releasing them back into the wild was no longer an option. Contact with humans had altered their natural behaviour, leaving them unable to survive on their own. Their rescuer therefore turned to Tbilisi Zoo for help.

Konstantin Pkhakadze, head of the zoo’s exotic animals department, said the pine martens arrived at Tbilisi Zoo about a month ago. He said such cases are quite common. People often assume that young animals found alone have been orphaned and need rescuing, but that is not always the case.

In most instances, the mother is nearby, hunting, searching for food or moving her young to a new location. Pkhakadze said intervening at that stage is the biggest mistake people can make. They should not even approach the cubs, as the mother may detect the scent of humans, see it as a threat and never return to her offspring.

Tbilisi Zoo currently has very limited capacity to take in new animals. Its existing site is overcrowded, while most of its resources are being directed towards the construction of a new zoo.

Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver were initially housed in the zoo’s exotics pavilion. However, the small enclosed space was unsuitable for such active and energetic animals. Zoo staff therefore built a temporary outdoor enclosure, giving the pine martens more space, fresh air and room to move freely.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Pine martens at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Georgia’s opposition launches campaign to restore voting rights for emigrants
World.content:
In Georgia, the opposition alliance Coalition for Change and the Strategy Aghmashenebeli party have launched the Emigrant’s Vote campaign, calling for the restoration of Georgian citizens’ right to vote from abroad in parliamentary and municipal elections.

Under the new Election Code, approved by the ruling Georgian Dream party on 17 December 2025, emigrants are no longer allowed to vote from abroad. Instead, they must travel to Georgia to cast their ballots.

One of Coalition for Change’s members, Tengo Tevzadze, announced the launch of the campaign, saying the initiative would culminate in a constitutional challenge seeking to restore emigrants’ right to take part in elections.

According to Tevzadze, the campaign aims to demonstrate that allowing emigrants to vote is consistent with Georgia’s constitution and that every Georgian citizen, regardless of where they live, should be able to take part in elections.

Tevzadze noted that Georgian Dream won just 13.4% of the overseas vote in the disputed 2024 parliamentary election, which the opposition says was rigged. He argued that this was why the authorities later moved to strip emigrants of their voting rights.

Tevzadze argues that depriving emigrants of the right to vote violates Georgia’s constitution and is unfair to a group of citizens that makes a significant contribution to the country’s economy.

The campaign’s organisers have set out two main demands: restoring emigrants’ right to vote and creating an electoral system that allows Georgian citizens living abroad to cast their ballots.

“We need as many emigrants as possible to sign the petition so that, alongside political efforts, we can also challenge the regime through legal means. Through a constitutional lawsuit, we will clearly demonstrate that emigrants’ participation in elections and their voting rights are protected by the constitution, and that Georgians, both at home and abroad, must be able to take part in free and fair elections,” Tengo Tevzadze said.

Voting rights for Georgian emigrants

World.title: Evening illuminations in South Ossetia: Video
World.content:
Evening illuminations in South Ossetia

Major reconstruction work has been completed in the South Ossetian capital, Tskhinval. The city centre has been renovated, dozens of streets repaired, and new utility networks installed.

The redevelopment of Theatre Square included new lighting, benches and marble planters, while boxwood and juniper shrubs were planted. Several school and college buildings, along with the Kosta Khetagurov State Drama Theatre, have also been restored.

The work was funded through Russia’s investment programme.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Evening illuminations in South Ossetia

World.title: Russian mass strike on Ukraine leaves several dead and dozens injured. Video from Lviv
World.content:
Russian strike on Ukraine: Video from Lviv

Russia launched a mass overnight attack on Ukraine on 30 July, according to Ukrainian authorities, firing a total of 74 missiles and 284 attack drones. Ukraine said its air defences intercepted a significant number of the incoming targets, but some missiles and drones struck their intended targets.

Several regions across Ukraine came under attack, including Lviv, Kyiv and the Dnipropetrovsk region.

In Lviv, one resident was killed. In the village of Radushne, near Kryvyi Rih, a ballistic missile struck the home of a large family. Six people were killed, including three children, while several others were injured.

Lviv Mayor Andriy Sadovyi said the city had suffered direct Russian missile strikes on residential buildings for the first time in a long period.

The heaviest damage was reported on Paton and Vyhovskoho streets, where more than 20 residential buildings, a school, two kindergartens and other civilian infrastructure were damaged.

Rescue workers recovered the body of a man from beneath the rubble.

According to the latest official figures, 34 people, including three children, were injured in the attack on Lviv. Nine people were rescued from damaged buildings. Emergency crews are continuing search and rescue operations and clearing the debris.

Lviv city authorities said some residents whose homes were damaged would be provided with temporary accommodation, while municipal services are assisting those left homeless.

Russian strike on Ukraine: Video from Lviv

World.title: German broadcaster ARD investigates Georgia’s rise as a crypto hub
World.content:
Crypto mining in Georgia

“Crypto war: How Putin is using bitcoin to wage war against us” is the title of a 45-minute investigative documentary by German public broadcaster ARD, which portrays Georgia as a major cryptocurrency mining hub and an alleged transit route used by Russia to circumvent Western sanctions.

The documentary focuses on bitcoin mining and crypto systems which, the journalists argue, have enabled Russia to adapt to international financial restrictions.

Georgia’s favourable conditions for crypto industry

The investigation’s authors say Georgia has developed a particularly favourable legal and tax environment for the cryptocurrency industry over many years. They argue that this was closely linked to political and economic decisions taken during the rule of the Georgian Dream party and its founder, Bidzina Ivanishvili, turning the country into what they describe as one of the world’s cryptocurrency “grey zones”.

The documentary focuses in particular on the free industrial zones in Poti and Rustavi. According to the journalists, Russia can no longer sell natural gas to Europe at pre-sanctions levels, with some of that gas instead being used to generate low-cost electricity. The filmmakers argue that this electricity powers large-scale bitcoin mining infrastructure, the ultimate financial benefits of which serve Russia’s interests.

The German journalists say they travelled to Georgia and visited cryptocurrency mining facilities themselves, including infrastructure in the Rustavi Free Industrial Zone.

Russia said using cryptocurrency to circumvent sanctions

Nino Bakradze, founder of the investigative journalism organisation iFact, says in the documentary that Russia has not been completely cut off from the international financial system and is increasingly using cryptocurrency for cross-border transactions.

Nino Bakradze

She says iFact investigated exports of dual-use goods to Russia by conducting an undercover experiment. The organisation contacted a Russian trading company and asked whether it could ship around 30 drones to Russia. According to Bakradze, the company replied that such a shipment was possible and said it had carried out similar transactions before despite the risks posed by sanctions.

Bakradze says the investigation found that companies involved in such transactions use cryptocurrency to settle payments in order to circumvent sanctions, often without being detected by Western authorities.

‘Bitcoin mining in Georgia is profitable’

The documentary also features local bitcoin miner Nikoloz Museridze, who says the main advantage of mining bitcoin in Georgia is the country’s relatively low electricity prices.

Nikoloz Museridze

Museridze says his mining farm consumes about 2 megawatts of electricity. He estimates that, at this capacity, it takes about a year to mine one bitcoin, while the cost of producing a single bitcoin in Georgia is around $30,000-$40,000.

The miner describes bitcoin as “borderless money” that can be transferred anywhere in the world at any time and which, he claims, cannot be blocked or frozen.

World.title: Nauru withdraws recognition of occupied Abkhazia and South Ossetia
World.content:
The government of the Pacific island nation of Nauru says it has formally withdrawn its recognition of the self-proclaimed republics of Abkhazia and South Ossetia as independent states.

“The Government of the Republic of Nauru declares that it has withdrawn its recognition of the ‘Republic of South Ossetia’ and the ‘Republic of Abkhazia’ as independent states.

Accordingly, the Republic of Nauru has immediately terminated diplomatic relations with South Ossetia and Abkhazia,” the Nauru government said in a statement.

On 29 July, Nauru severed diplomatic relations with the Russian-occupied Georgian regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

Georgia’s foreign ministry described the decision as a sign of respect for the principles of international law and said Tbilisi was ready to establish diplomatic relations with Nauru and strengthen bilateral cooperation on the basis of shared interests.

“The decision once again confirms that respect for and adherence to international law are the foundation of healthy international relations,” the ministry said in a statement.

The self-proclaimed Abkhaz foreign ministry claimed that Nauru had come under “unprecedented pressure” to end diplomatic relations with Abkhazia.

“The development of cooperation between the Republic of Abkhazia and the Republic of Nauru has consistently encountered resistance from Georgia and its Western partners. As joint initiatives turned into practice, a campaign of aggressive external pressure was unleashed against the Republic of Nauru.

For many years, states maintaining diplomatic relations with the Republic of Abkhazia have faced external pressure aimed at abandoning their independently determined foreign policy course. Small states, with limited resources to counter large-scale political, diplomatic, and economic instruments of influence, are particularly vulnerable to such pressure.

Such practice contradicts the fundamental principles of the UN Charter, including the principles of the sovereign equality of states and non-interference in their internal affairs.

The Republic of Abkhazia remains committed to strengthening its international subject status, protecting its national interests, and developing mutually beneficial cooperation with states that share the principles of sovereign equality, mutual respect, and international law,” the statement said.

Nauru recognised the independence of Abkhazia and Georgia’s Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia) in 2009, after Russia declared the two Georgian regions independent states. Nauru was one of only a handful of countries to support the move backed by Moscow.

Nauru is a small Pacific island state in the Micronesia region. It is one of the world’s smallest countries, both by land area and population. Covering about 21 sq km (8 sq miles), it is home to around 12,000-13,000 people.

World.title: Pashinyan: ‘Russia wants either exclusive ties or nothing’
World.content:
Pashinyan rejects exclusive ties with Russia

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has once again addressed the current state of relations between Armenia and Russia. He commented in particular on Russia’s restrictions on imports of Armenian goods, an issue that has caused growing concern in Armenia. During a briefing, Pashinyan said the country should view the situation not as a crisis but as an opportunity to diversify its economy.

Journalists asked him to address the political dimension of the issue, arguing that it clearly extends beyond economics. Pashinyan said the problem stems from Armenia’s search for alternatives that it previously did not have.

As an example, he pointed to the signing of strategic partnership agreements with China, the United States, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, France and other countries.

According to Pashinyan, Armenia had never before had — and could not have had — strategic relations with so many partners.

“I cannot speak about Russia’s feelings. I can say that Russia sees this as a problem. There is also an element of exclusivity here. The issue is this: either the relationship is exclusive, or there should be no relationship at all. We do not share that view,” he said.

Pashinyan said Yerevan’s position is “legitimate.” Armenia’s ties with Russia are not exclusive, he said, but the relationship should continue.

“I ask that our position be treated with understanding and respect, especially since its legitimacy is not questioned in practice,” he said.

Pashinyan also stressed that Armenia would continue discussions with Russia over the economic restrictions that Russia and the Eurasian Economic Union have imposed on Armenian goods.

“That would be the worst possible course of action,” he added.

“What was wrong with Armenia? What did Armenia do?”

Journalists asked why Russia places such importance on Armenia’s political orientation and whether Pashinyan had given Moscow any reason to doubt that Armenia remains a reliable partner. In response, the prime minister posed a series of questions:

“What was wrong with Armenia in 2022 that the Collective Security Treaty Organization failed to fulfil its obligations? What did Armenia do wrong? Whom did Armenia harm? What did Armenia do that justified what happened?” he said, referring to Russia’s and the CSTO’s failure to respond after Azerbaijani forces entered Armenia’s internationally recognised territory in 2021–2022, despite the alliance’s obligation to act in the event of an attack on a member state’s territorial integrity.

What was wrong with Armenia that the Russian peacekeepers in Karabakh failed to fulfil their mission? Was the problem October 2022?” he continued, referring to the 6 October 2022 statement signed by Armenia and Azerbaijan in Prague, in which the two countries recognised each other’s territorial integrity. “But there were incidents even before that. What was wrong with Armenia? And why is it always assumed that we are the bad partner?”

“We are showing who needs Armenia”

Continuing on the issue, Pashinyan referred to Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko’s remark, “Who needs Armenia?”

“Has Armenia harmed anyone? Has it harmed Belarus? How can anyone speak about a sovereign state like that?” he said.

Pashinyan argued that the Belarusian president had asked the question but failed to find an answer. Now, he said, Armenia is showing exactly who values relations with it.

“Armenia matters to China, the United States, the European Union and Iran. And Armenia needs all of those partners as well. Georgia needs Armenia, and Armenia needs Georgia. Armenia matters to France, Germany, Poland and the United Kingdom. That’s the whole story.”

“The alternative is not yet in place” for a referendum

In recent months, Moscow has repeatedly urged Armenia to choose between the Eurasian Economic Union and the European Union. Russian officials have insisted that Armenia should hold a referendum on the issue as soon as possible. At the end of May, the leaders of four EAEU member states issued a joint statement calling for such a vote.

“I respect the fact that, on 29 May, the leaders of four EAEU countries issued a statement supporting the idea of a referendum on EU membership. But there is still nothing to vote on,” Pashinyan said.

He reiterated that it would make sense to hold a referendum only after Armenia obtains EU candidate status or once the issue formally appears on the agenda.

According to the prime minister, Moscow does not challenge Yerevan’s right to pursue alternatives. Instead, it is telling Armenia: “Decide today which alternative you choose.”

“But the alternative is not yet in place. The process of creating it has only just begun. It would be dishonest to ask people now whether they support an alternative that does not yet exist. They would ask many questions that we simply cannot answer today,” he said.

Pashinyan said the government would continue working to answer those questions before asking the public to make a choice.

Pashinyan rejects exclusive ties with Russia

World.title: Grandfather and grandson pedal 5,300km from Broome to Bowral for MND
World.content:
After six weeks cycling through harsh headwinds and expansive deserts, Bob Montgomery, 82, and his grandson Tom Malcolm, 18, finally have a chance to catch their breath.

The pair clocked close to 5,300 kilometres as they crossed the finish line on Sunday afternoon to the roaring applause of Mr Montgomery's local community of Bowral, in the NSW Southern Highlands.

They left Broome on June 22 and pedalled across Western Australia, the Northern Territory, regional Queensland and outback NSW to raise $500,000 for motor neurone disease (MND) research and awareness.

The "shocking" disease strikes a personal chord for Mr Montgomery, who lost a cousin to the condition during his first charity distance ride at 70 years old.

"We get the pain riding the harsh winds we ride into and all that stuff. At the end of the day, we can put our feet up and sit back and have a drink," he said.

" But for people with MND, there's no end to what they've got. It's just a dead end. "

A finish line marked by balloons was set up and many people held up written messages of encouragement for the pair's final 50 metres. (ABC Illawarra: Brooke Chandler)

The pair averaged 160km a day and learned some harsh lessons along the way.

"I would next time reverse the course," Mr Montgomery said.

"[The wind] was basically in our face the whole time and it'd be pretty easy to give up and just put our bikes in the car.

"Tom and I would talk to each other, and we knew we were getting the support from others as funds came in. That was very, very helpful."

Bob Montgomery and Tom Malcolm stayed in local hotels during their six-week charity distance ride. (Supplied: Ethan Grahek)

Mr Montgomery said meeting people and enjoying a "beer or two" at each local stopover helped motivate him through his fifth MND charity distance ride.

"It seems like a long dream going back to Broome … there's so many stories and so many people we met along the way who put their hands into their pockets to throw some cash in, which is fantastic," he said.

Their cross-country effort was an idea pitched by Mr Montgomery and timed to coincide with Mr Malcolm's university break.

The pair experienced some mechanical setbacks and would often cycle for up to 12 hours a day. (Supplied: Ethan Grahek)

"It took many months to agree to," Mr Malcolm said.

"I definitely admire Pappa in all that he's done.

"He was the big catalyst for me coming on this ride."

The family-duo would mount their bikes by four o'clock most mornings in freezing conditions and ride alongside road trains on narrow single-lane highways.

Tributes for footballers

MND is a rare, progressive group of neurological conditions that damage the cells controlling voluntary muscle movement, leading to muscle weakness, loss of physical function, and a shortened life expectancy.

Both men paid tribute to AFL footballer and MND advocate Neale Daniher, who died shortly before their journey, as well as former South Sydney Rabbitohs player Jai Arrow.

Bob Montgomery and Tom Malcolm wore South Sydney Rabbitohs jerseys for former player Jai Arrow who retired earlier this year with an MND diagnosis. (Supplied: Rachel Kelly)

"Neil Daniher is my hero because he made himself available to the public all that time which was just amazing … and now of course Jai's got the same battle," Mr Montgomery said.

"It's so important for fighting this disease to have a whole community behind you."

Not the last adventure

Donations and messages of support have trickled in from Australia and countries like the UK, Switzerland and New Zealand, with one donor writing; "As a person living with MND, I can't ride so I appreciate all that you are doing."

Mr Montgomery has generated nearly $300,000 for MND over his five charity distance rides, and another $65,000 during this latest endeavour.

"We provide services, advisory, equipment provision, carer support and that money will go towards helping people right here, right now on the ground throughout NSW and the ACT," MND NSW CEO Liam O'Meara said.

" So what they are doing is huge and will have an effect on many, many lives. "

Dozens of family and friends, including federal MP Carol Berry, turned out to cheer the pair across the finish line on Sunday afternoon. (ABC Illawarra: Brooke Chandler)

Mr Montgomery's latest cross-country effort was dubbed "One Last Ride" by his wife Jenny.

"It won't be my last adventure … I always thought I'd love to do the Kokoda Trail," he said.

"That'd be a great thing for my grandsons to do."

World.title: Drivers brace for petrol price hikes as fuel excise cut comes to end
World.content:
Drivers are bracing for more pain at the fuel pump as the federal government's fuel excise cut comes to an end.

The excise, which for months was reduced to mitigate a fuel price spike, will return to its normal amount at midnight on August 3, adding 16 cents per litre to wholesale prices.

It is expected the change will take about 10 days to flow through to the bowser, with prices forecast to increase to about $2.20 a litre for unleaded and $2.60 a litre for diesel, according to RACQ principal economist Ian Jeffreys.

He advised motorists to "fill up as soon as possible" to avoid paying a premium.

Track the latest petrol and diesel prices around Australia See what's happening with petrol and diesel prices near you, updated constantly.

The end of the excise cut coincides with a jump in global oil prices from below $US85 a barrel to about $US90 in the past fortnight.

"If renewed tensions in the Middle East remain high, we could see these increased oil prices persist and ultimately push bowser prices up further," Mr Jeffreys added.

The fuel excise cut took 32 cents off each litre of fuel when it was introduced in March, but the reduction was halved to 16 cents in July.

The cost-of-living relief was implemented after the global oil trade was impacted by the Iran war, which has brought naval shipments through the Strait of Hormuz to a halt.

Australia imports the equivalent of about 90 per cent of its refined oil needs, including bowser fuel, from several sources that rely on crude oil movement through the Strait of Hormuz.

Prices have surged in the past fortnight since a wobbly ceasefire between the US and Iran collapsed.

Speaking to reporters on Saturday, Energy Minister Chris Bowen urged motorists not to stockpile fuel.

He said Australia had several weeks' worth of unleaded and diesel reserves, with more shipments on the way.

"Hoarding fuel will not help the situation and it's dangerous, so there's no need to buy more than you need," Mr Jeffreys said.

Extension ruled out

Mr Bowen said the government was not considering an extension of the cut.

"Obviously we always monitor the situation and take steps as necessary, but our policy decision is clear," he said.

Mr Bowen said fuel retailers could be penalised by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) if found to be price gouging.

"[The ACCC] are monitoring, they will take action and they have the powers to take action if they see actions they find illegal," he said.

How the Middle East war spiked Australia's fuel prices Here's a quick breakdown on how the Iran war caused fuel prices to jump in Australia.

Asked whether she supported the cut ending, Liberal Party deputy leader Jane Hume said the government had failed to offset the cost of the measure.

"That means that these cuts to the fuel excise are going to cost Australians more and more," she said.

Drivers who spoke to the ABC on Sunday were ambivalent about the end of the excise cut.

On the New South Wales South Coast, Vanessa Ward-Brown said while she understood the need to end the fuel excise, regional communities would struggle more with increased costs.

"We don't have access to public transport like metropolitan areas do so we don't have any alternative other than to drive," she said.

Vanessa Ward-Brown and Travis Fraser say fuel has been costly, even with the excise cut in place. (ABC News: Toby Hemmings)

Ms Ward-Brown recently bought a house in Batemans Bay with her partner Travis Fraser, but has been driving three and a half hours to Sydney every week for last two months to complete her postgraduate law degree.

She said even with the fuel excise, the cost of commuting over that time was more than $1,000.

"I've been literally trying to work out between here and Sydney where is the cheapest petrol along the way to save the most money," she said.

In Adelaide, a motorist who did not share his name, said he thought the government was doing what it could.

"It's tried to help out, but it's a big cost and, you know, we have to pay the price of the war, unfortunately," he said.

World.title: From playing on a rock to rocking out — the 'steep rise' of Wild Honey
World.content:
Under a tamarind tree by a beach in Arnhem Land, the lead singer of Yothu Yindi would strum his guitar and sing, as his grandsons sat watching in the sand.

Two of those grandchildren have now grown up and picked up instruments themselves, forming one of the Top End's hottest new musical prospects, with their band Wild Honey.

Yothu Yindi's leader singer, the trailblazing former Australian of the Year Dr M Yunupiŋu, passed away in 2013, but for his grandson Gawukawu Gurruwiwi, his memory lives strong.

The grandsons of Yothu Yindi's lead singer have ambitions to take Wild Honey to the MCG and beyond. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

"Sometimes my grandfather would bring us instruments; toy drums, bass, guitar, from when he was touring," he said.

"And we used to set up all the instruments on a rock, overlooking the water.

"We used to imagine that rock was our stage, and we used to play, and pretend we were Yothu Yindi. Playing for the trees, the crabs, the seagulls."

Now, decades since that breakthrough Australian act climbed the charts with their hit song Treaty, won ARIAs and toured the globe, Wild Honey are having their moment.

The seven-piece band secured a major slot at the Garma Festival in Arnhem Land, the nation's premier Indigenous event for the sharing of Yolŋu culture, music and ideas.

Wild Honey's red carpet ambitions

Guitarist Adrian Schmidt Mumm said he had been in many bands before, but with Wild Honey, felt like he was finally onto something special.

He had first come across his fellow band members while running an after-school music program in their remote community.

"It's felt like a very steep rise," he said.

"This is our second Garma and we already headlined Friday night, so that's very encouraging and inspiring, and makes you feel like, 'oh, maybe there is something in this'.

"It really feels like there's a substance to it, and an ambition, and the enthusiasm from the band is infectious and makes you want to keep on playing and writing and recording."

The band members are not shy of voicing that ambition — they want to be the next big thing.

Balumba Gondarra says Wild Honey wants to see the bright lights of the world. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Another of Dr M Yunupiŋu's grandsons, Balumba Gondarra, said Wild Honey wanted to make it out of their remote Northern Territory home and see the bright lights of the world.

"See the red carpet, ARIA, that's my dream," he said.

"Play the MCG in Melbourne, see the world.

"To be honest, we've never been to big cities. We grew up in the community. For me, I've never been to Sydney, Melbourne, Canberra."

'Music in our blood'

As they step deeper into the music game, Wild Honey members said they always try to pay homage to their Yolŋu musical heroes; as well as their originals, their set-list is peppered with classics from the Warumpi Band, King Stingray, and of course their grandfather's band.

They have also been mentored by some of those same bands, including King Stingray, who have broken through into the mainstream in recent years themselves with catchy singles like Camp Dog and Milkumana.

Gawukawu Gurruwiwi says he grew up with music in his blood. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

"We grew up with music in our blood," Gurruwiwi said.

"That special tamarind tree, we'd chill around, playing music, watching old man play.

"His legacy, what he left, we can light the pathway to the next generation to come."

As well as Wild Honey, the 2026 Garma stage was graced with some of Australia's finest musicians, from Emma Donovan to the Andrew Gurruwiwi Band, and headliner Baker Boy.

Wild Honey will hit the stage again later this month for the East Arnhem Live festival on August 29, alongside talented artists including Gurruwiwi's musical mum, Dhapanbal.

World.title: Trump, Kushner, oligarchs and flamingos. Welcome to Albania's revolution
World.content:
Inside Albania anger is brewing at a level not seen since the fall of Communism.



The people are protesting for the preservation of a free and fragile paradise.



They’re also protesting against an allegedly "corrupt" government with ties to oligarchs and the underworld, as well as one name in particular … Trump.



Albania's Zvërnec Peninsula is framed by picturesque, tree-covered mountains and, in the distance, is the small island of Sazan which sits like a fortress at the edge of the Adriatic Sea.

People at the beach in Zvërnec, Albania. ( )

The beach here is sparsely populated.

Local fishermen lazily launch dinghies from the shallows, families relax under broad umbrellas, and a handful of local teenagers play football in the wet sand.

In the water between the coastline and the island swim endangered monk seals and rare loggerhead turtles.

Behind the beach lies the vast Narta Lagoon, a thriving ecosystem home to 200 species of precious birdlife — including flocks of flamingos that snack on the shrimp in the briny waters.

Flamingos live in the Narta Lagoon in Zvërnec. ( )

The area is home to endangered monk seals. ( )

Rare loggerhead turtles also swim in the local waters. ( )

The Flamingo Revolution is named after the Narta Lagoon flamingos. ( )

While much of the Mediterranean coastline is lined with luxury hotels, high-end shopping strips and packed beach clubs and bars, Zvërnec remains untouched by modern development.

It is why a controversial proposal has lit the wick for protests in the Albanian capital of Tirana.

"This is one of the last stretches of the Mediterranean that is void of intensive human intervention," Aleksander Trajce, an Albanian environmentalist, told 7.30.

"It's one of the last natural gems we have."

But Zvërnec's status as a wild, untouched paradise may soon be over after the Albanian government green-lit a $6.5 billion luxury resort to be built on the shores of the eastern side of Sazan Island and next to the Narta Lagoon.

Tender and draft design documents leaked online show plans for the opulent resort include thousands of rooms in a luxury complex, featuring a casino and a water park — with rooms and restaurants catered by Carbone, the chic, A-list New York Italian eatery.

Jared Kushner shared this concept art of the project to his X account in 2024. ( )

Concept art of rooms in the proposed resort. ( )

Prestigious Swiss hoteliers Aman have been mooted as the operators of the resort.

Rooms at its properties in the French Alps and Venice fetch about $1,000 a night — the median monthly salary in Albania.

Backing the secluded five-star retreat is Jared Kushner and his wife Ivanka Trump, the daughter of the US president.

Mr Kushner is closely intertwined with his father-in-law's administration and has been a key shadow mediator in peace talks in the Middle East and Ukraine — but is not a government employee.

This technicality has allowed him to continue running his highly profitable private equity firm, Affinity Partners, where, with the backing of Saudi sovereign wealth, he pours billions of dollars into Israeli tech and European real estate.

Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump want to build a sprawling luxury resort. ( )

People on a beach in Vlore. ( )

People cross a wooden footbridge to St Mary's Monastery on Zvërnec Island in Narta Lagoon. ( )

Visitors relaxing by the water. ( )

Investment in Albania's coast has been a key driver of the nation's economy since the communist regime fell in 1990. And successive governments have been eager to bring in foreign cash to build up its scenic coastline.

Mr Trajce, who despite being the executive director of Protection and Preservation of Natural Environment in Albania and one of the country's leading environmentalists, was blindsided by the project.

Aleksandër Trajçe, executive director of Protection and Preservation of Natural Environment in Albania. ( )

"We were never consulted. We were never approached," he said.

"And to our knowledge, nobody — no other serious or reputable organisation or research group that deals with the environment — has been approached."

Kept completely in the dark, Mr Trajce has been forced to piece together the resort's massive scale through incremental media leaks.

What he sees terrifies him.

"Eight stories high, resorts, with apartments, with villas — it feels very much like a real estate development project rather than a tourism development project," he said.

Concept art showing part of the resort on the Zvërnec peninsula. ( )

"It would be the complete destruction of the ecosystem here.

"We are talking about the most fragile part of this protected area.

"The consequences can be as unpredictable and as catastrophic that it's very hard to imagine any other scenario than a complete alteration of the ecosystem."

A dodgy Trump story?

The provenance of the idea for the resort is the subject of heated debate, but according to Ivanka Trump, she and her husband dreamt up the idea while on a glamorous summer sojourn.

In May, speaking on the David Senra podcast, Ms Trump — who works in the family real estate business — recalled the dreamy discovery.

Loading...

"[Jared and I] were on a friend's boat, and we stopped for a swim," she said.

" Effectively, that's how we found it. We swam to the islands. "

The friend was millionaire British financier and earl, Nathaniel Rothschild, and the boat was the baron's 73-metre superyacht Planet 9, which hosted the pair in 2021.

Sazan Island in Albania. ( )

She went on to tell the podcast's host that Sazan was "an unbelievable, beautiful 1,400-hectare private island in the middle of the Mediterranean".

She then claimed she and Mr Kushner climbed across the craggy terrain of the island to reach its peak.

Ms Trump's account has been widely derided in Albania, with critics questioning the veracity of the anecdote.

"When Ivanka said she walked around the island barefoot, I was quite surprised, because the terrain is quite rough," Mr Trajce told 7.30.

Old military buildings are still found on Sazan Island. ( )

A boat off the coast of Sazan Island. ( )

"Even for us as experienced field workers, it's very hard to walk that terrain with proper hiking boots.

"To me it was clear she didn't have a proper connection to the place.

" Yes, the island is beautiful but it's beautiful because it's wild. "

Ms Trump's claim that the island is private and was "found" by her and Mr Kushner is dubious.

The island is public land and was home to a military base for decades.

People on a beach on Sazan Island, Albania. ( )

It has also been a major tourist destination since the beach was opened to the public in 2015.

When 7.30 visited the island, it was clear it was no secret.

Loud music blasted from rented powerboats moored at the shore and hordes of tourists were arriving on passenger ferries — with guides taking them to a small swimming beach.

One group of holiday-makers was eating a catered lunch as their large water taxi completed a leisurely lap of the island.

It's not just the credibility of Ivanka Trump's story that has angered many Albanians — it's the way in which her husband's firm has been given the green light to build on one of the last protected parts of the Mediterranean.

Laws for oligarchs and the underworld

Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama. ( )

In February 2024, the Albanian government led by Prime Minister Edi Rama passed sweeping changes to laws protecting the environment and Albania's protected beaches and parks.

The new legislation allowed Mr Rama's administration to permit (at their discretion) five-star resorts to be built in areas that were previously off-limits.

The laws were passed just three days after the initial plans for the resort were quietly made public by the Kushner team.

It's also since been reported that Mr Rama met Ms Trump and her husband on that 2021 boat trip.

Jared Kushner, far left, and Ivanka Trump, third from left, pose with a group including Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama, second from right. ( )

The government has denied tailoring the laws for the American couple but Albanians are suspicious of the statutory changes.

Redi Muçi, an academic who left his job at Albania's top university to become a representative in the Albanian parliament, told 7.30 that corruption is endemic in Albania, where valuable land sales are often subject to shady deals.

Mr Muçi is particularly alarmed by the government-linked committee headed by Mr Rama that gives him personal oversight of land deals.

He says it is concerning that land often ends up in the hands of figures accused of being connected to the Albanian underworld.

Albanian politician Redi Muçi. ( )

"The Special Investigation Unit issued more than 20 arrest warrants for people related to drug trafficking who have acquired more than a million square metres of construction permits," Mr Muçi told 7.30, in Tirana.

"It's not a problem of the Trump family developing in Albania itself. It's more to do with the corruption that's behind it."

In the case of the Trump-Kushner development there are serious questions surrounding the ownership of the glittering coastline.

The development company backed by Mr Kushner reportedly acquired a portion of the development rights from Arthur Shehu, a Miami-based Albanian businessman.

Mr Shehu is wanted by authorities in Tirana over allegations of drug smuggling and money laundering.

Albania's anti-corruption watchdog is now alleging that Mr Shehu forged the property deeds to the land before selling it for development.

There is no allegation that Mr Kushner, Ms Trump or Affinity Partners committed any wrongdoing.

There are questions over the ownership of the coastline where Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump want to build their resort. ( )

Mr Kushner and Affinity did not respond to the ABC's request for comment.

Villagers in the area are also claiming ancestral ownership of the land, with a case currently before the courts.

Mr Muçi fears the case will languish in the judicial system for years and said precedent suggests locals are often overpowered by large corporations and powerful Albanians when land is contested.

"What happens to the local residents is that they carry on a long legal fight that spreads for decades, but that never concludes with them receiving what they're due," he said.

The Albanian government has been contacted for comment — but Prime Minister Edi Rama has previously dismissed suggestions the development will have a highly adverse effect on the coastline's environment.

Enter the revolution

The government says that its law changes and liberal approach to granting development permits are in the name of tourism and economic development.

In 1990, when Communism fell in Albania, the country was destitute.

Demonstrators at a rally in Tirana in December 1990. ( )

A statue of Albania's former communist leader Enver Hoxha is pushed over in Tirana in February 1991. ( )

Gradually, conditions improved as governments used tourism to bring in cash.

Under Mr Rama, the tourism boom has accelerated, with buildings along the Mediterranean springing up regularly.

Vlore, the bustling beachside city next to the earmarked Trump-Kushner site in Zvërnec, is packed with hotels, restaurants, and tourism infrastructure, including a controversial airport, which is currently under construction.

People on a beach in Vlore, Albania ( )

Over summer, the beaches are packed as Albania's modest population of 2.6 million people swells to about 11 million.

"Of course we need to have tourism," Mr Muçi told 7.30.

A man sits at the beach in Vlore, Albania. ( )

"We need to benefit from the fact that Albania has its mountains, its coastline, good weather. But alongside that, this cannot be the sole economic input in the Albanian economy."

For years Albanians have watched concrete take over their once-untouched beaches with mounting sadness.

Resistance was small in scale.

But that small activist movement was just the prologue to a historic wave of public fury.

'They want to take our nature'

A protester waves the Albanian flag. ( )

On a Friday night in Tirana hundreds of people gather in the main square, under the rich orange glow of the evening sun.

Skanderbeg Square is the main stage for the protest.

Flamingo signs are a common sight. ( )

The protest takes place in Tirana's Skanderbeg Square. ( )

A Flamingo Revolution protest takes place in the capital Tirana. ( )

When 7.30 attended, it was the 41st protest against Albanian development and the Trump-Kushner resort.

Twenty-five-year-old Sona Faudi and her friend, 23-year-old Najada Dafa, went to the square as soon as they finished work.

They attend every day from 7pm.

Sona Faudi regularly attends the protests. ( )

"We need to protect our land. Ivanka Trump wants to buy Sazan Island, but we don't want our land to be treated like private land," Ms Faudi told 7.30.

"They want to take our nature from us.

"Albanians won't profit anything from this because it is being built for rich people, and we have other things we need to be concerned about."

The protests having been taking place since May. ( )

The protests are considered the largest anti-government demonstrations in Albania since the fall of communism. ( )

A man holds up a sign at a protest in Tirana. ( )

The protests began in May when footage surfaced of security personnel restraining a demonstrator at the Trump-Kushner development site.

Widespread public outrage triggered massive protests across Albania, mobilising hundreds of thousands of citizens.

Known as 'The Flamingo Revolution' it is now widely considered the largest anti-government display in the country since Communism fell.

Najada Dafa wears a Flamingo Revolution pin on her shirt. ( )

Ms Dafa, who works as a scientific researcher, said Ms Trump's comments about "finding" the island were also a flashpoint for many Albanians.

"She made it sound like she was Christopher Columbus," she told 7.30.

"It's isolated, of course, but we know it exists — we have been there."

The night 7.30 joined Ms Faudi and Ms Dafa, organisers said about 3,000 people descended on central Tirana to protest.

Albania's capital, Tirana. ( )

"We will never stop protesting because we are Albanians, we are Balkans, and Balkans are very stubborn people," Ms Faudi said.

The demonstrators hope global attention can heap pressure on the Albanian government, and that the EU (of which Albania aims to be a member by 2030) can step in to halt the resort.

But not everyone disapproves of the tourism money rushing into the country's economy.

Some Albanians are relishing the country's willingness to open itself up to the world.

"We were in Communism for 50 years and completely isolated in a country. You cannot imagine how happy we are when we see people from every place of the world," one local told us.

Hotelier Kujtim Devershi supports the proposed development on the coast. ( )

"I think the development has been done in a very nice way. If you go to Spain, you see a similar thing. If you go to Miami, you see a similar thing. Why not in Albania?" he said.

Those within Albania's hospitality industry, including hotelier Kujtim Dervishi, say tourism has been a boon for business.

"The media in Albania and internationally are making too much of a negative issue of Albania's seaside," Mr Derivishi told 7.30.

"The coast is beautiful and great for tourism ... they've been investing in it and that's a good thing, it's strategic."

There is still no timeline on when Mr Kushner and Ms Trump's island dream will become a reality.

But surveyors have been spotted on the beach and a service road has already been constructed.

And while the government has granted the couple preliminary approval, court cases, protests, and concerns from the EU could delay the project for several years.

Activists say the Flamingo Revolution will roll on for as long as it takes.

Reporter: Elias Clure

World.title: Three incidents keep search and rescue crews busy in Tasmania
World.content:
A man and a woman from southern Tasmania have been helped to safety after their four-wheel drive became stuck on a remote track south of Queenstown on the state's west coast.

"The man and woman told police they had been driving for several hours and became disoriented on the tracks, eventually becoming stuck on a very difficult section which they were unable to pass," Tasmania Police said in a statement.

Police said they were told one of the two people had a physical disability, which meant they could not walk without assistance.

Influencers and winter hiking Don't plan a bushwalk based on what an Instagram influencer may have supposedly achieved, a veteran rescuer says, ahead of Tasmania's winter season.

Police from Queenstown and Rosebery set off about 5:30pm yesterday, finding them about 7:45pm last night.

"There were no injuries and the vehicle was successfully recovered and driven back to Queenstown," police said.

Search and rescue crews were also called to help two bushwalkers — one in the state's north, the other on Flinders Island — yesterday.

"A 44-year-old northern Tasmanian man spent about five hours lost in the Meander Falls area on Saturday night after becoming separated from his walking companion and veering off the track back to the car park," police said.

"Tasmania Police Search and Rescue officers were deployed to the scene and, supported by State Emergency Service personnel and using drone technology, were able to safely locate the man about midnight.

"He was walked out with no significant injuries."

The rescue helicopter was also sent to the area but the weather conditions meant it was unable to fly.

Going hiking? You should take a locator beacon — here's how to use it When you go hiking, experts say a personal locator beacon should be a non-negotiable. So how do they work, and where do you get one?

Earlier yesterday, the helicopter was used to winch a walker to safety after she got into difficulty on Mount Killiecrankie, on Flinders Island.

Police said the Queensland woman, aged in her mid-50s, called police using a mobile phone late yesterday afternoon, telling them she was unable to walk out after a solo bushwalk to Mount Killiecrankie.

The helicopter crew found her about 7pm. She also had no significant injuries.

"Police are reminding bushwalkers and motorists of the need to be prepared for trips into the Tasmanian bush, and to always carry appropriate safety equipment," Tasmania Police said.

World.title: Trump holds off on new strikes against Iran amid emerging 'deal'
World.content:
US President Donald Trump says he will order American forces to hold off on new strikes against Iran, saying Middle East allies have reached the parameters of a deal to end the five-month old war.

The emerging deal "would include the Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT, and an end to Iran's nuclear threat," Mr Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Trump threatens more strikes on Iran Iran says any aggression by the US and Israel will be met with a proportionate response.

"Based on this request, I have agreed, for the future benefit of the WORLD and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL."

Israel had agreed to join the US in the commitment to try to complete the agreement with Iran that would bring about an end to the war, he added.

Saudis concerned about Iran retaliation

Prior to the announcement, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the kingdom's de facto leader, spoke with Mr Trump by phone and raised concerns about the US potentially escalating the conflict with Iran, according to a person familiar with the leaders' discussion.

The Saudis, according to the person briefed on the substance of the call but not authorised to comment publicly, are concerned that Tehran could respond with attacks on the energy infrastructure of the kingdom and other Gulf countries.

War leaders navigate Trump's moods Volodymyr Zelenskyy must have felt a little triggered when he walked into the Oval Office this week. But Trump's public anger is now often directed at another at-war ally.

The crown prince during Saturday's call sought clarity from Mr Trump on what potential new action he was considering to take against Iran, the source said.

A White House official, who was not authorised to comment publicly and requested anonymity, confirmed the leaders spoke on Saturday but did not offer any detail.

Kuwait said on Saturday it responded to a new round of drone attacks from Iran while a tanker was struck in the strategic waterway.

Israel carried out heavy strikes on the Gaza Strip after the Palestinian militant group Hamas agreed to disarm.

US threatened new strikes before announcement

Mr Trump on Friday had threatened more strikes on Iran as the US pressed for the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.

Speaking to reporters during a meeting with members of his cabinet at the Camp David presidential retreat in Maryland, Mr Trump said "we just want to win" in Iran and that the US would hit Iran "very hard" until it couldn't "take it anymore".

Later that day, White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt expressed the US administration's frustration that Tehran had last month signed a memorandum of understanding on a truce but then quickly "broke it, shot at commercial ships, and killed American soldiers".

At Camp David, Donald Trump said the US would hit Iran "very hard" until it could not "take it anymore". (Reuters: Daniel Heuer)

On Saturday, the US State Department issued new security alerts for Americans in 10 countries in the region to exercise heightened caution due to the escalating tensions with Iran.

The warnings, covering Bahrain, Israel, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, urged US citizens to prepare for the possibility of flight cancellations, temporary airspace closures and other travel disruptions.

New attacks on Kuwait and shipping

Kuwait's military said on Saturday that its forces were responding to drone attacks, which were part of Iran's assaults on the country.

In a statement, Major General Saud Abdulaziz Al-Otaibi, spokesperson for Kuwait's Defense Ministry, said the drones hit "a number of vital facilities", including a government structure in the country's north.

He said there were no casualties.

The British Navy said on Saturday that a tanker was struck and a separate explosion hit close to a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Oman.

From coffee to commute, the Iran war is shaping our morning routines This century's biggest oil shock is entering its sixth month, with no end in sight as war in Iran continues. Is it showing up in your daily budget?

No casualties were reported in either incident.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Organisation said an unknown projectile hit the vessel on Friday, 11 nautical miles north-east of Lima, Oman.

The attack damaged the vessel's engine room.

The group said that on Saturday a large splash and an explosion were reported close to another tanker while it was sailing 21 nautical miles north-west of Khasab city.

Separately, crude oil appeared to be leaking and spreading in recent days from a sanctioned tanker grounded off the coast of Oman, close to a marine protected area, satellite images reviewed by the Associated Press show.

Iran has repeatedly attacked vessels attempting to transit through the Strait of Hormuz without its authorisation as part of its ongoing conflict with the US.

Israel strikes Gaza after Hamas says it will disarm

Intense Israeli strikes on Friday night and Saturday killed at least four people in central and northern Gaza and wounded dozens more, according to local health officials.

The strikes in Gaza followed evacuation warnings by Israel's military, which said on Saturday that it had struck Hamas targets across the territory and dismantled five Hamas storage facilities.

The strikes came after Hamas confirmed on Friday that it would disarm in a potential breakthrough for ending the war in Gaza, although major obstacles remain.

Iranian hackers suspected in US cyber attack Cyber attacks on several local water systems in the US carry telltale signs of a hacker group affiliated with Iran, in what is an increasingly common type of warfare.

Palestinians in Gaza, most of whom are displaced or live in camps, received the news with both hope and scepticism.

A 24-year-old tuktuk driver, Abdel Moneim Aboul-Roos, who lost his leg in an Israeli strike, said he did not care about "talk about withdrawal and disarmament" as long as essentials such as food and medicine remained lacking.

Israel has not officially commented on the Hamas deal, which is part of a US-brokered ceasefire announced last October.

That agreement called for Hamas to disarm and hand over power to an independent Palestinian administration.

Israel was to withdraw and an International Stabilisation Force was to be deployed.

In a post on X, Israeli far-right lawmaker Itamar Ben-Gvir called the deal "unacceptable" and said the killings in Gaza must continue.

"Israel must win," he said.

Egypt, a key Gaza ceasefire mediator, lauded Hamas and other Palestinian groups for "their positive response" in the phased peace plan, Egyptian state-run media reported.

World.title: Australia's Rhiannan Iffland becomes greatest cliff diver of all time
World.content:
Australia's Rhiannan Iffland has officially become the greatest cliff diver of all time after winning the penultimate event of the season in Mostar, in southern Bosnia and Herzegovina.

The 34-year-old from Newcastle arrived at the historic bridge knowing that victory on Saturday local time from the 21m platform would seal her 10th World Series title in a row and 48th victory of her career.

An estimated 23,000 fans turned out across three days of competition to see Iffland tally 363.20 points, finishing ahead of Canada's Molly Carlson (361.60) and Australian Xantheia Pennisi (345.80) to again lift the King Kahekili Trophy.

Pennisi's 10th career podium came thanks to a personal best total score, while Stella Forsyth (276.15), the third Australian participating, came 10th in the 12-woman field.

Rhiannan Iffland is now a commanding 27 points ahead of her nearest rival in the standings. (Getty Images: Dean Treml)

"I'm super stoked, and I guess it's time to process and then celebrate," said Iffland, who entered the final round just 1.6 points ahead of Carlson in sweltering conditions.

"I knew deep down in my heart that it wasn't going to be an easy one today. I knew Molly wasn't going to leave without putting up a good fight."

Iffland's triumph — her 48th in 59 stops — moved her to 77 points after four of the five stops on tour, an unassailable 27 clear of Carlson, with compatriot Pennisi (35) fifth.

The win — thanks to a stunning inward three somersaults half twist tuck dive into the Neretva River — also moved Iffland ahead of Englishman Gary Hunt on the all-time wins list.

It is the third time she has wrapped up the title with a stop to spare.

Romania's Constantin Popovici (right) joined Australia's Rhiannon Iffland in celebrations after winning the men's event in Mostar. (Getty Images: Romina Amato)

"Forty-eight out of 50-something starts, it's nuts," the five-time high diving world champion added.

"But I guess the recipe really comes down to passion, and drive and hard work. There is no secret recipe to being so consistent. Practice, practice, practice, and it paid off for me."

The men's event was won by Romania's Constantin Popovici, who edged out Britain's Aidan Heslop and James Lichenstein of the United States.

Heslop leads the standings on 68 points, followed by Lichtenstein (57) and Popovici (55).

Divers now have an extended two-month break before the final event of the 2026 calendar takes place in Polignano a Mare, Italy — the home of European cliff diving — from September 27.

World.content:
The Cronulla Sharks have continued their rich vein of form, overcoming a slow start to claim an impressive 32-16 win over fellow top-eight side South Sydney.

The Sharks conceded the first try, and had a player in the sin bin early, before scoring five tries to consolidate their position inside the NRL's top four.

Sharks halfback Nicho Hynes was a perfect six-out-of-six in front of goal, taking his current goal-kicking streak to 32 consecutive successful attempts.

That is a new club record, and now has Hynes just three shy of the all-time NRL record held by Canterbury Bulldogs great Hazem El Masri.

World.title: Tigers can breathe easy again, find third win as West Coast rue inaccuracy
World.content:
In today’s AFL Briefing, your wrap of footy news: A West Coast player went to ground in obvious pain after a gut punch from a Richmond opponent.

Surgery for Swan after suffering a sickening lower leg injury. Tiger in the gun for behind-the-play blow Marc McGowan Richmond may have dodged a second wooden spoon in three years with a second win this season over a wayward West Coast as Tigers defender Luke Trainor faces match review scrutiny for a gut punch. Adem Yze’s men had lost eight matches in a row by an average of almost 50 points, and were on the bottom, behind Essendon on percentage with a miserable 2-17 win-loss record.



But Richmond took advantage of the visiting Eagles’ yips in front of goal at the MCG on Sunday to climb above the Bombers and within one win of 16th-placed West Coast, who were 3.17 at one stage before losing 12.12 (84) to 9.19 (73). The result eases pressure on coach Yze, who has presided over only 10 victories in 66 matches in what is a full-blown rebuild at Tigerland. Yze re-signed until the end of 2028 in November last year, and chief executive Shane Dunne said he had the club’s backing. There were only 12 points between the sides at three-quarter-time, but goals to Richmond premiership veterans Tom Lynch and Toby Nankervis blew the margin out before they hung on for a narrow win.



The Eagles, who have been competitive most weeks despite their lack of success, have plenty to be rueful about, with spearhead Jake Waterman’s 2.6 day – on top of putting another kick out on the full – headlining their woeful goalkicking. Elliot Yeo had a chance to slice the difference to six points with a gettable set shot inside the last two minutes, but sprayed it to the left, only for No.1 draft pick Sam Lalor to seal the contest at the other end not long after. View post on X West Coast were trying to beat Richmond at the MCG for the first time since 2015, but the 33,737 crowd instead were able to celebrate a rare Tigers triumph this season. Tim Taranto led Richmond’s charge all afternoon with 32 disposals and a game-high 11 clearances, while Harley Reid was excellent in a losing cause with 34 touches, 20 contested possessions and nine clearances. Mid-season draftee Marcus Herbert (34 disposals) was also prolific for the Eagles.



Trainor’s behind-the-play gut punch to West Coast’s Jack Williams came in the second quarter of the clubs’ clash after they engaged in a standing wrestle. Once Trainor broke loose, he wound up and struck the Eagle with a clenched left fist. The second-year Tiger, playing his 30th career game, instantly jogged away while Williams went to ground in obvious pain and went to the bench soon after. It is the type of incident the AFL aimed to stamp out when it announced tribunal changes in February, revealing that incidents where a player strikes another in the chest or stomach were more likely to be graded medium impact and result in at least a one-game suspension. Match review officer Michael Christian has typically graded these incidents as low impact, which led to fines rather than bans. Trainor’s gut punch was also an intentional action.



Richmond have a lengthy injury list that includes key defensive options Noah Balta, Josh Gibcus and Campbell Gray, so losing Trainor would present the Tigers with more challenges down back. More to come Surgery for ‘devastated’ Swan after leg injury Peter Ryan Sydney Swans defender Will Edwards had surgery on Sunday after suffering a sickening lower leg injury against the Saints on Saturday.



Will Edwards was taken from the ground with a broken leg. AFL Photos Edwards appeared to dislocate his ankle and was carted from the field having received pain medication during the Swans’ 19-point win at Marvel Stadium. Coach Dean Cox described the injury as “devastating” for the 23-year-old, who made his debut this season following a series of leg fractures and infections. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 If the Crows fade away yet again, could this Essendon contender step up? The club is expected to provide more information about the injury and his prognosis after the operation. Midfielder James Rowbottom will also have surgery to repair a broken hand sustained during the match against St Kilda. For the Saints, Jack Silvagni (dislocated shoulder) and Tom De Koning (hip pointer) are in doubt for next Sunday night’s match against their former team, Carlton.
