World.title: Quick hits: Sprinter's surprise, a bored prince and a stunning upset
World.content:
An Australian sprinter receives a surprise visit, Jamaica celebrates in style after beating the Diamonds and Prince George looks bored at the cycling.

Here are the quick hits from day nine of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Surprise guests shock Aussie sprinter

Chloe Mannix-Power (right) had some fans she was not expecting to see in the stands. (Reuters: Phil Noble)

Chloe Mannix-Power somewhat controversially missed out on an individual 100-metre berth at these Games, but hit the track for the first time in the women's 4x100m heats.

In the moments after she and teammates Ebony Lane, Monique Hanlon and Georgia Harris made it through to the women's 4x100m final, Mannix-Power looked up into the stands and received quite a shock.

"I thought [my parents] were at home watching on the lounge, but no they're up in the top of the grandstand cheering me on," she said.

"My parents love a surprise moment, they've done it before, so to be honest I kind of had a little feeling they would be up there, but they never tell me they're here until the end of the race."

Mannix-Power later helped Australia finish fourth in the final.

2. Prince George bored?

Prince William, Princess Catherine and their three children took in a few of the sports on day nine.

Prince George, however, seemed as though he wanted to be anywhere else when they visited the velodrome.

Prince George watches on at the velodrome. (AP: Andrew Milligan)

Earlier, the royals watched on as the Diamonds lost 46-45 to Jamaica in a major upset in the netball semifinals.

The Prince and Princess of Wales took to Instagram to thank the athletes for putting on a show.

The Prince and Princess of Wales and their family watching the netball at the Hydro in Glasgow. (Getty Images)

"Incredible atmosphere at the Commonwealth Games today," a post from their official Instagram account read.

"Watching world-class talent compete and seeing the power of sport to bring people together is truly special.

"Thank you to everyone involved for such a wonderful day."

3. 'Absolute scenes'

Jamaica celebrates its win over the Diamonds. (Getty Images: Lintao Zhang)

Not only did the Royals take in Jamaica's shock victory, but they also witnessed some of the wildest celebrations seen at the Commonwealth Games.

After Sophie Dwyer missed the shot that would have sent the semifinal to extra time, the entire Jamaican squad celebrated like they never had before.

We lost count of how many social media videos featured the caption: "Absolute scenes."

Loading Instagram content

For the Jamaicans, this was personal.

They were still hurting from their loss to the Diamonds in the 2022 Commonwealth Games final in Birmingham.

"We're carrying a bit of vengeance from the last Commonwealth Games," Jamaica captain Shamera Sterling-Humphrey said.

"We've graduated from bronze medals. We didn't want bronze this year."

Jamaica faces New Zealand in the final, while the Diamonds meet England in the bronze medal play-off.

4. Montag admits to being 'selfish'

Elizabeth McMillen led Jemima Montag for most of the race, but did not win gold. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

It was an Australian sweep of the medals in the women's 10,000m race walk, but the fight for the gold medal between teammates was a fierce one.

Australian Elizabeth McMillen and Jemima Montag broke clear from the pack early and led for the entire race.

McMillen was at the front, with Montag her shadow just behind.

Montag's strategy was to use McMillen as protection from the wind, a tactic which worked to perfection.

McMillen's lead for the better part of 23 laps of the 25-lap race, before Montag ducked out from behind her and put on the burners in a decisive attack to claim gold.

It was a move she had no regrets over.

"In a race you have to be selfish. Unfortunately it's an individual sport, not a team," Montag said.

"If it was cycling or something with drafting, where you do change the lead around then absolutely.

"But as much as I would love to, sometimes you have to forget it's a teammate that you care about and just remember it's another competitor and it's another body that in front of you and to ultimately be selfish."

McMillen was not particularly happy, but understood.

"What can you do? That's racing for you," McMillen said.

"I did look back a few times thinking, 'Are you going to help out here?', but no. I was the rabbit today, so what are you going to do?"

5. Indian boxer explains celebration

Arundhati Choudhary celebrates in her unique way. (Getty Images: Francois Nel)

India boxer Arundhati Choudhary is a beacon of positivity inside and outside the ring.

Choudhary, who won gold in the women's 70-kilogram category in Glasgow, takes inspiration from a Hindu deity, Lord Rama.

This is why she opts for a bow and arrow celebration.

"In India we have Lord Rama, who killed negativity with his bow," Choudhary explained.

"Last year I was suffering from surgery and my family was also suffering from many problems.

"So I just throw the bow and arrow and shoot all the negativity out."

World.title: 'Pattern of missteps': Football bodies launch stunning Infantino rebuke
World.content:
Successfully stopping Gianni Infantino's FIFA plan to sell World Cup profits to private investors was the first half of a high-stakes game in global soccer politics.

The second half kicked off overnight with what seemed a clear aim of ending Infantino's decade-long presidency.

"No option should be off the table," said European soccer body UEFA, whose president Aleksander Čeferin has led the fight against Infantino in a seismic week for FIFA.

"The current FIFA leadership has not only lost UEFA's confidence but also that of many other members of the football family."

Aleksander Čeferin (left) has been a vocal critic of Gianni Infantino's latest quest to privatise part of FIFA. (Getty Images: Nicolò Campo/LightRocket)

After that comment, the governing body for North and Central American and Caribbean soccer (CONCACAF) called for accountability, saying: "A [World Cup] proposal of this magnitude does not reach that stage by accident. It is a symptom of leadership that has stopped putting football first. This recent unilateral and egregious act of poor governance and leadership follows a pattern of missteps and similar behaviour. A full review of this leadership must now take place."

Mr Infantino had proposed creating a $US20 billion ($28.5 billion) company to run the World Cup with private investors but drew backlash that grew every day since Tuesday's announcement.

The FIFA president was forced to scrap the plan early Saturday after his senior adviser who sat on a White House panel resigned and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), joined Europe and North America in opposing it.

UEFA's blistering statement

UEFA, the governing body of European soccer, issued its blistering statement hours after FIFA announced it was withdrawing its private equity plan.

"We cannot keep going on like this with secret schemes on fast-track timescales, cooked up by faceless individuals and of dubious benefit to the game," UEFA said.

"We must identify those responsible and hold them to account.

"It is right that, in the coming days and weeks, UEFA will work with its associations and in close cooperation with other confederations to reflect on how this happened and devise a plan to make sure that it cannot occur again."

Lise Klaveness (right) looks on as Gianni Infantino takes a selfie with a fan during the World Cup. (Getty Images: Jean Catuffe)

Norwegian soccer federation president Lise Klaveness, an elected member of the UEFA executive committee, said steps must be taken to protect the integrity of the sport.

"The entire framework of international football cooperation was unnecessarily put at risk in pursuit of individual interests rather than the best interests of the game," Mr Klaveness said.

"This has been visible to many for a long time, including those of us elected to positions intended to safeguard checks and balances and provide ongoing oversight. We have to recognise that these mechanisms have not worked well enough."

Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa (right) also criticised the way the privatisation plan had been rolled out. (Getty Images: Kevin C. Cox)

The president of the AFC, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, said, "The future of global football must always be shaped through proper consultation, collective dialogue and respect for the established governance structures of our game."

Mr Infantino's audacious bid fell apart after UEFA's 55-member nations agreed Thursday to boycott the World Cup and all other FIFA competitions. CONCACAF and the AFC also said they opposed the plan.

CONCACAF's statement added that FIFA leaders have "a duty of service over power. Where that duty is not upheld, accountability cannot be optional".

FIFA's internal revolt

There was also an internal revolt.

Mr Infantino's senior adviser, Carlos Cordeiro, a former Goldman Sachs banker who represented the soccer body on the White House Task Force for the World Cup, resigned and urged other senior FIFA staff to speak out.

Hours later, FIFA chief operating officer Kevin Lamour issued a statement to the Associated Press, saying FIFA staff were deceived by Infantino's lack of openness in planning the sale over recent months and that the project must not continue.

Kevin Lamour says the FIFA plan is a project of "one person". (Getty Images: Joosep Martinson)

"It is the project of one person," wrote Mr Lamour, a longtime colleague of Mr Infantino at both FIFA and UEFA.

"Not only must this project not go ahead … but the time has now come for football political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions."

Mr Infantino had proposed spinning off FIFA's commercial businesses — including World Cups and Club World Cups for men and women — into a $US20 billion subsidiary with 20 per cent owned by private investors.

The "anchor investor", described by FIFA, is a New York-based investment firm launched by Joshua Kushner, the younger brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner.

This is not Infantino's first big plan to flop

A tumultuous week in international soccer is at least the third time Mr Infantino has rocked it with an ambitious plan many in the sport saw as reckless.

But the fallout from FIFA's Joshua Kushner-backed plan is the first time UEFA has acted quickly to create momentum for removing the man who was its former long-time employee.

In 2018, Mr Infantino pushed a secretive offer of $US25 billion from Japan's SoftBank to create new competitions, which posed a long-term risk to continental events for clubs and national teams.

Vladimir Putin awarded an Order of Friendship to Gianni Infantino after the 2018 World Cup in Russia. (Getty Images: Mikhail Metzel/TASS)

In 2021, Mr Infantino proposed playing World Cups every two years instead of four — an idea that also angered the International Olympic Committee where he is an elected member.

Both plans created big rifts in the sport and were eventually dropped by FIFA.

Despite the turmoil, Mr Infantino was re-elected unopposed in 2019 and 2023.

The third time is shaping up to be different.

November 18 is the deadline for candidates to enter the next presidential contest, exactly four months ahead of the vote in Rabat, Morocco, where FIFA has its African headquarters.

FIFA statutes allow Mr Infantino one more four-year term in office. The failed spin-off venture seemed like a way to create a commissioner-like role for Mr Infantino beyond 2031, likely paying much more than his current annual salary and a bonus deal of more than $US6 million.

Gianni Infantino with Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al-Thani and Jordan's Crown Prince Hussein at the FIFA Arab Cup 2025. (Getty Images: Noushad Thekkayil/NurPhoto)

It would take 106 votes to ensure a majority in a contested election. Continents surely do not vote uniformly en bloc, but most of Europe's 55, plus Asia's 46 and CONCACAF's 35 FIFA members would be a solid base.

The Qatar FA issued a statement in support of Infantino on Saturday.

Its president, Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa bin Ahmed Al Thani, said: "We welcome FIFA President Gianni Infantino's decision to withdraw the FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal in the interest of the global football community.

"While the proposal had merit, we applaud the wisdom behind prioritising unity among Member Associations. The Qatar Football Association fully supports president Infantino's efforts to continue growing and strengthening the game globally."

World.title: One final clean sweep proves Aussie track stars are the real deal
World.content:
The main event for most of the crowd at Scotstoun Stadium lived up to the hype.

Scottish world record holder Josh Kerr utterly bossed a chaotic men's mile final, teaching Australian hope Cameron Myers a lesson in competition racing.

Twenty-year-old Myers came into the Games in phenomenal form and pledged to not let the hometown favourite out of his sight in the final, but once he was boxed in and Kerr got a break, it was curtains with half a lap to go.

Josh Kerr lit up Scotstoun. (Getty Images: Ross MacDonald/SNS Group)

"He smashed me," a visibly disappointed Myers said.

The inexperienced young gun pledged to learn from it and clearly enjoyed his time in the "electric" atmosphere.

But the finale for a historic athletics program for Australia came about half an hour later, when three Australian stars lined up in the women's mile.

We're used to see it in the swimming, but this time it was an international track meet that staged a replay of the Australian championships as Abbey Caldwell, Jess Hull and Claudia Hollingsworth went around the track four times.

Stunning day of Comm Games success for Australia Australia stuns the field to claim gold in the men's 4x100m relay for the first time since 1974 on a packed night final night of athletics action.

When they ran the equivalent 1,500 metres at the national championships in April, it was a debacle.

Hollingsworth tripped Hull, which held up Caldwell, who was pipped by Sarah Billings.

Hull and Caldwell lodged protests, Hollingsworth was disqualified, and Billings was installed as national champion.

After her unusual elevation to the crown, Billings chose to only race the 800m in Glasgow, winning bronze, and her competitors from that night in Sydney stepped in as the clear fastest milers in the country.

The women pulled off the triumph Camweon Myers (right) could not. (Getty Images: Ross MacDonald/SNS Group)

Lining up in the Commonwealth Games final right next to Hull, Caldwell burst off the line, while Hull held back and watched as Hollingsworth settled into the pack ahead of her.

Like the nats, it was a slow race, raising the risk of another late calamity.

Instead, with 200 metres to go, Caldwell burst clear and Hull joined her.

Hull couldn't match Caldwell but, just like when she won silver behind Rose Davies in the 5,000m, she was beaming as her teammate crossed the line ahead of her.

Abbey Caldwell crossed ahead of Jess Hull, the woman who paved the path for her. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

Meanwhile, the in-stadium announcer broke the news that the podium sweep was on as Hollingsworth, seemingly boxed in with the typically rambunctious peloton, found the space and energy to burst past Naomi Korir and claim bronze.

Caldwell had predicted a podium sweep before the athletics program started in a manner portraying matter-of-fact confidence, rather than arrogant bluster.

Even after the prediction came true, it was the importance of their presence on the start line, 9.34 metres behind the spot where Caldwell snared gold 4 minutes and 39.31 seconds later, that Hull remarked upon.

"The Aussies are a force; on that start line we're a threat," she said.

"We've done it at Commonwealth level and the next step is to do it at [world] championships, get three of us in the final and then the odds are pretty high that you're gonna bring home a couple of medals."

The women's middle distance has been the jewel in the Australian track crown before the sprinters joined the party in the past couple of years.

But this podium sweep in the first female Commonwealth mile in history, Caldwell said, truly "put [them] on the map".

"We are the best and I think we can prove that we are the best and we will come and compete for those [Olympic and world] medals," she said.

"We do all wanna keep competing and we are worldwide competitors.

"Jess paved that path for us; we're here to compete internationally, we've accomplished the Commonwealth and now we move onto the big world stage."

If Glasgow 2026 was the coming-out party for Australia's new short-track guns, it marked the coming of age for Caldwell, Hull, Hollingsworth and Billings, who were holding up the tartan long before it was cool.

World.title: Riders sent flying in spectacular crash as Aussie avoids carnage to medal
World.content:
A Malaysian rider was stretchered off the track and two others also needed medical attention after a mass pile-up in Commonwealth Games cycling.

As riders jockeyed for position with one lap left in the men's 10 kilometre scratch race, a crash in the back half of the bunch took down seven riders, with all who crashed not finishing the race.

The three Australians dodged the carnage and Tom Cornish went on to win silver behind England's Henry Hobbs.

But Malaysian New Joe Lau was taken from the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome on a stretcher. Red Walters of Grenada has a suspected broken collarbone and Canadian Jonathan Hinse was also in the hands of medical staff for several minutes before he was able to walk gingerly back to the team pits.

It was the first major crash after three days of track cycling at the Games.

"In racing, we're pretty used to the chaos. When you hear something like that and it's behind you, it's almost a sigh of relief — just because you're in front of it and you don't have to dodge anyone," Cornish said.

"So that was quite lucky.

"At that point, it's an all-out sprint anyway and there's not really much you can change.

"I was lucky to hold it up, I think."

Australia's Tom Cornish holds up his silver medal after avoiding the carnage in the men's 10km scratch race. (Getty Images: Molly Darlington)

The old maxim in cycling is that there are two types of riders — those who have crashed and those who are about to crash.

Cornish has crashed five times this year already and knows he is lucky not to break any bones.

"If it just happens to be one person further forward, you crash. If it doesn't then you make it through and that's kind-of how it is," Cornish said.

"It's something we're used to. I've been doing the sport for almost 20 years and it just becomes part of it."

Fellow Australian Oli Bleddyn did well to avoid the falling riders, while Blake Agnoletto was clear of the carnage.

"I was lucky enough to have the boys working for me today. Both of them are so strong in their own right, they probably could have been up there as well," Cornish said of their team riding.

"I was pretty lucky to have them."

World.title: The new wave of working women taking up golf
World.content:
Melissa Miegel found a new love at 37 years of age.

It happened when she least expected it on a quiet Sunday about five months ago.

At her father's invitation, she tagged along to his weekend activity.

She and golf have not been apart for a weekend since.

She is one of a growing cohort of women who have started spending time on the green.

Melissa Miegel has been playing golf for almost six months. (ABC Riverland: Shannon Pearce)

According to Golf Australia, women's participation is increasing at almost double the rate of men.

It estimates around 60 per cent of people who started playing golf in the past two years were women.

As a mental health worker, Ms Miegel has found the pace and setting of golf to be a safe space.

"I have a very busy brain a lot of the time, so I think it's been a really good opportunity to get outside and actually be more focused on the thing that's directly in front of me," she said.

"For me it's about practising, being more present in what I'm doing and in the moment and slowing down.

"It's a good way to challenge myself as well."

Melissa Miegel is working with a local coach to encourage more women in her region to try the sport. (ABC Riverland: Shannon Pearce)

Encouraging more women to join her in her home region of South Australia's Riverland has become a focus for Ms Miegel.

She believes it is a space where women who are already juggling family, work and life commitments can slow down and find time for themselves.

"I've done a lot of questioning about what it actually looks like for golf because I think people have perceptions of 18 holes, going out there [and] spending hours on end," Ms Miegel said.

Women finding their way

While golf has had a long history as a sport for men that takes hours to play, women are finding ways to make it work around life's busyness.

For this reason, driving ranges and simulators have become popular with women, making up 50 per cent of users with an average age of 38.

Most new golfers begin playing off-course. (ABC News: Dallas Freedman)

Women are also playing three times more nine-hole rounds of golf than men.

"You can play a round of golf in two hours, you can play the driving range, and you still get that social connection that you're really craving," said Golf Australia's head of women and girls Tamara Mason.

"You can wear what you want, you can show up with whoever you want, when you want, and you can fit that in."

She said those less traditional formats were also more accessible.

"You can show up 10 minutes later if the kids are late to school or if the meeting ran over," she said.

"You don't have that fear of disappointing people if you don't show up at your tee time."

Tamara Mason says regional golf clubs are finding the most success at fostering community to welcome in women. (ABC News: Dallas Freedman)

Beyond the format, Ms Mason said there was also a need for change around the culture of many clubs.

"We do have some work to do with our clubs and venues that perhaps only see things a particular way," she said.

"We know that there's a whole other customer base out there looking for something different.

"We know that women being physically active don't want to be judged when they're playing the sport."

Driving the change

Back in the Riverland, ex-PGA professional and coach Jamie Clutterham has been working with Ms Miegel, trying to break stereotypes by running clinics and programs for women and girls.

Jamie Clutterham believes including women in the golf community makes it stronger. (ABC Riverland: Anita Ward)

"In the past 21 months we've activated some programs, and we're seeing the start of, hopefully, a new women's golf world up here in the Riverland," he said.

" A lot of them will say to me 'I'm never going to get off the ground' and they walk away half an hour later happy that they've hit a shot. "

He said around 90 women have become regular golfers in the region across four local clubs.

Women now make up 42 per cent of all golfers in Australia, according to Golf Australia. (ABC Riverland: Shannon Pearce)

A group of community coaches also help him run the sessions to try and make a space in the sport that does not require competition.

"I try and bring new golfers into a coaching space and give them some confidence and competence, and hand them over to some mentors who help with the golf course play, become comfortable with the etiquette and the club environment," Mr Clutterham said.

"If we can activate even just a few people to enjoy that, enjoy some golf and be in a happy space, then I think we're ticking a box there."

Ms Miegel's advice is to give it a go.

"You don't have to be good enough to start playing, but I think you have to start playing to be at least trying to improve yourself and get better," she said.

Tech.title: Angela Nissel faces down grief with a laugh
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Angela Nissel’s latest book, Good Grief, Pass the Bread, Mom Is Dead, is my kind of memoir. Sure, it’s a deeply emotional tale about caring for a terminally ill parent. But it’s delivered with the sort of gallows humor that I often turn to to get me through tough times.

Of course, that sort of dark humor should come as no surprise from Nissel. She first made a splash with The Broke Diaries, which grew out of a blog she kept in college detailing her daily struggles and, at times, embarrassment at being a broke student. Eventually she went on to produce and write for hit shows including Scrubs and The Boondocks.

One of her most lasting contributions is undeniably Okayplayer, which she co-founded with Questlove. Though, as we’ll find out shortly, being involved with one of the most important online outlets in hip hop is something of a bittersweet memory for Nissel.

Oh, and she has my favorite GIF submission yet.

What is your most indispensable tool?

A knockoff Swiss Army Knife. It was a gift from the Scrubs grips over 20 years ago. I always have a screwdriver, a knife, and a corkscrew in my pocket. I feel like a badass.

Which is the most underappreciated?

My dog. He’s analog and breaks down my cardboard boxes in seconds. Now they all fit in the recycle bin.

What is the first app you install on a new phone or computer? (Do not count preinstalled software like Gmail.)

Craigslist. Youngins sleep on Craigslist. I’ve found a free patio set and in the early aughts when I was lonely and new in L.A. I made a friend to go clubbing with. I forgot my wallet, and she thought I was scamming her and we never hung out again, but I still love Craigslist.

What is one thing you wish you could change about your phone?

That I somehow still butt dial people. The phone biometrically knows my face, but can’t tell when it’s my wallet accidentally dialing someone?

What sites do you have pinned to your tab bar?

Wordle. Connections. Essays I swear I’m going to get around to reading but never do. Now I feel badly. I’m going to read one.

How many tabs do you have open right now?

I limited myself to four or my anxiety starts skyrocketing.

Which social media platform do you use the most (if any)?

Instagram, because I’ve been told by my book publisher that in 2026 I have to make “charismatic vertical videos” to sell my latest book. I’m working on being both vertical and charismatic.

What is your happy place online?

A small corner of Reddit where we laugh at the shenanigans of one celebrity wife. I love that place so much I even thanked our group by nickname in my latest book’s acknowledgments.

What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?

My first Fitbit. For a person who grew up on Commodore 64s that took an hour to load video games, wearable tech that instantly tells you how lazy you are seemed like something out of The Jetsons. Now robots are performing surgeries, and the goalpost for futuristic tech has moved.

Which was the most disappointing?

Wearable tech that was supposed to shock me into breaking bad habits. I was like, “Why am I doing this to myself?”

What game do you have the fondest memories of?

Castle Wolfenstein! The mechanics of that game on the Commodore 64 blew me away! Of course, now, it looks like Pong compared to newer games, but when I played it with my brother, I remember feeling like I was in the future, yet killing Nazis from the past.

What is one thing you wish you had created?

I wish I’d created The Blackening. It’s a movie. It’s so brilliant that I’m unsure how they got it made. A lot of brilliance tends to die in development out here in Hollywood to make way for “sure money bet” reboots.

What creation are you most proud of?

The groundbreaking site I created with Questlove.

Which are you least proud of?

The groundbreaking site I created with Questlove. For 25 years, I’ve had to answer questions about why the only woman involved isn’t mentioned in the creation of the website, why the man I hired suddenly replaced me, or why I don’t know who owns the site. I’ve also learned of how many women — mostly of color — have been erased from their creations as the Internet moved from “cool place to hang” to corporate megamall. I’m proud of my part in Internet hip-hop history, but I hate how many women I meet who have been erased.

What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received?

Be interesting and interested! That means get offline and have things to talk about besides what social media is talking about. Despite us being so connected, we have a loneliness problem in the US. Getting offline, taking local community college classes, and free birdwatching groups has taught me so much and given me new acquaintances, both bird and human.

What do you do when you need to focus?

Take an edible. I’m an experienced user now. They used to make me paranoid, but now I’m like an edibles master, and I know just the right dose to take so my anxiety disappears, and I can relax into making some art without the voice in my head that says “This sucks! Everyone is going to hate this, and you’ll die broke!”

What do you do when you’re feeling stuck?

Give myself permission to relax and take in someone else’s creation. Permission to be stuck and get inspiration from someone else’s book / movie / Substack has been a big help for me. There’s so much amazing art around, and when I look at other people’s, it reminds me why I feel the drive to create.

When was the last time you went somewhere without your phone?

Every day I go to the dog park without it. I feel we can learn so much from just watching nature, including our beloved mutts. I feel we stole the game of American football from how dogs play. My dog is always defense, btw.

What’s the last piece of physical media you bought?

Books! Last book purchase was If I Ruled the World by Amy Dubois Barnett.

What do you think is worth splurging on?

Anything that gives you more free time to just relax. So, again, books, lol. For $20-$40 bucks, I get DAYS of brain relaxation.

What would the tagline for your biopic be?

She had jokes, trauma, and a very suspicious relationship with pigeons.

What’s the last GIF or meme you used?

Tech.title: Is this Billboard Hot 100 hit AI slop?
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Fenix Flexin is best known as a member of Shoreline Mafia, a rap duo from Los Angeles. But he’s recently found solo success with the track “Rubberz,” which has climbed to number 58 on the Billboard Hot 100. Almost immediately, though, questions were raised about the song’s origins, with many speculating that it was largely, if not entirely, generated by AI. Fenix has denied those accusations, but done little to dispel them.

Part of the suspicion is certainly due to the fact that the song is a dramatic left turn. Fenix has primarily trafficked in trap-influenced West Coast rap. “Rubberz,” on the other hand, is heavily influenced by ‘80s UK synth pop. The vocal melody is clearly influenced by Morrissey, with Fenix even adopting a fake British accent. But artists are allowed to evolve and experiment. That alone doesn’t prove anything.

Perhaps more telling is the simple quality of the recording. Close inspection reveals a number of artifacts and anomalies that are commonly found in AI-generated music. Hi-hats have a certain brittle quality, the chorus vocals sound like a low-bitrate MP3, and reverb tails haphazardly cut off.

Speaking with The Verge, songwriter and co-host of the Switched on Pop podcast, Charlie Harding, highlighted the giveaways. “Ghostly backing vocals duck in and out unexpectedly. The drum reverb is full of unnatural digital artifacting reminiscent of a 64kbps MP3 downloaded off of Napster. Because most generative AI companies have trained their model on low-quality MP3s of unlicensed copyrighted material, we hear audibly degraded instrumentation.”

Feeding the song into an AI music detector doesn’t deliver a smoking gun. I ran the track through five different tools, and they all said that there was between 20 and 30 percent chance that it was AI or at least AI-assisted. But those sorts of tools are not necessarily super reliable and advance much more slowly than music-making models themselves.

Some of the supporting materials, however, have tripped up AI detectors. The single’s cover art and a post celebrating its success were both flagged as being AI-generated with over 97 percent certainty by multiple AI image detectors. Similarly, I fed the lyrics into multiple AI writing detectors and Gemini, which agreed they appeared to be written by AI. Producer and YouTuber Curtiss King dropped the lyrics into Claude, and it also flagged multiple signs that the lyrics appeared to be AI-generated.

The lyrics are the sort of logical near-gibberish that AI often spits out. The rhymes are simple and clean in a way that you wouldn’t expect from someone who is a reasonably accomplished rapper. There are no near rhymes or internal rhymes. Instead, everything sticks to a basic AA, BB format that clearly prioritizes the rhyme scheme over actual meaning or narrative development.

Swipin’ cards and stackin’ chips, I saw you sinkin’ ships Left me standin’ in the pourin’ rain, now I bought a heavy diamond chain

Who is sinking ships? Are we the sinking ships? No clue, this idea never comes back up. Similarly, the individual lines of the chorus might make sense, but when combined are meaningless.

Bankrolls on the table Watchin’ local cable Hatin’ that I’m able Hatin’ that I’m able

Ignoring the “local cable” bit, which is just awkward (and nearly sent King into a rage spiral), what is Fenix able to do? Why does he hate it? The lyrics raise more questions than they answer.

The way the lines are delivered is also odd. Verse three seemingly ends mid-thought on the line, “Not the jewelry.” Harding noted that it has a “complete lack of flow.” He says that, “No half-competent rapper would ever sing the title line ‘I just let the rubber band snap’ in such an awkward manner. The syncopation is highly unusual, emphasizing all the wrong syllables.” He goes on to explain that, “by smashing so many syllables together, it forces the word the onto the downbeat, instead of the word rubber, forcing all of the subsequent syllables to accent with unnatural syncopation.”

Live “performances” of “Rubberz” haven’t done Fenix any favors. The first couple of in-studio appearances featured the rapper awkwardly lip-syncing. At times it seems like the awkwardness of the flow and the lyrics trip him up, as if he can’t remember his own song. Honestly, he’s not even trying that hard to convince anyone that he’s actually singing.

Things only get worse when Fenix actually does sing. It’s abundantly clear in multiple clips that he is incapable of recreating the vocal range and accent from the recording (and that he doesn’t know the lyrics). In many of the clips of live performances, even when he’s singing, they’re simply playing the original vocals over his. His real vocals are kept extremely low in the mix, and the DJ strategically drops out the backing track briefly in an effort to prove the authenticity of the song, but fails.

Fenix has defended himself, saying the difference between the recorded version and any in-the-flesh performance is down to vocal processing, including AutoTune. However, multiple people, including Harding, King, and Anthony Fantano, have disputed this assertion. King compares AutoTune to spellcheck, and that’s not a bad analogy. While yes, it can be pushed to its limits to create unique robotic textures, it’s designed to clean up errors — it would not extend a performer’s vocal range or introduce an accent, as Fantano points out.

Perhaps the most compelling argument for “Rubberz” being authentic is just how bad it is. Harding says, “I would assume it was written by someone who has never written a song using an ‘80s kids practice keyboard.” If the song was indeed created using generative AI, it was clearly made with an inferior model. “I am concerned that audiences find this song interesting when it is created by one of the lesser generative AI music companies with a terrible model. More sophisticated models have already made big improvements in the audible artifacts and awkwardly sung rhythms.”

Fenix has posted clips of what he says are Pro Tools session files. But that doesn’t actually prove anything. Unless he shares the original recording and project files publicly, it’s likely he’ll never shake the AI allegations. And I don’t see that happening anytime soon.

Tech.title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day leak racks up millions of views
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

A bootleg of Spider-Man: Brand New Day was up on X for over seven hours before eventually being pulled. During that time, it reached over 5.9 million accounts and accumulated over 143,000 likes. Other accounts have reposted the leaked film, but none have lasted particularly long, as Disney now seems to be on top of issuing takedown requests.

The leak is unlikely to slow down the box office juggernaut, which is already shattering records. It raked in $72 million in previews this week. The previous record holder was Avengers: Endgame, which grossed $60 million during its previews way back in 2019. Endgame went on to set staggering records for opening weekend, grossing over $1.2 billion worldwide and over $350 million in the US. Spider-Man: No Way Home currently holds the number two spot on the all-time US opening weekend list with $260 million.

Brand New Day could potentially usurp Endgame, though it certainly faces an uphill battle. Between previews and opening day, it’s already grossed $168 million, which puts it ahead of Endgame’s $157.4 million. Sony is keeping its estimates somewhat conservative, saying it expects the latest Spider-Man to pull in $325 million.

Tech.title: Trump blames Tim Walz for water hacks even though it’s probably Iran
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The FBI, the EPA, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) have stopped short of officially blaming Iran for a spate of cyberattacks on Minnesota’s water systems, but consensus is that Iran is likely behind them. That, of course, hasn’t stopped Donald Trump from sharing his own theory — that Governor Tim Walz is to blame and telling reporters that “I don’t think there was an Iranian cyberattack.”

Trump’s comments come shortly after the FBI issued a warning that the cyberattacks on American infrastructure were spreading to other states. In Minnesota alone, at least 30 community water systems had been targeted in what appeared to be a coordinated attack. The CISA has linked similar attacks earlier in the year to Iran, which has been the target of an on-again-off-again war waged by the US government. With limited military options, Iran has repeatedly turned to digital efforts to become a thorn in the side of the Trump administration and wage a PR war.

Trump has lashed out frequently at Minnesota and Walz during his second term and even threatened to invoke the Insurrection Act against it during a surge of ICE enforcement efforts in the state that left multiple people dead.

Tech.title: You could be taking way better photos on your phone
Tech.content:
is a technology reporter who has been covering the industry since 2007. He co-hosts the Waveform podcast with MKBHD. A former engineer, he now specializes in topics like computational photography and social media protocols.

Your smartphone photos can look way better. If you’re willing to put in a little extra work, use third party apps and spend a bit of time editing, it’s possible to take photos that — under the right circumstances — can rival dedicated digital cameras.

I post a lot of smartphone photos online, and “How do I take better photos on my phone?” is a question I get practically every day. It makes sense. As the saying goes, “The best camera is the one you have on you,” and we practically always have our phones on us these days.

Over the last few years, smartphone camera sensors have gotten bigger, with better light gathering capabilities and higher resolutions. But even though the sensors have gotten bigger and better, the straight-out-of-camera quality through default camera apps hasn’t improved much, if at all. In some respects, smartphone photos have actually gotten worse — aesthetically, at least.

iPhone 17 Pro Max iPhone 17 Pro Max iPhone 17 Pro Max iPhone 17 Pro Max

The reason driving this is what people generally use their smartphone cameras for. Smartphone cameras are mostly optimized for information transfer — sending photos of menus, signs, faces and objects that are clear and easy to see. This means phones will usually pull down highlights and pull up the shadows, creating a flatter image that makes it easier to see more information in the frame. But showing more information does not automatically make a photo better. In fact, much of our perception of aesthetics in a photo has to do with its ability to present depth. A photo with too much information in the shadows and highlights will appear washed out. Phones also introduce artifacts like over-sharpening and noise reduction to compensate for their small sensors, which further contributes to the “muddy” smartphone camera look you’re used to seeing by now. This is less necessary now, but many smartphones still do it.

But that doesn’t mean phone cameras are bad. The sensors in modern smartphones have actually gotten so good, many of them can rival dedicated point-and-shoot options on the market today. Knowing how to utilize those sensors is the part most people don’t know how to do, and it really comes down to utilizing some third-party camera and editing apps.

The apps

Moment

There are plenty of apps available today that will give you an instantly “aesthetic” photo. Apps like Dazzcam and Hujicam try to emulate film aesthetics like light leaks and polaroid borders (and honestly, if that’s what you’re looking for, they do a fantastic job). There are also apps like Moment Pro Camera II and Halide that offer “Natural” and “Process Zero” modes, which apply far lighter processing than the default camera offers.

Those options are great if you want your pictures to look better instantly without needing to do any additional editing, but if you want the best possible photo, you’ll need to shoot RAW or DNG.

A RAW vs the edited photo

RAW files are a bundle of practically all the information your camera collects, with extremely minimal processing. In most cases, RAW photos won’t necessarily look better than photos straight from the default camera app right away, but that’s because the default camera app makes a lot of creative decisions for you. If you want the highest-quality photo, it’s best to make these creative decisions yourself.

There are tons of apps available that let you shoot RAW, but the apps I use frequently and that I recommend to other people are Moment Pro Camera II and Halide on iOS, and VWFNDR and Zerocam on Android.

I wouldn’t recommend shooting RAW on every photo you take on your phone. Your phone camera is, after all, optimized for what you are probably taking photos of every day. I generally shoot RAW when I see a nice landscape or city scene that I want to share, or if I’m trying to take a portrait of someone and don’t want all the automatic computational phone processing to apply. Really, I shoot RAW when I’m trying to take a photo for artistic purposes, not for informational purposes.

When you’re shooting, you’ll want to tap on your subject in the viewfinder to get the best possible exposure for it. If the rest of the image is a little bright, or a little dark, don’t worry too much. RAW photos retain a lot of information. I should note, though, that under extremely dark circumstances, RAW on smartphones won’t always be the best option. Physics is still physics, and sometimes it’s better to use the computational photography capabilities your phone offers, which mostly shine in low-light environments by stacking multiple frames to reduce noise.

You’ll notice that when you shoot in RAW, the apps will force you to stick to the native focal lengths your phone offers. That’s because RAW images are information straight off the sensor, and cropping applies processing. Photos from the main sensor will often be the best quality, since it usually has the biggest sensor on your phone, so I recommend shooting with it if you can. I do often shoot with the telephoto lens while traveling though, because sometimes you want a little more reach or a little more compression, and you can usually get good photos from that lens as well.

Editing

After you take your photos, you’re going to need to edit them. Most phones won’t show RAW images in the camera gallery, so in order to get them in an editing app, it’s best to use the share sheet and share directly to your editing app of choice. I suggest Snapseed, since it’s totally free and recently got a wonderful visual overhaul. If you’re an Adobe subscriber, Lightroom Mobile is also great, especially if you’re already used to Lightroom’s tools on your computer.

RAW photos don’t usually look great right away, and the magic of RAW is just how much you can tweak the files. Once I have the photo imported, I usually hit the auto button, just to see what the general boundaries are for the image. Auto mode tries to make everything a mid-tone, meaning it will pull down the highlights and pull up the shadows. This will already look better than straight-out-of-camera from your phone’s default camera app, because it isn’t applying noise reduction or sharpening, just highlight, shadow, contrast, and saturation tweaks, but it usually still needs more, or different, adjustments.

Once I see what auto mode wants to do, I’ll either edit from there, or hit the back button and edit myself. A good photo has a natural amount of contrast, with relatively deep shadows and bright highlights. You usually don’t want to go too hard on either of these things, and having a little bit of detail in both of these is usually preferred, but honestly, this is subjective. Occasionally, it’s preferable to crush the highlights and shadows completely, if you’re going for an ultra high-contrast look.

For color, RAW images are usually flatter than most people find pleasing, and you can fix this with either the saturation or vibrance sliders. I generally prefer vibrance. Saturation will increase the saturation of all colors in the image linearly, where vibrance is weighted, increasing saturation of flatter colors more than already-saturated colors. You can overdo this pretty easily, so I recommend having a light touch when it comes to saturation. You can also use white balance to color your image, and many people find a warmer white balance more pleasing, especially when taking photos outside.

RAW Edited RAW Edited

Another color tool I love to use is the color mix, or selective editing tool. This allows you to tap on a portion of the image and change some of its values. In Snapseed, you can change the brightness, contrast, saturation, and structure. If you’re in Lightroom mobile, you’ll have access to selective hue shifts, which I use all the time. This allows you to shift a yellow tone towards more orange or green, or shift a blue tone more cyan or purple.

Most editing apps also include geometry or perspective tools. These tools allow you to adjust distortion, aspect, scale, and offset. If you don’t know what that means, try hitting the auto button in the geometry or perspective setting. You might be surprised how distorted your phone captured a scene compared to what it looks like in reality, but this is image-dependent. If you want to straighten lines in your photo, some editing apps offer a guided tool that allows you to manually add guidance lines to tell the program what lines should be straight in the image.

The tools you’ll want to use are going to depend heavily on what you want the image to convey. For example, when I’m doing architectural photography, I rely a lot more heavily on the perspective tools, because the aesthetic of the image is heavily dictated by its geometry. If I’m photographing a landscape, I’m more focused on tone and color. Not every scene needs to be tweaked with every tool, and how you edit comes down to personal taste. That taste can also take a while to develop, so study the photos you like and try to figure out how they were edited.

RAW Edited RAW Edited

When you’re done with your edits, many editing apps like Snapseed and Lightroom Mobile also come with a handy tool to put a matte (or border) around your image. I think that photos look better with a white border, as it isolates the image for your eyes. You obviously don’t have to use this tool, but I really like it. Have some whimsy!

This process is a lot more work than just opening your camera app and snapping, but the results are worth it. I am continuously blown away by the quality of images I’m able to get off smartphones, and just how close they can be to a dedicated camera. If you don’t believe me, check out this video I did comparing RAW photos from the iPhone 17 Pro to the Leica M11.

Photography by David Imel / The Verge

Tech.title: The Mermaid Mask is a perfect vacation murder mystery
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

The Mermaid Mask, the next point-and-click game from Tangle Tower developer SFB Games, has everything you could ask for in a great murder mystery.

It starts with a compelling setup: The captain of a submarine is found dead in a locked room, his body next to a mysterious cauldron with blood trickling across the floor. The colorful cast of suspects stationed aboard are delightful to talk to, including a grumpy author trying to draft a sequel to his hit novel, an actor playing the lead in a movie based on that novel, a young woman who puts on elaborate illusion performances, and even a man who studies dreams. The submarine works as an excellent setting that elevates the mystery — in a vehicle that already has such a small footprint, how does a locked-door crime happen in the first place?

Image: SFB Games

Like other crime-solving games, such as the Ace Attorney series, The Mermaid Mask is essentially a visual novel. As Detective Grimoire and his partner Sally, the returning protagonists from Tangle Tower, you’re primarily talking with suspects, investigating rooms, poring over objects, and solving puzzles. But each room is packed with nooks and crannies and knickknacks to click around on, investigate, and learn about, so there’s almost always something to dig into.

The whole thing is backed by excellent voice acting; I often went out of my way to click on every detail I could find just to hear what the characters would say. The puzzles, which have you doing things like turning dials in exactly the right way or organizing skulls on a shelf, also do a good job breaking up what would otherwise be a whole lot of text conversations.

Even though I haven’t played Tangle Tower, I didn’t feel like I was missing any meaningful context. The Mermaid Mask borrows a tried-and-true model from other franchises starring a returning detective, like with Knives Out’s Benoit Blanc: You can come into this story cold without missing anything important, but Detective Grimoire and Sally are a fun hang that make a few nods to their previous work together.

Sometimes, you’ll have to puzzle together clues to form a conclusion. Image: SFB Games

Eventually, after you gather enough evidence about somebody, you’ll confront them in Ace Attorney-like sequences where you’ll be able to make observations or accusations that the suspect rather wished you wouldn’t. These were extremely satisfying; it always felt good to figure out a tiny detail that would break someone’s facade wide open. Whenever the opportunity to do another one came up, I couldn’t wait to jump in.

I had a few issues with The Mermaid Mask, but they’ll be familiar to anyone who likes playing these sorts of games. Presenting every clue to every suspect to get their reaction can be tedious. It’s not necessary, but I didn’t realize that until about halfway in my 10-hour playthrough when I spotted the hint system that suggests what you might want to show someone. Sometimes you have to make your case by presenting evidence in a specific order, even if you have already worked out where it might lead, so that the characters can talk things out as the script demands. At one point, I ran out of leads to explore and couldn’t figure where to go next until I manipulated one clue in one specific way that opened up a bunch of leads. More than once, I couldn’t figure out the exact clue that would advance things, so I just brute-forced guesses until I could move forward.

These roadblocks were frustrating. But that’s mostly because they stopped me from moving forward in a story that had me staying up way past my bedtime. When I reached the game’s finale — which begins with a classic murder mystery parlor room scene — I could hardly put my Steam Deck down because I wanted to see how all the pieces came together. When I finally finished The Mermaid Mask after a three-day tear, I felt like I had just closed the book on a satisfying murder mystery novel.

The Mermaid Mask is out now on Nintendo Switch, PC, and PS5.

Tech.title: Inside the London hacker house taking a stand against founder burnout
Tech.content:
Six twentysomethings in East London have built what they say is the anti-San Francisco hacker house. The goal is a “holistic improvement in life,” rather than “12 weeks, Demo Day is coming,” Rowan Aldean, 26, explained.

Intrigued, I spent an afternoon visiting the house, meeting its residents, and doing a vibe check. I arrived after Aldean escorted me through the clean sidewalks of a new East London development to where the six-story building stood facing the water.

The house is called the London Island Founder House — or “Lift House” — and Aldean and his wife, Zahraa, 22, an upcoming pharmaceutical research PhD candidate, have lived there since May, just a few months after it officially launched in March. Aldean sold his previous company last year for millions, he said, and now runs an “applied AI” startup that helps companies learn how to deploy agents.

Like all hacker houses, Lift House is part startup workspace, part co-living space. The house is named after both its lift — that is, its elevator — and its mission to uplift tech founders, Aldean said. It’s one of the very few co-living hacker houses to exist in London (compared to San Francisco, where dozens — if not hundreds — are scattered around the city at any given time).

Lift House is a bet that U.K. founders can build successful companies without mimicking the over-the-top hustle culture of Silicon Valley.

Founders have described stories of San Francisco hacker houses illegally running in warehouses, throwing full-on galas, or setting up in a tent or espousing punishing, 72-hour sprints typical of the “996” work culture.

“I don’t expect the performative and over-the-top events will be a thing here,” Aldean said, and pointed to one of London’s most successful AI companies, DeepMind. “They’ve won Nobel prizes and built frontier innovation without any song and dance.”

Instead, Lift House is part of a trend called “Londonmaxxing,” in which founders attempt to optimize everything the London tech scene offers. The London ecosystem feels less showy and less startup bro-y than San Francisco, but its founders share similar ambitions: success, wealth, and market domination.



London AI startups have raised $12 billion so far in 2026, out of $14.7 billion raised by all London startups, according to Dealroom. Six companies have raised more than $500 million: Wayve, Superintelligence, ElevenLabs, Recursive, Ineffable Intelligence, and Isomorphic Labs, the latter three of which were founded by DeepMind alumni.



The excitement from AI has boosted the morale of the U.K. tech scene, inspiring a new generation of founders, like those in the Lift House, to take big swings.

LIFT Tour Image Credits:TechCrunch

Journaling vs. demo day

The timeline for living on Lift House is flexible — some people have stayed for a month; others intend to stay for at least six months. They buy their own groceries, Aldean said, although they often cook together and share ingredients. Cleaning is split among the group. Everyone declined to share information about the rent they pay.

The residents of Lift House aim for a balanced approach toward ambition, each one of them tells me — an almost unheard-of idea by San Francisco startup standards.

On Sundays, the group will journal together, a practice introduced by David Amor, 28, who runs a brain coaching and training company, helping founders and business leaders understand more about their brain and how it can help optimize business performance. The idea of journaling is to help everyone track how much time they spent in nature that week, how well they ate, and how much they moved their bodies.

“I’m eating healthier, working out more, and sleeping more,” Luke, 27, who runs an AI-marketing company, said about living in the house. “I always make sure to have lunch now, which is something that is simple, but I wasn’t doing before I lived here.” (Luke asked that his last name be withheld.)



Tuesdays evenings are for volleyball, where the founders play on the house team in a local league.

After dinner on other evenings, Wan Ying L, 25, who just left an AI startup and is working on a new idea, might play the piano in the living room. Sometimes the group plays Catan or visits art exhibitions together.

Presence Plumb, 25, is a tech strategist. She likes to host rooftop dinner parties, serving dishes that reflect the different nationalities in the house — from Iraqi to Spanish — while invited founders, researchers, investors, and operators chat about tech trends and investments.

“It’s a bit calmer, balanced, authentic in a way,” she said of people in the London ecosystem. “They don’t want too much of that only startup tech bro vibe. They want a bit of balance.”

Each founder follows their own schedules for a typical workday. Amor, for example, is up by 8 a.m. and gives himself exactly 30 seconds after waking up before jumping into his morning work. “I have a clear objective of ‘this is what I want to do in the first half of the day, when there’s no distractions.’” After his morning work routine, he takes a cold shower, “because it increases your dopamine by 250% and that gives me that motivation, that spark,” he said.

Wan playing the piano Image Credits:TechCrunch

Luke, meanwhile, is up at around 8:30. His co-founder, Varun, 27 (who asked that his last name be withheld), typically travels to the Lift House to co-work, and the duo starts work at around 9 a.m. with a team call.

Aldean rarely wakes before 10 a.m. unless something big is happening, like a “crazy angel [investor] call,” he said.



When asked what makes this house uniquely British rather than a wellness-focused Silicon Valley founder house, Aldean joked: “Well, we drink tea together like Brits, and in SF folks just drink filtered coffee.”



More seriously, he spoke of how British founders face a different kind of pressure than those in the U.S. They must navigate a cultural aversion to risk, an inclination toward humility, and a shame associated with failure. Instead of forgoing sleep for hustle and grind, they deal with what they call the “tall poppy syndrome,” when the media builds one up only to ruthlessly tear them down should they become too successful, investors and founders say. It makes some founders in the ecosystem wary of displaying too many wins.

Still, Luke said London is a strong choice for an early-stage founder: There’s a good network, ample early capital opportunities, and an option for a life outside of tech. In many ways, it is much more like New York culturally for founders than in San Francisco.

“London is so diverse that if you look properly enough, you’ll always find something fun to get involved with,” Amor added, “whether that’s a founder-run club, wellness events, [or going] to jazz nights.”

Luke and Varun write marketing terms on the whiteboard. They stand for top of funnel (TOFU), middle of funnel (MOFU), and bottom of funnel (BOFU). Image Credits:TechCrunch

Luke and Varun largely avoided venture capital funding by taking advantage of the U.K. government’s SEIS/EIS, which is supposed to help attract more angel investments into local startups. “There’s people who will pay basically the same rate of tax if they give us the money versus if they pay income tax,” Luke explained as another reason he liked starting out in London.

Aldean also feels the London ecosystem is less cutthroat than the Valley. He recalls his days living in a hacker house in the Bay — everyone’s desk had to face the wall, and it was heads-down, product-building. He felt the ecosystem, at times, was too willing to gossip, which is apparently done quite differently in the U.K.

“There’s nothing like ‘oh my god did you hear that the CTO just, like, did this,’” Aldean said. “It’s like you’re always worried,” he said, that someone would spread negative stories, especially if it benefited them.

Aldean also thinks London startups, more than Silicon Valley ones, sell into slow-moving large corporations rather than to each other, meaning one could build without having to kiss up or posture to get their peers to like them.

To the selling point, Varun and Luke mentioned another difference between the U.S. and U.K. ecosystem. “It’s a relatively fleeting market,” Varun said of the U.S. “You get quick wins. Here, it’s hard to close a customer, but if they close, they stay with you longer.”

Coming to America

Eventually, though, the road for many U.K. startups goes straight to the U.S.

In the U.K., founders have access to affordable top talent from universities like Oxbridge and a time zone that makes it easier to work with the rest of Europe, the Middle East, Asia, and parts of North America. In the U.S., however, they have access to the world’s largest economy and, most importantly, a lot of investors willing to write large checks, from pre-seed to growth stages.

“It’s almost like a factory line in a way,” Varun said. “You start here, and then you expand there or vice versa.”

American investors are also playing a role in luring British talent away from the country. I told the Lift House residents about one startup founder who said a top investor wouldn’t even back the company unless she relocated to the U.S. She ended up doing so, though decided to keep her family based in the U.K. to raise her children.

“We had an investor in Miami who said the same thing,” Luke said of an investor trying to get him and Varun to move to the U.S. “It’s quite a common practice.” He and Varun have already begun their U.S. expansion, and despite loving London, the duo hasn’t ruled out moving to the U.S. to be closer to their customers.

David, who has a brain coaching startup, is the one who introduced journaling into the household. Image Credits:TechCrunch

That’s the tension bubbling beneath not just the U.K.’s tech ecosystem but most of Europe’s. “I work with a lot of people trying to support the European ecosystem more,” Plumb said.

Yet, founders “talk about London; everyone is bullish on the country until they get the opportunity to leave,” Aldean added.

The Lift House lease has about a year left, and there is sentiment in the house to keep it going for as long as they can. After all, there aren’t too many in London, though the city sees many short-term gatherings, like the Solana Hacker House meet-up series. Some of the more public co-living hacker houses are part of a global chain, like the San Francisco-based network The Residency, which expanded into London last year, and BaseJump, which is announcing a London version of its hacker house program soon.

In 2024, two founders tried the opposite version of the Lift House called “The London Founder House,” which Sifted covered under the headline “The people here don’t want work-life balance.” That home is noted as London’s first-ever hacker house, and though it wound down last year, it left an influence through its concept, events, and connected players around the ecosystem. To even be considered for the London Founder House, one had to have raised at least half a million dollars.

For Lift House, prospective residents need to show a hobby outside their companies and an interest in fitness. It’s the same pitch many in the Londonmaxxing ecosystem are using to keep people from leaving: That here one can have it all.

“The culture is to build something that lasts,” Aldean said, “not necessarily burn out chasing a flash.”

Tech.title: Judge denies xAI’s request to block Minnesota ban on ‘nudify’ apps
Tech.content:
In Brief

Despite a lawsuit from xAI, a Minnesota ban on apps that allow users to “nudify” images can move forward, according to NBC News.

U.S. District Judge Donovan Frank’s ruling focused as much on the timing of xAI’s lawsuit as on the substance of the law itself. Frank wrote that xAI filed its request for a temporary restraining order “on July 29, 2026, nearly three months after the law was signed, and only three days before the law is set to take effect” on August 1.

“Such a delay in bringing the action and the motion suggests that harm is not immediate,” Frank said.

This isn’t the end of xAI’s lawsuit against the ban; it only means that the law can take effect while the lawsuit proceeds. In the suit, xAI argued that the ban — the first of its kind in the United States — is “overinclusive” and that “there are far less restrictive alternatives that function to achieve the same ends.”

Earlier this year, users of Elon Musk’s social media platform X (both X and xAI, are now part of SpaceX) used xAI’s Grok chatbot to flood the platform with non-consensual sexualized images, leading to investigations and bans.

Tech.title: YouTuber Hank Green says his AI usage is ‘not healthy’
Tech.content:
Hank Green, a novelist, comedian, and YouTuber with 3.2 million subscribers, recently apologized to his audience for his growing reliance on AI chatbots.

The controversy started when, in the middle of a video posted on the educational channel Complexly, Green incongruously used the phrase “I appreciate the pushback,” leading viewers to speculate that he’d written the script with a chatbot — and, in the process, accidentally included its response to one of his prompts.

In a since-deleted post on X, Green acknowledged that he’d produced the video “under a ton of pressure” and used ChatGPT “for research on this script.” At the same time, he said the “pushback” line was actually a response to the episode’s guest.

Green then offered a more in-depth apology on Reddit, where he said he was “mortified” that he’d “let so many people down” and that he plans to reduce his video production as a result.

Green insisted that he’s only used ChatGPT to “locate papers and other resources for learning about topics,” and that the words and the “takes” have still been his. At the same time, he admitted it was fair to criticize him for “diluting” himself.

He also clarified that he’s “not a pure AI-hater,” while also listing a number of concerns about the technology, including its impact on climate change and “the speed at which these companies are trying to consolidate economic power.”

“Ultimately, what I am most scared of is ruining myself for people, but I have not been managing my impulses well,” he said. “You need to know that my words are mine. I don’t think that this hasn’t been true, but I’ve been moving so fast that my own process isn’t actually clear to me and I want to have it be a guarantee moving forward.”

It sounds like Green is going to take some time to figure out how to make that guarantee a reality. In the meantime, he’ll be pausing or posting less frequently to his various YouTube channels. Green said he wants to do more work like a recent meditative video “where the writing was the whole thing and I felt it all the way down.” Green also said he’ll probably make more videos with his “dumb unscripted straight to camera thoughts.”

“But mostly I need to come to terms with the fact that the level of dopamine I’ve been getting from interacting with LLMs…with doing more and more and more and more…is not healthy for me or good for the world,” Green said. “It is careless, and has disconnected me from where people are on this.”

Tech.title: Should you still buy your next smartphone — or subscribe to it instead?
Tech.content:
The smartphone industry’s next battleground may not be the phone itself, but how consumers get it. As premium devices become more expensive, Apple, Samsung, and others are betting that leasing, subscriptions, and guaranteed buyback programs can make upgrading more attractive.

This week, Apple launched Apple Upgrade in the U.S. in partnership with Klarna, allowing consumers to lease an iPhone, Mac, iPad, or Apple Watch for a monthly fee with the option to upgrade, return, or eventually purchase the device. Samsung, meanwhile, has been offering its Galaxy Forever program in India, combining financing with a guaranteed buyback to let consumers upgrade flagship Galaxy smartphones more predictably.

On its earnings call on Thursday, Apple CEO Tim Cook said the Upgrade program is intended to make it easier for customers — particularly those who prefer upgrading on a regular schedule — to access the company’s latest products through a leasing plan. He also said Apple’s relatively high resale values make the model well suited to such plans.

The shift comes as consumers keep their smartphones for longer, driven by rising prices as tighter supplies push up memory and other component costs, and incremental hardware improvements that have kept older devices capable for longer. That has given manufacturers fewer opportunities to sell new devices while also reducing the flow of handsets into the booming refurbished market. Analyst firm Counterpoint Research expects the average global replacement cycle to stretch to four years in 2026, up from 3.5 years in 2025.

The trend is evident in the United States, where premium smartphone owners now keep their devices for an average of 42 months, up from 38 to 40 months in previous years, according to market intelligence firm IDC. That has prompted smartphone makers to experiment with leasing, subscriptions, and guaranteed buyback programs.

“These programs fundamentally do not work unless a secondary market exists,” said Max Weinbach, an analyst at Creative Strategies. “The only way to sustain a used or refurbished market is to make sure devices enter that market, and leasing and guaranteed buyback programs make that possible.”

The industry’s challenge, however, is not just to get consumers to upgrade more often — it is also to persuade them that these new ownership models make more financial sense than buying outright.

When leasing makes sense

“Leasing definitely isn’t for everyone, but it can make sense, especially for someone who upgrades often,” Matt Schulz, chief consumer finance analyst at online lending marketplace LendingTree, told TechCrunch. Consumers who keep their phones for three, four, or five years, however, are often better off buying them outright than opting for a subscription or leasing model, he said.

For those who upgrade every year or two, however, the economics can be closer than they appear. “It’s important to stress the fact this is an upgrade program that’s done via a lease, rather than just a leasing program,” Weinbach said. “The intent is that the user will turn in their device every 12 to 36 months because they intend to upgrade regardless.”

Based on his analysis of Apple’s new program, Weinbach told TechCrunch that consumers who already replace their phones frequently could pay roughly the same — or, in some cases, even less — than they would by buying a device outright and trading it in later, particularly on higher-storage models whose trade-in values do not always reflect their higher purchase prices.

Image Credits:Apple

The programs, however, are not just about making premium smartphones more affordable. Smartphone makers also see them as a way to keep customers within their ecosystems as devices become more expensive and replacement cycles lengthen.

“The real driver isn’t shorter upgrade cycles; it’s protecting margin and retention as pricing pressure mounts,” IDC’s associate vice president of devices research Navkendar Singh told TechCrunch.

Rather than simply trying to get consumers to replace their phones more often, brands are increasingly trying to turn costly smartphone purchases into more predictable monthly payments that keep customers within their ecosystems, Singh said.

The idea of paying monthly for a smartphone is not new, particularly in the U.S., where wireless carriers have long offered financing and upgrade plans tied to service contracts. However, what is changing is that phone makers are increasingly trying to own that relationship themselves.

Carrier financing has long helped make premium smartphones more affordable in the U.S. “It’s the interest-free financing of 36 months and aggressive trade-ins of up to $1,100 that have made the U.S. the region with the highest smartphone average selling prices,” Nabila Popal, senior research director at IDC, told TechCrunch.

The existing financing and trade-in offers have helped Apple and Samsung dominate the U.S. smartphone market with a combined share of more than 80%, per IDC.

The shift toward subscriptions and other alternative ownership models is also creating opportunities for startups. BytePe, which offers subscription-style plans for smartphones and other consumer electronics in India, said more than 80% of its customers opt for subscriptions over outright purchases or traditional EMI plans.

Founder and CEO Jayant Jha told TechCrunch that BytePe’s typical customers are young professionals in their first or second jobs who want access to premium smartphones without paying the full price upfront or committing to long ownership cycles.

The trend is not limited to the U.S. and India. Companies such as the UK’s Raylo and Germany’s Grover have built businesses around leasing smartphones and other consumer electronics through monthly subscription plans.

Analysts expect more companies to follow. “The primary objective is to increase customer lifetime value by improving retention, creating predictable upgrade cycles and securing a steady pipeline of trade-in devices for certified refurbishment and resale,” Tarun Pathak, research director at Counterpoint Research, told TechCrunch.

Pathak expects such initiatives to become more common in the premium smartphone segment, although he believes financing will remain the more important tool for improving affordability.

Nonetheless, outright ownership is unlikely to disappear anytime soon. Mandeep Manocha, co-founder and CEO of Indian smartphone trade-in and refurbishment platform Cashify, expects leasing, subscriptions, and outright purchases to coexist rather than replace one another.

“All three business models have a place to exist, and they will continue to do so,” Manocha told TechCrunch. “There is a natural transition that may happen from complete ownership to leasing, but it’s a long journey.”

That may be especially true in the U.S., where carrier financing has long dominated premium smartphone purchases.

IDC’s Popal expects Apple’s new Upgrade program to have a bigger impact on Mac sales than iPhones, saying the offering is more likely to expand financing options than fundamentally change how Americans buy their next smartphone.

Tech.title: Sam Altman is still making the case for parenting via ChatGPT
Tech.content:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman seemed excited to share what he called a “cool use case” on Friday, posting that parents could “connect your family calendars and explain your kids’ interests” to the company’s new product ChatGPT Work, then “every morning for the drive to school, have it make a podcast that talks about one kid’s soccer game that afternoon, one kid’s upcoming birthday, some news, etc.”

Altman’s post prompted lots of virtual eye-rolling, including a simple response from Alex Hirsch, creator of the animated series “Gravity Falls”: “What if you just talked to your children”?

Hirsch’s question seems to have gone even more viral than Altman’s initial post — while Altman’s comment has been reposted around 300 times and liked around 9,600 times (as of Saturday morning), Hirsch’s response has been reposted 9,000 times and received 122,000 likes.

This isn’t the first time a tech CEO has promised that AI can shield users — and specifically users’ morning commutes — from the messiness and inefficiency of human experience. Last year, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said he’d stopped listening his favorite podcasts during his morning drive; instead, he asked an AI chatbot about those podcasts.

Altman’s post also echoed comments he’s made about parenting in the past, most notably when he appeared on “The Tonight Show with Jimmy Fallon” and declared, “I cannot imagine having gone through figuring out how to raise a newborn without ChatGPT.” (Though he was also quick to acknowledge, “Clearly, people did it for a long time, no problem.”)

Getting parents on-board seems to be a priority for OpenAI, which recently posted a job listing for a product manager with experience building trust-sensitive consumer experiences for parents and families. Meta, meanwhile, is testing an AI-powered app that tells bedtime stories.

But while OpenAI has added safety features for parents, it also faces multiple lawsuits from parents and families alleging that ChatGPT played a role in loved ones’ delusions and suicides. (The company has said it’s “continuously improving how our models respond in sensitive interactions.”)

Tech.title: This $9 key physically locks your most addictive apps
Tech.content:
Screen-time apps aren’t effective for many people because, in the end, they depend on your willpower. They remind you to stop scrolling or let you set timers, but such notifications can be easy to ignore.

Autonomous Key takes a different approach to this issue simply by being a physical device. It’s an NFC key that pairs with a companion app to let you lock away distracting apps. So instead of tapping a button to bypass the block, you have to physically scan the key with your phone to regain access to your locked apps. Each unlock session can last for up to 60 minutes before the apps are automatically locked again.
